members.name: dedupe
members.doc:
Share one in-flight fetch between concurrent GET/HEAD calls with equal path, params,
query, body, and headers (default true). Mutations are never deduped. In the browser the
in-flight table is per client instance; during SSR it is per request (never shared across
requests), and off outside a request.

members.name: batch
members.signature: batch?: boolean | { maxItems?: number; mutations?: boolean; forwardHeaders?: readonly string[] }
members.doc:
Coalesce the calls made in one tick into a single `POST /_denext/api-batch` (default true;
`{ maxItems }` caps a batch, default 20). Reads (GET/HEAD) run concurrently on the server;
mutations (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) each run alone, in the order they were called, with their
route's CSRF checks — `{ mutations: false }` sends them as their own requests.
`{ forwardHeaders: ["x-tenant"] }` lets calls carrying those headers ride too, each item with
its own value (the server must list the same names in `apiBatch.forwardHeaders`; credential,
framing and proxy headers never ride). A read with any other custom header or a body, a
mutation with a header other than `x-csrf-token` or a forwarded one, or a call with
`batch: false` always goes alone; a single pending call skips the batch framing entirely.

(native session mode) or your own provider. Batching is off for an authenticated client
(the batch endpoint is same-origin only).

symbols.name: cache
symbols.signature: cache<A, R>(fn: (...args: A) => R): (...args: A) => R
symbols.doc: React.cache — memoize a function by its arguments.
symbols.docFull:
`React.cache` — memoize a function by its arguments.

React's server `cache()` scopes results to a single request via async context;
denext already provides that request-scoped variant in `src/server/cache.ts`
(which pulls `node:async_hooks`). This is the **client-safe** surface exposed on
the `react` package: a plain persistent memo keyed by argument identity, using a
nested Map/WeakMap tree (object args keyed by reference, primitives by value) so
libraries importing `cache` from `react` resolve and dedupe correctly without
dragging server-only APIs into the client bundle.

**Lifetime (React's semantics):** during SSR the memo is **request-scoped** (keyed
on the current request context, so one request's result is never served to
another — matching React and avoiding a cross-request data leak), and the
per-request root is garbage-collected with the request. **Server code outside a
request** (a scheduled task, a script, module init) is **not memoized** — `fn` runs
on every call, exactly as React's `cache()` does with no dispatcher active — so a
result can never persist across logical calls. **In the browser** (the client
bundle, where React memoizes per render pool) it is a persistent per-function memo
whose distinct **primitive** args are bounded per node ({@link CACHE_MAX_PER_NODE},
evicting the oldest) so they can't grow without limit (object args use a WeakMap
and are freed with the arg). Request-scoped roots stay uncapped (freed with the
request, matching React). A throwing `fn` is not cached (it re-runs next call).
symbols.returns: A memoized function returning the cached result for equal arguments.

symbols.name: choose
symbols.signature: choose<K, R>(value: K, cases: ChooseCases<K, R>, defaultCase?: () => R): R | undefined
symbols.doc: choose(value, cases, defaultCase?) — pick a branch by value and run it.
symbols.docFull:
`choose(value, cases, defaultCase?)` — pick a branch by value and run it.

A pure control-flow helper for rendering, borrowed from Lit's `choose`. It looks
`value` up in `cases` and calls the matching zero-argument function, returning its
result. When no case matches it calls `defaultCase` if one was given, otherwise it
returns `undefined`. Only the selected branch runs — the others are never invoked —
so it reads as a lazy `switch` you can drop straight into JSX.

Only `cases`' OWN keys match (`Object.hasOwn`): inherited names such as `toString`,
`constructor`, `valueOf`, `hasOwnProperty` or `__proto__` fall through to
`defaultCase` unless `cases` declares them itself. An own key whose value is
`undefined` also falls through to `defaultCase`.

Because `defaultCase` is a separate argument rather than a `"default"` key, a `value`
of the literal string `"default"` matches a `default` entry in `cases`, not the fallback.

params.name: value
params.doc: The key to look up in cases (own keys only).

params.name: cases
params.doc: A partial map from key to a zero-argument branch function.

params.name: defaultCase
params.doc: Run when no case matches; omit it to get undefined instead.

symbols.returns: The selected branch's result, or undefined when nothing matched and no defaultCase was given.

symbols.docFull: A streaming render: the HTML byte stream plus React's `allReady` signal.

members.name: allReady
members.doc:
Resolves once the shell and every Suspense boundary have **rendered** — independent of
how far the consumer has read (the flush is demand-gated, the rendering is not), so
`await stream.allReady` before reading never deadlocks. Rejects with the error when the
shell fails, or with the abort reason when `signal` aborts before every boundary rendered.
Always carries an internal handler, so an unobserved rejection never crashes the process.

members.name: shellReady
members.doc:
Resolves once the shell has rendered — React's `onShellReady` point — without reading
it: the shell is written on the first read, with every boundary rendered by then inline.
Rejects with the error when the shell fails. Pre-handled, like {@link allReady}.

symbols.name: renderToReadableStream
symbols.doc: Render a VNode tree to a streaming HTML ReadableStream<Uint8Array>, resolving Suspense boundaries progressively.
symbols.docFull:
Render a VNode tree to a streaming HTML `ReadableStream<Uint8Array>`,
resolving Suspense boundaries progressively.

The stream is **pull-gated**: nothing is produced ahead of a read. The first read gets the
shell — every Suspense boundary that has finished by then inline, as React writes it, the
rest as fallback placeholders — and each later chunk (a batch of settled boundaries, then
the tail) is produced only when the consumer asks for more, so a slow consumer applies
backpressure instead of the whole document queueing in memory as encoded chunks. Boundary
rendering is not gated — see {@link RenderStream.allReady}: a consumer that awaits it before
reading gets every boundary inline.

symbols.name: renderToString
symbols.doc: Render a VNode (or renderable child) to an HTML string. This is the primary SSR entry point.
symbols.docFull:
Render a VNode (or renderable child) to an HTML string.
This is the primary SSR entry point.

The renderer appends into a single shared buffer and stays **fully synchronous**
for synchronous subtrees — a promise is only allocated when a child actually
returns one (an async server component, or a Suspense/error-boundary that must
await). This avoids one promise frame per node and the per-array `Promise.all`,
and building the HTML in one buffer (joined once) avoids the old bottom-up
O(n·depth) string re-copying. Output is byte-for-byte identical to before.

symbols.docFull:
Define a server action. Give it a **stable, explicit id** (unique per app) so
the client stub and the server handler agree across the boundary.

On the server the returned function runs `handler` directly and registers it
for RPC dispatch. In the browser it returns a stub that POSTs the arguments to
the action endpoint and resolves with the JSON result.

The handler runs with the request's async context, so it may read
`cookies()`/`headers()`, call `revalidatePath`/`revalidateTag`, or `redirect()`.
It **must** authorize and validate its own input — registration alone exposes
it to any same-origin caller.

symbols.name: startTransition
symbols.doc: Run callback as a low-priority "transition": the callback runs synchronously (like React), but any state updates it triggers are scheduled at transition priority — flushed after the reconciler yields to the browser, so urgent updates and paint/input happen first. Without the client scheduler it just runs the callback. The transition render is time-sliced and interruptible: a higher-priority (sync) update abandons the in-flight transition and restarts it (see the Async transitions guide: /docs/rendering#async-transitions).
symbols.docFull:
Run `callback` as a low-priority "transition": the callback runs synchronously
(like React), but any state updates it triggers are scheduled at transition
priority — flushed after the reconciler yields to the browser, so urgent updates
and paint/input happen first. Without the client scheduler it just runs the callback. The transition render is time-sliced and interruptible: a
higher-priority (sync) update abandons the in-flight transition and restarts it
(see the Async transitions guide: /docs/rendering#async-transitions).

An **async** callback (`startTransition(async () => { await x; setState() })`) is
supported: the transition stays active across the `await`, so updates scheduled
after it still land at transition priority. By default denext entangles by a time
window while the returned promise is pending; enable `asyncContext` in
`denext.config.ts` to scope by transition identity instead, so an unrelated urgent
update in that window keeps its priority (see the Async transitions guide /
KNOWN-LIMITATIONS).

`React.SuspenseList` — coordinates the reveal order of sibling `<Suspense>`

all until the last resolves). `tail="collapsed"` shows only the next boundary's
fallback, `"hidden"` shows none.

buffered server rendering every boundary has already resolved, so order is moot.

symbols.name: useWakeLock
symbols.doc: Keep the screen awake via the Screen Wake Lock API, as a hook. Call WakeLockControls.request request to add this instance's claim and WakeLockControls.release release to drop it; the claim is also dropped automatically on unmount. Because the screen is device-global, the lock is refcounted: it stays on while any instance has a claim, and WakeLockControls.count count/WakeLockControls.active active report the shared state to every instance. WakeLockControls.releaseAll releaseAll drops every claim at once.
symbols.docFull:
Keep the screen awake via the Screen Wake Lock API, as a hook. Call
{@linkcode WakeLockControls.request request} to add this instance's claim and
{@linkcode WakeLockControls.release release} to drop it; the claim is also
dropped automatically on unmount. Because the screen is device-global, the
lock is refcounted: it stays on while any instance has a claim, and
{@linkcode WakeLockControls.count count}/{@linkcode WakeLockControls.active active}
report the shared state to every instance. {@linkcode WakeLockControls.releaseAll releaseAll}
drops every claim at once.

The lock is re-acquired automatically when the page returns to visible (the
browser drops it while the tab is hidden). On the server, or in a browser
without the API, `isSupported` is `false` and the actions are no-ops.

symbols.name: ViewTransition
symbols.signature: ViewTransition(props: { ref?: ((instance: ViewTransitionInstance | null) => void | (() => void)) | { current: ViewTransitionInstance | null } | null; name?: string; default?: string | Record<string, string>; enter?: string | Record<string, string>; exit?: string | Record<string, string>; update?: string | Record<string, string>; share?: string | Record<string, string>; onEnter?: ViewTransitionCallback; onExit?: ViewTransitionCallback; onUpdate?: ViewTransitionCallback; onShare?: ViewTransitionCallback; children?: VNodeChildren }): VNode
symbols.doc: React.ViewTransition (experimental) — the client-driven view-transition wrapper. It is transparent (no DOM node of its own) and carries its config by stamping the DNX_VT_ATTR attribute onto its **nearest host nodes** (a DOM attribute survives server rendering AND the Flight boundary, unlike a VNode marker): a host child, every host in a Fragment or a list (the first keeps name, the others get React's name_<i> suffix), and the hosts a component child renders. Text directly inside is not animated (it can't be named). The import-gated marking runtime finds these elements and applies real view-transition-name (an automatic one when name is unset) and view-transition-class (enter/exit/update/share, else default; "none" opts out):
symbols.docFull:
`React.ViewTransition` (experimental) — the client-driven view-transition wrapper. It is
transparent (no DOM node of its own) and carries its config by stamping the {@link DNX_VT_ATTR}
attribute onto its **nearest host nodes** (a DOM attribute survives server rendering AND the
Flight boundary, unlike a VNode marker): a host child, every host in a Fragment or a list (the
first keeps `name`, the others get React's `name_<i>` suffix), and the hosts a component child
renders. Text directly inside is not animated (it can't be named). The import-gated marking
runtime finds these elements and applies real `view-transition-name` (an automatic one when
`name` is unset) and `view-transition-class` (`enter`/`exit`/`update`/`share`, else `default`;
`"none"` opts out):

- **Same-page updates** (React's triggers): a commit made only of Transition work — a
  `startTransition` update, a `useDeferredValue` catch-up, a Suspense reveal — runs inside
  `document.startViewTransition` when a wrapped element enters, exits, is shared (a `name` that
  leaves one place and enters another) or updates (its content mutated or its layout moved).
  An urgent update never animates, and neither does a `useSyncExternalStore` change (React
  renders a store change synchronously even inside `startTransition`).
- **Soft navigations** commit inside `document.startViewTransition` (see `withViewTransition`
  in `src/client/nav-document.ts`), so a `name` shared across routes morphs one element into the
  other; the route-level cross-fade applies regardless.

A hidden `<Activity>` going hidden in a Transition animates its boundaries as exits, and a
boundary entirely outside the viewport (before and after) is not animated, as in React.

`onEnter` / `onExit` / `onUpdate` / `onShare` run once the transition's pseudo-elements exist
(`ready`), with the boundary's `ViewTransitionInstance` (`name`, and `group` / `imagePair` /
`old` / `new` handles with `animate()` / `getAnimations()` / `getComputedStyle()` on its
`::view-transition-*` pseudo-elements) and the transition types; a returned function runs
when the transition finishes. `onShare` runs on the side that leaves. On a soft navigation a
boundary that persists runs `onUpdate` when its content changed or its box moved. A `ref`
receives the same instance once the boundary's first host mounts. Callbacks and `ref` need a
client-rendered `<ViewTransition>` (a function can't cross from a Server Component).

Where the browser lacks the View Transitions API the commit simply applies.

symbols.name: VirtualList
symbols.doc: A virtualized list: renders only the rows near the viewport, so 1M–10M rows scroll as fast as 100. Rows are measured as they render (estimatedItemSize is only a hint), rows keep their identity (and state) across data changes, and content changes above the viewport never move what you are looking at — including on iOS, where the list never writes the scroll offset during a fling. Past the browser's element-height limit the scroll space is scaled, and scrollToIndex still lands exactly.
symbols.docFull:
A virtualized list: renders only the rows near the viewport, so 1M–10M rows scroll as fast
as 100. Rows are measured as they render (`estimatedItemSize` is only a hint), rows keep
their identity (and state) across data changes, and content changes above the viewport
never move what you are looking at — including on iOS, where the list never writes the
scroll offset during a fling. Past the browser's element-height limit the scroll space is
scaled, and `scrollToIndex` still lands exactly.

**Bottom-anchored lists** (messages, logs, feeds): `anchor="end"` starts at the bottom,
bottom-aligns short content, stays pinned while at the bottom (appends, a streaming last row,
the keyboard opening with `keyboardInset`), and `onStartReached` loads history without a
jump. **Sections:**
`stickyIndices` (the real row sticks, so it stays focusable; the next header pushes it up).
**Grids:** `numColumns` + `gap`. **Accessibility:** `role="list"` / `"listitem"` with
`aria-setsize` / `aria-posinset`, Arrow / Page / Home / End (and optional typeahead)
navigation into rows not yet rendered, and the focused row stays mounted while scrolled
away. **SSR:** the server renders the first window (at `initialScrollIndex`, or the end
for `anchor="end"`), which hydrates without moving. **React Native parity:**
`onViewableItemsChanged`, `onScroll` / momentum events, `refreshControl`,
`contentContainerStyle`, `ListHeaderComponentStyle`.

**Testing:** without a `ResizeObserver` (as under `denext/testing`) nothing is measured:
sizes come from `getItemSize` (exact) or the estimates, and the viewport from the scroller's
`clientHeight`, else `viewportSize` (default 800) — so `render(<VirtualList>)` shows a
deterministic set of rows with no layout engine.

members.name: anchor

`"end"` for a bottom-anchored list: start at the end, align short content to the end, and stay pinned to

members.name: pinEndOn
members.signature: readonly pinEndOn?: { readonly data?: boolean; readonly items?: boolean; readonly layout?: boolean; readonly footer?: boolean }
members.doc:
With `anchor="end"`, which changes keep a view that is at the end pinned there: a data change
(`data`), a row's size (`items`), the scroller's size (`layout`), and the size of what follows
the rows (`footer`: `ListFooterComponent`, a docked text field's inset). Each defaults to `true`; a change
whose flag is `false` keeps the visible rows in place instead (LegendList's
`maintainScrollAtEnd.on`). `{ footer: false }` keeps the visible rows still while a text
field in the footer grows. With all four `false` the list still opens at the end: its first row sizes
and viewport size land there, until the first data change or scroll away from the end.

members.name: maintainVisibleContentPosition
members.doc:
Keep the visible rows in place when rows are added or removed above them (anchored by
key). Default `true`. With `false`, a data change above the view shifts what is visible
(React Native's default: a view at the very top shows new first rows). Size refinements —
a row measured taller or shorter than its estimate, a resize — never move the visible rows
either way, and a pending `scrollToIndex` holds its target either way.

(A list with no size information renders at most 10 rows until its first measurement
either way.)

symbols.name: withWebLock
symbols.signature: withWebLock<T>(name: string, fn: () => T | Promise<T>, options?: WebLockOptions): Promise<T | undefined>
symbols.doc: Run fn while holding a same-origin lock named name, coordinating across every tab, iframe, and worker of the origin (the Web Locks API). Only one holder runs an exclusive lock at a time; the lock is released automatically when fn settles — or when the holding context is destroyed — so a crashed tab can never deadlock the others.
symbols.docFull:
Run `fn` while holding a same-origin lock named `name`, coordinating across
every tab, iframe, and worker of the origin (the Web Locks API). Only one
holder runs an exclusive lock at a time; the lock is released automatically
when `fn` settles — or when the holding context is destroyed — so a crashed
tab can never deadlock the others.

It degrades gracefully: on the server (SSR) and in any browser without the Web
Locks API (an insecure context, or a very old browser) `fn` is simply run
without coordination, so the same call works in every environment.

The canonical use is cross-tab single-flight: an auth-token refresh that must
not stampede a one-time-use refresh cookie, a once-per-origin client bootstrap
or migration, or electing a single leader tab to own a shared connection.

params.name: name
params.doc: The lock name — any string; scope it, e.g. "auth:refresh".

params.name: fn
params.doc: The work to run while holding the lock.

params.name: options
params.doc: Lock mode, ifAvailable, and an optional abort signal.

symbols.returns: The result of fn, or undefined when ifAvailable is set and the lock was already held (so fn did not run).

symbols.name: ApiBatchConfig
symbols.doc: Limits for the typed-API batch endpoint (POST /_denext/api-batch).
symbols.docFull: Limits for the typed-API batch endpoint (`POST /_denext/api-batch`).

members.name: enabled
members.doc: Serve the endpoint at all (default true; `false` → 404).

members.name: mutations
members.doc:
Batch mutations too (default true): the client sends the POST / PUT / PATCH / DELETE calls a
page makes in one tick in the same batch as its reads, and the server runs each one alone,
in call order, with its route's CSRF checks. `false` refuses mutation items (the whole
batch is a 400), so the client must send them as their own requests
(`createApiClient({ batch: { mutations: false } })`).

members.name: forwardHeaders
members.doc:
Request headers a batched call may carry, each item with its own value — a tenant or
locale header such as `["x-tenant"]` (default none). The client batches a call carrying
one only when it lists the same name (`createApiClient({ batch: { forwardHeaders } })`);
a call with any other custom header goes as its own request. A header reaches only its own
item's handler, never another item's, and never comes from the batch request itself. Names
are lower-cased; a credential (`cookie`, `authorization`, `apikey`), framing or hop-by-hop
header, `origin` / `referer` / `host`, a method override (`x-http-method-override`), a
header a proxy, CDN, hosting platform or auth proxy sets (`forwarded`, `x-forwarded-*`,
`x-real-ip`, `cf-*`, `fly-*`, `x-vercel-*`, `x-amzn-*`, `x-envoy-*`, `x-azure-*`,
`x-appengine-*`, `x-goog-*`, `x-ms-client-principal*`, `x-auth-request-*`, …), Next's
internal `x-middleware-*`, `x-denext-*`, `sec-*` and the app's `rateLimitHeader` are refused.
Each value is one line of at most 1024 characters; anything else fails the whole batch.

members.name: maxItems
members.doc: Max items per batch (default 20, at most 100).

members.name: maxBodyBytes
members.doc: Max batch request body in bytes (default 1 MiB).

members.name: concurrency
members.doc: Items run concurrently per batch (default 4).

members.name: maxItemResponseBytes
members.doc: Max bytes of one item's response body carried back (default 4 MiB; over → a 500 item).

members.name: maxTotalResponseBytes
members.doc:
Max bytes of ALL items' response bodies together (default 16 MiB; over → the rest are
500 items).
