members.doc: Purge every cached page rendered for `path` (an exact pathname).

members.name: expireByTag
members.signature: expireByTag?(tag: string, timing: CacheEntryTiming): void | Promise<void>
members.doc:
Optional: **soft-expire** every entry carrying `tag` — rewrite its
`staleAt`/`expiresAt` (stale-while-revalidate) instead of deleting it, so a
`revalidateTag(tag, profile)` serves stale while refreshing. A store that omits
this falls back to a hard {@link deleteByTag} (correct, just not SWR).

members.name: sweepPages
members.doc:
Optional: delete every cached **page** whose key does not start with `keep` — the
entries of other builds and older page-cache formats, which a {@link PageCache} never
reads again. `denext start` passes its own prefix (`v2:<buildId>:`) once, after startup.
Data entries (`unstable_cache` / `"use cache"`) and the kept pages' tags are untouched.
Returns how many pages were deleted. A store that omits this is never swept; its
unreachable pages age out through its own eviction.

members.name: takeData
members.signature: takeData?(key: string): DataEntry | undefined | Promise<DataEntry | undefined>
members.doc:
Optional: **atomically** read and delete one data entry — a single-use record (a passkey
ceremony's challenge) that must be consumed exactly once even when several instances race
for it. Returns the entry when it was fresh, and then no other call (on any instance sharing
the store) ever returns it; an expired entry is removed and missed. A store that omits this
is not used for such records (they stay in the instance's memory).

members.doc:
Drop THIS instance's publishes of `key` that its Live hub has not yet sent to a subscriber:
those inside the hub's coalescing window, or still in the transport. Later publishes are
delivered as usual. Per instance: another instance's publishes of the key — in its hub's
window, or on their way through a shared transport — are not reached, nor are frames already

({@linkcode ChannelPublishOptions.grant}); `discard` is the local complement, not that
guarantee.

symbols.doc: What ChannelConfig.authorize answers to admit a subscriber under a grant: an opaque, short text for what it may read (a digest of its role and claims, say — never the claims themselves: it travels between instances). The Live hub then sends it a publish stamped with a grant (ChannelPublishOptions.grant) only when the two are equal, and every unstamped publish as before. The grant is recorded again at each re-authorization, so a subscriber whose claims changed is matched against what it may read now.

members.name: authorize
members.signature: authorize: (ctx: ChannelContext, key: string) => boolean | ChannelAdmission | Promise<boolean | ChannelAdmission>
members.doc:
REQUIRED: may this subscriber receive `key`? Runs in the subscriber's session. `true` admits
it, `false` refuses; `{ allow: true, grant }` admits it under a grant
({@linkcode ChannelAdmission}), so a publish stamped with another grant is not sent to it.

members.name: authTtlSeconds
members.doc: Re-authorize a subscriber lazily after this many seconds (default: `live.limits.channelAuthTtlSeconds`).

members.name: history
members.signature: history?: number | { size: number; ttlSeconds?: number }
members.doc:
Keep a replay log of each key's publishes: the last `size` (1–1000) for `ttlSeconds`
(default 24 hours). A subscriber passing `since` (`useChannel(ch, key, { since: "0" })`)
receives what it missed after `authorize` allows it, a reconnect resumes from its last
cursor, and a burst is delivered whole rather than latest-wins. The log is this instance's
(in memory, bounded) unless the transport brings a shared one (`redisChannelTransport`).

members.name: ordered
members.doc:
Deliver every publish, in order, instead of the latest one: two publishes to a key within the
hub's coalescing window both go out, and while a subscriber's frames are held (a slow socket,
a re-authorization in flight) up to 256 of them are kept in order
rather than the last one only. Past that the oldest are dropped, so a payload that must not
be lost silently should carry its own sequence number for the subscriber to check. For a
stream of deltas (each publish a batch of changes), not a state value.

members.name: onActive
members.doc:
Called when `key` gets its first subscriber on THIS instance (after `authorize` allowed it
and the subscription was registered). Runs in the root context; a throw is logged.

members.name: onIdle
members.doc:
Called when the last subscriber of `key` on THIS instance leaves (unsubscribed, revoked,
denied on re-authorization, or its connection closed) — the place to release per-key state
a channel keeps for its subscribers. Runs in the root context; a throw is logged.

`reason` is `"disconnect"` when the last subscriber's connection closed (or the hub shut
down) — it may come back with the same key — and `"unsubscribe"` otherwise (unsubscribed,
revoked, or denied on re-authorization).

members.name: publisher
members.doc:
A supervised producer for each active key: started when `key` gets its first subscriber on
THIS instance (in the root context), its `signal` aborted when the last one leaves. A throw
restarts it with exponential backoff (see `publisherRestart`); subscribers stay connected
throughout and simply receive nothing until it publishes again. Returning ends it for good
(until the key goes idle and active again).

members.name: publisherRestart
members.doc:
How a throwing `publisher` restarts (default: 5 restarts a minute, 250 ms doubling to 10 s,
20% jitter). Past `maxRestarts` within `period` it gives up for that key (logged); the
subscribers stay connected, and the key's next activation starts it afresh.

symbols.name: clientIp
symbols.doc: The client's IP address for the current request. Throws outside a request context (like headers); undefined when the request has no recorded peer (a handler invoked directly in a test, not through denext's server loop).
symbols.docFull:
The client's IP address for the current request. Throws outside a request context
(like {@linkcode headers}); `undefined` when the request has no recorded peer (a handler
invoked directly in a test, not through denext's server loop).

When the app trusts a fronting proxy ({@linkcode AppConfig.trustForwardedHeaders} /
`DENEXT_TRUST_PROXY=1`), the last hop of `x-forwarded-for` is returned; otherwise the
socket peer the server saw. Never read `x-forwarded-for` yourself without that flag — any
client can set it. {@linkcode AppConfig.rateLimitHeader} does not change it: that header names
the address per-address limits key on ({@linkcode clientIpForLimits}), nothing more.

Reading it makes the render **dynamic** (per-request), exactly like {@linkcode headers}:
a page that branches on the client IP cannot be statically cached. Use it in a route
handler, a Server Action, or middleware where that is already the case.
symbols.returns: The client IP, or undefined when the request has no recorded peer.

symbols.name: clientIpForLimits
symbols.doc: The client address to key a **per-address limit** on (a quota, a connection cap): clientIp — or undefined when that address is the socket peer and a loopback, private, link-local or unique-local one while the proxy is not trusted. Behind a reverse proxy without AppConfig.trustForwardedHeaders (or DENEXT_TRUST_PROXY=1) every visitor arrives from the proxy's address, so limiting on it would make one limit site-wide; key the limit on something else (a session, a connection) instead. A directly connected public peer and a trusted proxy's hop are returned as clientIp returns them — or, with { bucket: true }, as their limit bucket (an IPv6 address's /64), which is what a limit should key on.
symbols.docFull:
The client address to key a **per-address limit** on (a quota, a connection cap):
{@linkcode clientIp} — or `undefined` when that address is the socket peer and a loopback,
private, link-local or unique-local one while the proxy is not trusted. Behind a reverse proxy
without {@linkcode AppConfig.trustForwardedHeaders} (or `DENEXT_TRUST_PROXY=1`) every visitor
arrives from the proxy's address, so limiting on it would make one limit site-wide; key the
limit on something else (a session, a connection) instead. A directly connected public peer and
a trusted proxy's hop are returned as {@linkcode clientIp} returns them — or, with
`{ bucket: true }`, as their limit bucket (an IPv6 address's `/64`), which is what a limit
should key on.

Two app settings widen it (the model is Supabase Auth's `GOTRUE_RATE_LIMIT_HEADER`):
{@linkcode AppConfig.rateLimitHeader} (`DENEXT_RATE_LIMIT_HEADER`) names a header the proxy sets
to the client address (`cf-connecting-ip`, `fly-client-ip`, `x-real-ip`) — its last value is the
answer whenever it holds an IP address, local or not; a request without it falls back to the
rule above. {@linkcode AppConfig.rateLimitLocalAddresses}
(`DENEXT_RATE_LIMIT_LOCAL_ADDRESSES=1`) answers a loopback/private socket peer as itself instead
of `undefined` — for a host where those peers are real clients (a LAN, a VPN).

Throws outside a request context and makes the render dynamic, exactly like
{@linkcode clientIp}.

params.name: options
params.doc: bucket: true answers the address's **limit bucket** instead of the address: an IPv4 address as it is, an IPv6 one normalised and collapsed to its /64 prefix (2001:db8:1:2::/64) — the allocation one client controls, so rotating within it does not mint a fresh budget, and every spelling of one address shares one. Default false.

symbols.returns: The address (or bucket) to limit on, or undefined when per-address limits should not apply.

members.name: sign
members.doc:
Code-sign the binary after the compile (`denext build --compile --sign` asks for it once).
A macOS target is signed with `codesign` (the Hardened Runtime, a secure timestamp and the
JIT entitlement V8 needs) as `DENEXT_CODESIGN_IDENTITY`, then notarized when notary
credentials are set; a Windows target is Authenticode-signed with `signtool` (Windows) or
`osslsigncode` (macOS / Linux) with `DENEXT_WINDOWS_CERT`. Credentials come from the

where `--sign` fails.

symbols.name: composeMiddleware
symbols.doc: Compose an ordered list of entries into a single MiddlewareRunner.
symbols.docFull:
Compose an ordered list of entries into a single {@linkcode MiddlewareRunner}.

Entries run in array order. A `Response` short-circuits the chain; a
`rewrite` threads its URL into every subsequent entry (so later matchers see
the rewritten path); `next({ headers })` accumulates headers cumulatively
across the chain. If any entry rewrote, the final outcome is a `rewrite`;
otherwise it is `next` with the accumulated headers.

default is gzip only (Next.js's `compress`); list `"br"` to send brotli to clients that
accept it (quality 5: markedly smaller output for about two to three times gzip's CPU).

symbols.name: cors
symbols.doc: An allowlist-driven CORS policy for the endpoints a chain defines — the same exact-origin, fail-closed rules as the app's cors config (origins, methods, headers, exposeHeaders, credentials, maxAge), scoped to one endpoint. The framework answers a preflight for the method the policy guards (204, before middleware.ts and before this chain runs) and decorates every response the endpoint produces, errors included, with the headers the request's origin is granted. It REPLACES the route's export const cors and the app's cors for that method. The policy is validated here, so a bad one fails at import.
symbols.docFull:
An allowlist-driven CORS policy for the endpoints a chain defines — the same exact-origin,
fail-closed rules as the app's `cors` config (`origins`, `methods`, `headers`,
`exposeHeaders`, `credentials`, `maxAge`), scoped to one endpoint. The framework answers a
preflight for the method the policy guards (`204`, before `middleware.ts` and before this
chain runs) and decorates every response the endpoint produces, errors included, with the
headers the request's origin is granted. It REPLACES the route's `export const cors` and the
app's `cors` for that method. The policy is validated here, so a bad one fails at import.

CORS only tells a browser which origins may READ a response; pair it with {@link csrf} on a
cookie-authenticated endpoint to refuse the cross-site writes a browser still sends.
symbols.returns: A middleware carrying the resolved policy (no context extension).

Origins match EXACTLY (scheme + host + port, byte for byte); there are no wildcards, prefixes or suffixes, and "null" is refused.

symbols.name: createOtaHandler
symbols.doc: Build a handler that serves an OTA UI export to checkForUiUpdate / the native DenextOta plugin, following the serving rules every OTA server must keep:
symbols.docFull:
Build a handler that serves an OTA UI export to `checkForUiUpdate` / the native
`DenextOta` plugin, following the serving rules every OTA server must keep:

1. serve `_denext/ota.json` and ONLY the files it lists (anything else resolves `null`,
   so a request can never reach a file the manifest does not name);
2. put it behind the same auth as the app's API (wrap the handler; it does no auth);
3. send `Cache-Control: no-store`, so no cache serves a stale manifest or file.

Only `GET`/`HEAD` are answered (plus an `OPTIONS` preflight from an origin `cors` allows).
The manifest is re-read when its mtime changes, so a re-stamp (`denext ota manifest`, which
replaces the file atomically) needs no restart. Re-exporting in place is not atomic (a phone
could fetch a new manifest and old files, which then fail their hash check): export into a
new directory and point the handler at it, e.g. through a symlink you swap.

With `channels` instead of `dir`, each request is served from the release its channel (and,
during a staged rollout, its install id's bucket) selects; the rules above hold per release.

params.name: options
params.doc: The export directory (or the channels file), the path it is served under, and CORS.

symbols.returns: (request) => Response | null: null for a request that is not for the UI.

symbols.name: createPushSender
symbols.doc: Create a push sender for your APNs and/or FCM credentials. Keep one per process: it caches the APNs provider JWT for 50 minutes (Apple refuses one older than an hour, and throttles refreshing it more often than every 20 minutes) and the FCM access token until a minute before it expires. A refused provider token (ExpiredProviderToken / InvalidProviderToken, FCM 401) is re-signed and the send retried once.
symbols.docFull:
Create a push sender for your APNs and/or FCM credentials. Keep one per process: it caches
the APNs provider JWT for 50 minutes (Apple refuses one older than an hour, and throttles
refreshing it more often than every 20 minutes) and the FCM access token until a minute
before it expires. A refused provider token (`ExpiredProviderToken` /
`InvalidProviderToken`, FCM 401) is re-signed and the send retried once.

`ios` targets go to APNs, `android` targets to FCM HTTP v1. Delivery failures are results
(see {@linkcode PushErrorCode}); prune the token on `"invalid-token"`. A malformed config
throws a `TypeError` here, and a key that is not a PKCS#8 PEM rejects the first send with one.

members.name: authorize
members.signature: authorize?: (credentials: Record<string, string>) => Promise<AuthUser | null> | AuthUser | null
members.doc:
Validate submitted credentials and return the user, or `null` to reject.
MUST NOT leak whether an account exists (return `null` for an unknown account and
a wrong password alike) and must compare passwords in constant time — store hashes
from `hashPassword` and check with `verifyPassword` (both from `denext/server`).
Failed attempts are rate-limited by the framework (see `AuthConfig.rateLimit`).

Optional: without it, the framework verifies against the configured adapter's
credentials group (`getUserByEmail` → `getCredential` → `AuthConfig.hasher`).

symbols.name: CspSetting
symbols.doc: How a scope's Content-Security-Policy is decided (three-state): - "strict" — denext's default hash-based strict policy. - "off" — emit **no** CSP header for this scope (e.g. Next.js-compat, or to set the policy entirely at the edge/proxy). - a RouteCsp object — the strict policy plus the listed external opt-ins.
symbols.docFull:
How a scope's Content-Security-Policy is decided (three-state):
- `"strict"` — denext's default hash-based strict policy.
- `"off"` — emit **no** CSP header for this scope (e.g. Next.js-compat, or to set
  the policy entirely at the edge/proxy).
- a {@link RouteCsp} object — the strict policy plus the listed external opt-ins.

Settable globally (`denext.config` `csp`) and per file (a route's `csp` export);
the per-file setting overrides the global one for that route.

symbols.name: csrf
symbols.doc: Refuse cross-site state changes on a cookie-authenticated endpoint. A non-safe method (anything but GET/HEAD/OPTIONS) must come from the app's own origin, allowedOrigins (app config or these options) or the app's Deno Desktop origin — the Origin header, else Referer, and neither present is a refusal: the same gate Server Actions, the typed-API batch and denextAuth apply. With doubleSubmit the request must also echo the token cookie in a header. A refusal is a 403 csrf_failed envelope, before any schema runs; the code is folded into the endpoint's documented errors for @denext/openapi.
symbols.docFull:
Refuse cross-site state changes on a cookie-authenticated endpoint. A non-safe method
(anything but `GET`/`HEAD`/`OPTIONS`) must come from the app's own origin, `allowedOrigins`
(app config or these options) or the app's Deno Desktop origin — the `Origin` header, else
`Referer`, and neither present is a refusal: the same gate Server Actions, the typed-API batch
and `denextAuth` apply. With `doubleSubmit` the request must also echo the token cookie in a
header. A refusal is a 403 `csrf_failed` envelope, before any schema runs; the code is folded
into the endpoint's documented errors for `@denext/openapi`.

— the prefix stops a sibling subdomain from planting a token of its own — and
`denext-csrf` over plain http. Either name is read; a secure request ignores the
unprefixed one. A name set here is used as given.

members.doc:
Rendering mode. Omit (the default) for the App Router (SSR/SSG) pipeline.
`"spa"` builds {@link SpaConfig.entry} as a pure client-side-rendered app —
React but not Next: no `app/` directory, no SSR, no Flight. denext bundles the
entry, emits an HTML shell around it, serves it with a history-API fallback, and
(via `denext export` / `deno desktop`) packages it as a static app. Use it to
host an existing Vite-style React SPA on denext's toolchain and runtime.

members.name: scheduledJobs
members.doc:
Cron schedules for background jobs: a map of a 5-field cron expression to the job name(s)
to run on it (a job is `jobs/<name>.ts` exporting `defineJob(...)`). Registered at server
startup via `Deno.cron` when the runtime exposes it (Deno Deploy, or `--unstable-cron`) and a
dependency-free minute-tick scheduler otherwise. A task may also declare its own `schedule`.

```ts
scheduledJobs: { "0 3 * * *": "cleanup", "0 0 * * 1": ["digest", "warm-cache"] }
```

members.name: jobs
members.doc:
Scheduled/background job behaviour. Currently run history, which is off unless asked for.

```ts
jobs: { history: true }
```

members.name: images
members.doc:
Image-optimization config. Remote sources are refused by default (local-only,
SSRF-safe); allowlist hosts here to enable optimizing remote images.

members.name: tailwind
members.doc:
Tailwind CSS integration. When set, denext manages the Tailwind v4 standalone
binary and compiles `input` → `output` automatically on `dev`/`build`.

members.name: mdx
cache
members.doc:
Cache Components / ISR data + page cache store. Omit to let denext resolve the
default at startup — the durable `node:sqlite` store when a writable filesystem is
available, else the in-memory store. Set {@link CacheConfig.store} to force a choice,
or pass your own {@link CacheStore}.

members.name: hsts
members.doc:
`Strict-Transport-Security` (HSTS) header tuning, applied to responses served
over HTTPS. Defaults to `max-age=31536000` (1 year, host-only — no
`includeSubDomains`/`preload`, a safe default that can't brick sibling
subdomains). Set fields to opt into a stronger policy, or `false` to omit the
header entirely (e.g. when your edge sets it).

members.name: csp
members.doc:
App-wide Content-Security-Policy default (three-state), overridable per file:
- `"strict"` (default) — denext's hash-based strict policy on buffered pages.
- `"off"` — emit no CSP header at all (set your policy at the edge, or for
  Next.js-style "CSP is the app's job" behavior). A route can still opt back in
  with its own `csp` export.
- a {@link CspSetting} object — the strict policy plus these global opt-ins
  (`scriptSrc`, `styleSrc`, `imgSrc`, `connectSrc`, `fontSrc`, `frameSrc`,
  `mediaSrc`, `workerSrc`; e.g. `{ frameSrc: ["https://js.stripe.com"] }` for
  Stripe's Payment Element iframes).

A route's `csp` export overrides this for that route. Streamed responses (PPR /
incremental streaming) carry the **same** strict hash-based CSP, computed from the
buffered shell prefix plus the hashed swap-runtime constant (see
{@link resolveStreamingCsp}); the one inherent limit is that an inline
`<style>`/`<script>` appearing inside a streamed hole (flushed after the head) is
not covered by the header — see [KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md]. Absent ⇒ `"strict"`.

members.name: publicEnv
members.doc:
Public-env vars to always embed in the page island, in addition to the ones
the build detects the client references. Use this to force-include a key the
client reads via a computed expression (`publicEnv()["NEXT_PUBLIC_" + x]`),
which the build can't see. Referenced keys are shipped automatically; this only
adds to that set.

members.name: streaming
members.doc:
Incremental (Suspense) streaming, **on by default**; set `false` to opt out.
A page with a pending Suspense boundary flushes its shell first and streams each
boundary's content as it resolves; a fully synchronous page (no holes) is still
delivered buffered, so it stays shared-cacheable. Streamed responses carry the
same strict hash-based CSP as buffered ones (the swap runtime is a hashed
constant), survive a failing boundary (its fallback stays), and cover Flight
routes. ISR/PPR-cacheable routes (revalidate/force-static) and soft navigations
take their own path first, so streaming never bypasses the page cache. A shipped,
default-on capability — not an experiment.

members.name: live
members.doc:
Live Server Components security policy: authorization hooks and resource caps
for the `<Live>` / `useLive` / `usePresence` WebSocket hub. See {@link LiveConfig}.
Presence/data are default-deny in production without a policy here — so this is a
**security-policy** field, not an on/off experiment.

members.name: apiBatch
members.doc:
The typed-API batch endpoint (`POST /_denext/api-batch`: N GET/HEAD calls from
`createApiClient` in one round trip). Same-origin only; caps on items, body, fan-out
concurrency, and per-item response size. See {@link ApiBatchConfig}.

members.name: apiMaxBodyBytes
members.doc:
The request-body cap for route handlers (`route.ts`), in bytes — default 1 MiB. A route
raises or lifts its own with `export const maxBodyBytes = N | false`; a `defineApi`
endpoint with `maxBodyBytes` in its definition overrides both. Over the cap → 413.

members.name: cors
members.doc:
Cross-origin (CORS) access to route handlers and the native `denextAuth` endpoints —
what a Capacitor shell or a front end on another origin needs. Off by default (no CORS
headers at all). A route overrides it with `export const cors = { … } | false`. See
{@link CorsConfig}.

members.name: appLinks
members.doc:
The domain-association files for the app's universal links (iOS) and App Links (Android):
`denext start` and `denext dev` serve `/.well-known/apple-app-site-association` and
`/.well-known/assetlinks.json` from it (`application/json`, `200`, never redirected), and
`denext export` writes both into the export. Pair it with `denext mobile add deep-links
--domain <host>`. See {@link AppLinksConfig}.

members.name: actionMaxBodyBytes
members.doc:
The request-body cap for Server Actions, in bytes — default 1 MiB (Next's default). Raise
it only for actions that accept large payloads (multipart uploads); over the cap → 413
before the action runs. `denext start`/`dev` forward it to the server; a custom server
passes `actionMaxBodyBytes` to `createApp()` itself.

members.name: canonicalOrigin
members.doc:
The app's public origin (e.g. `"https://example.com"`), pinned outright: absolute URLs
(canonical, `og:image`), the Server Action origin check and HSTS all use it instead of
the `Host` / forwarded headers — the robust choice behind a proxy that rewrites `Host`.
A full origin (scheme + host, no path). Unset, the `DENEXT_CANONICAL_ORIGIN` env var is
read at boot (config > env > derived from the request).

members.name: trustForwardedHeaders
members.doc:
Trust `X-Forwarded-Proto` / `X-Forwarded-Host` from a reverse proxy when deriving the
request origin (absolute URLs, the Server Action origin check, HSTS), and
`X-Forwarded-For` / an inbound `X-Request-Id` for `clientIp()`, `requestId()` and the
rate limiters (`denextAuth` and `rateLimit()` inherit it unless they set their own). Enable
ONLY when clients cannot reach denext directly — a client that can spoofs them. The origin
part is ignored when {@link DenextConfig.canonicalOrigin} is set. Unset,
`DENEXT_TRUST_PROXY=1` turns it on (config > env > `false`).

members.name: rateLimitHeader
members.doc:
A request header the fronting proxy sets to the client address — `"cf-connecting-ip"`
(Cloudflare), `"fly-client-ip"` (Fly.io), `"x-real-ip"` (nginx) — that every **per-address
limit** keys on: `rateLimit()`, `denextAuth`'s per-IP budgets,
`live.limits.maxConnectionsPerIp`, `@denext/backend` realtime's signed-out quota and
`clientIpForLimits()`. Supabase Auth's `GOTRUE_RATE_LIMIT_HEADER`, for denext. When a request
carries an IP address in it (its last comma-separated value), that address is the limit key,
IPv6 bucketed by /64 and an IPv4-mapped address as its IPv4 — a loopback/private one too.

A request **without** it (or with a value that is not an IP address) did not come through
the proxy that sets it, so it falls back to the rule without this option (the trusted
`x-forwarded-for` hop, else the socket peer) and one warning is logged — where Supabase Auth
applies no limit at all to it, which would let anyone who reaches the server directly skip
every limit by leaving the header out.

The header is believed only from a **trusted proxy**: a socket peer inside
{@link DenextConfig.rateLimitTrustedProxies}, or — with none listed — a loopback/private peer
while {@link DenextConfig.trustForwardedHeaders} is on. From any other peer it is ignored and
the limit keys on that peer (one warning), so a client that reaches the server directly (a
leaked origin IP, an exposed app port) cannot pick a fresh bucket per request by sending its
own value. Supabase Auth's `GOTRUE_RATE_LIMIT_HEADER` trusts the header from anyone; denext
does not, because that one misconfiguration fails open silently. With neither trust rule set
the header is never believed and a warning says so at boot.

It only names the LIMIT address: `clientIp()` still follows `trustForwardedHeaders`. Unset,
the `DENEXT_RATE_LIMIT_HEADER` env var is read at boot (config > env > none).

members.name: rateLimitTrustedProxies
members.doc:
The proxies whose {@link DenextConfig.rateLimitHeader} is believed: CIDR ranges or single
addresses (`["173.245.48.0/20", "2400:cb00::/32"]` for Cloudflare's published ranges,
`["10.0.0.0/8"]` for an nginx or Fly proxy on a private network). A request whose socket peer
is outside every range keys its per-address limits on that peer instead. Unset (or empty):
a loopback/private peer when `trustForwardedHeaders` is on, else none. Unset, the
`DENEXT_RATE_LIMIT_TRUSTED_PROXIES` env var (comma-separated) is read at boot
(config > env > none).

members.name: rateLimitLocalAddresses
members.doc:
Apply per-address limits (`rateLimit()`, `denextAuth`'s per-IP budgets,
`live.limits.maxConnectionsPerIp`, `@denext/backend` realtime's signed-out quota,
`clientIpForLimits()`) to a loopback, private, link-local or unique-local socket peer too,
counted by its own address. Default `false`: such a peer is usually a reverse proxy every
visitor shares, so its limit would be site-wide, and the limits are skipped for it with a
warning. Turn it on where those peers are real clients — a LAN or VPN deployment, a
container network with no proxy in front. A trusted forwarded hop or a
{@link DenextConfig.rateLimitHeader} address still takes precedence. Unset,
`DENEXT_RATE_LIMIT_LOCAL_ADDRESSES=1` turns it on (config > env > `false`).

members.name: allowedDevOrigins
members.doc:
`denext dev` only: extra hosts allowed to reach the dev server's `/_denext/*` assets (the
bundles, the module graph, the reload stream, the Live hub), beyond loopback. Each entry is
an origin (`"http://192.168.1.5:3000"`) or a bare host (`"192.168.1.5"`, `"mac.local"`,
`"mac.local:3000"`); matching is on the hostname. Wildcards are not supported: list each
host. Mirrors Next.js's `allowedDevOrigins`. An entry may also be a Deno Desktop app's
custom-scheme origin (`"myapp://app"`, validated as `desktop.app.origin` is), which admits a
request whose `Origin` is exactly that value — for a backend project that a separate desktop
app talks to. The project's own `desktop.app.origin` is admitted without listing it.

Without it the dev server refuses those assets to any non-loopback `Host` (the DNS-rebinding
defense, cf. CVE-2025-48068), so a phone or another machine gets a dead page. You rarely
need to set it by hand: `denext dev --lan` and an explicit `--host` allow the address they
bind, and `--allowed-dev-origin <origin>` adds entries for one run. A listed host is
trusted as a dev client: anything on the network that can reach it (and send that `Host`)
can read the app's transformed source, as a loopback client can. Ignored by `denext start`.

members.name: requestTimeout
members.doc:
Per-request deadline in milliseconds — default 30 000. A request still running past it
is aborted and answered `503`; the per-request `AbortSignal` fires so cooperative work
(`fetch(url, { signal })`) cancels. `0` disables the deadline. Unset, the
`DENEXT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` env var is read at boot (config > env > default).

members.name: maxConcurrency
members.doc:
In-process concurrency ceiling: the max number of client requests one instance handles
at once. A request arriving at capacity is shed immediately with `503` + `Retry-After`
(never queued). Bounds work up to the point the `Response` is produced (a streaming
body's client-read time is not counted); background ISR regeneration is exempt. A
complement to — not a replacement for — the edge/load-balancer ceiling. Default: no
limit. Unset, the `DENEXT_MAX_CONCURRENCY` env var is read at boot (config > env >
unlimited).

members.name: slotBackstop
members.doc:
With {@link DenextConfig.maxConcurrency} set and {@link DenextConfig.requestTimeout} `0`,
the milliseconds after which a never-settling request's concurrency slot is force-freed
(default 120 000). It frees only the slot — the render is not aborted, since the request
timeout was opted out of. Inert while a request timeout is in place.

members.name: cacheKeyParams
members.doc:
Allowlist of query-parameter names that fork the ISR page-cache key. When set, only these
params make a distinct cached entry; every other param (`?utm_*`, `?fbclid`, a random
cache-buster) is ignored for keying — but still reaches the render via `searchParams`, so
list every param whose value changes cacheable output. Unset, every param participates.

members.name: cdnCacheHeaders
members.doc:
Send shared-cache headers with ISR pages — **off by default** (opt-in). With `true`, a page
served from the ISR cache (and the render that stores it) answers `Cache-Control: public,
s-maxage=<seconds it stays fresh>, stale-while-revalidate=31536000` (`public,
s-maxage=31536000` for `force-static`), so a CDN in front caches it as long as denext would.
Never for a request carrying a `Cookie` or `Authorization`, a response that sets a cookie, a
non-200, a dynamic render, a response whose `Cache-Control` middleware or a `headers()` rule
already set, or a request a `middleware.ts` matched (`{ evenWithMiddleware: true }` sends it
there too).

The risk: a CDN keys a page on its URL alone, so a page gated on anything else the cached
render didn't read — an IP allow-list, an auth proxy's header, geolocation,
`Accept-Language` — is served from the CDN to everyone once one allowed visitor fetched it.
Turn it on only for pages every visitor may see.

members.name: compress
members.doc:
Compress dynamic responses (rendered HTML, Flight/JSON payloads, route-handler text/JSON/
JS/CSS/SVG/XML) — **on by default**, like Next.js's `compress`. gzip by default (as
Next.js); brotli (quality 5: markedly smaller output for about two to three times gzip's
CPU) only when listed in `{ encodings }` (`{ encodings: ["br", "gzip"] }`). Negotiated from
`Accept-Encoding` (q-values; a tie goes to the earlier listed coding) through `node:zlib`,
flushed explicitly; streamed (Suspense/PPR) HTML is compressed chunk by chunk with a
flush per chunk, so it still reaches the browser progressively. Skipped for bodies under
1 KiB, `text/event-stream`, already-compressed types (images, fonts, video, archives),
a response that already has a `Content-Encoding`, `Cache-Control: no-transform`, range
responses, `HEAD` and `204`/`304`. A page, layout or route handler opts out with
`export const compress = false`. Build-time precompressed client bundles (`.gz`) are
served as-is. Set `false` when a proxy in front (nginx, Cloudflare, a CDN) compresses.

members.name: nodeResolve
members.doc:
denext's tolerant node_modules resolver for the compat (npm-React) build — default ON.

Every bare npm specifier is resolved straight from the app's installed `node_modules`
using denext's own resolver, a strict superset of Deno's `npm:` loader: it honors
`exports` wildcard globs, falls back to a plain subpath, and returns nothing on a miss
(so the deno-loader still gets its shot). This is what makes an unmodified
pnpm/npm/yarn/bun app build with no catalog-concretizing and no hand-patching of
dependency `exports` — the "seamless migration" contract. Set `false` only to force
app deps back through Deno's strict `npm:` loader (escape hatch). The pre-2.0 home,
`experimental.nodeResolve`, was removed in 3.0 (setting it is a config error).

members.name: cacheComponents
members.doc:
Cache Components (Next.js 16): the `"use cache"` directive is compiled into
cross-request caching on the server (`src/build/use-cache-transform.ts`), plus the
PPR render path — dynamic-by-default rendering with cacheable `use cache` islands (a
cached shell with per-request dynamic holes spliced in). A stable, **opt-in**
feature, deliberately **off by default**: caching stays a choice, because a cache
bug's failure class (a poisoned or cross-user shell) is severe and must not be
imposed on apps that never asked. When off, every `"use cache"` directive is inert
(a plain no-op string statement) and rendering is unchanged.

Documented bounds (see KNOWN-LIMITATIONS): as in Next.js, reading request data
(`cookies()`/`headers()`) inside `use cache` throws (`"use cache: private"` may read
them); a streamed hole can't add an
inline `<style>`/`<script>` or hoist an in-boundary `<title>`/`<meta>` into the
already-flushed head. With `cacheKeyParams` set, reading a `searchParams` name outside
it postpones like `cookies()` (outside every Suspense boundary, the page renders per
request and is not stored).

Next.js's `experimental.cacheComponents` spelling is kept as an obsolete alias for
migrated Next apps (see {@linkcode resolveCacheComponents}); this top-level field wins.

members.name: cacheLife
members.doc:
Named `cacheLife()` profiles (Next.js 16's `cacheLife` key), each `{ stale, revalidate,
expire }` in seconds (`Infinity` for never): `cacheLife("biweekly")` inside a
`"use cache"` function picks one. A name that matches a built-in profile (`default`,
`seconds`, `minutes`, `hours`, `days`, `weeks`, `max`) overrides it; a field left out of
a custom profile falls back to the `default` profile's. Validated at load as Next.js does
(`false` is refused, `expire` must be at least `revalidate`).

members.name: reactCompiler
members.doc:
The build-time auto-memoization compiler (a React-Compiler-style pass), an opt-in
optimization that is off by default. Conservative by construction: it bails to
identity whenever a transform isn't provably safe, so it only ever adds memoization,
never changes behavior.

Next.js 15's `experimental.reactCompiler` spelling is honored, with a dev warning, when
this field is absent (the pre-2.0 `experimental.compiler` was removed in 3.0).

members.name: asyncContext
members.doc:
Scope async `startTransition` by transition IDENTITY instead of a time window, so a
post-`await` update is attributed to its transition while an unrelated urgent update in
the pending window keeps its priority. Off by default.

Enables a build-time transform that makes denext's first-party {@link AsyncContext}
survive `await` (src/build/async-context-transform.ts). It instruments every `await`
in client code (a small per-await cost); the default time-window behavior is unchanged
when off. Removes the async-`startTransition` gap in KNOWN-LIMITATIONS when on.

Graduated from `experimental.asyncContext` in 2.5; that spelling was removed in 3.0
(setting it is a config error).

members.name: features
members.doc:
Compile-time feature flags: `feature("KEY")` (from `denext/feature`) always returns the
configured value, and a call with a string-literal KEY is folded to a literal where the
build can, so the bundler dead-code-eliminates the untaken branch. A key not listed
reads `false`.

The server and every client bundle are seeded with this map. The fold (DCE) covers the
native App Router's component (`.tsx`/`.jsx`) modules, the SPA bundle, and dev; the
compat drop-in App Router path and non-component modules on the native path read the
seeded value without DCE. Flag names and states are embedded in the client bundle.

Graduated from `experimental.features` in 2.5; that spelling was removed in 3.0
(setting it is a config error).

members.name: optimizePackageImports
members.doc:
npm packages whose barrel (`index`) imports are rewritten to the files that define each
name, as Next.js's `optimizePackageImports` does: `import { Check } from "lucide-react"`
becomes an import of `lucide-react`'s `icons/check.js`, so the bundler never loads the
barrel. Your list is ADDED to a built-in default (lucide-react, date-fns, lodash-es, …);
a `"!pkg"` entry removes a package from it, and `false` turns the optimization off.

That keeps an icon library's thousand re-exports out of the module graph — and, when the
package also code-splits every icon (`lucide-react/dynamic`), out of the startup chunk
list. Applied to the esbuild bundles (the compat client and server bundles and SPA mode,
in production builds and compat dev rebuilds), for app source and for npm modules that
import a listed package. The unbundled per-module dev server and the native `deno bundle`
path do not apply it.

The built-in default is `lucide-react`, `date-fns`, `lodash-es`, `ramda`, `rxjs`,
`@tabler/icons-react`, `@heroicons/react/{20,24}/solid`, `@heroicons/react/24/outline`,
`react-icons/*`, `@mui/icons-material`, `recharts`, `react-use`, `@headlessui/react`,
`effect`; an entry ending in `/*` matches every subpath of the package, and `"!pkg"`
removes exactly the entry `pkg` (`"!react-icons/*"` drops the wildcard). Only named value
imports are rewritten, and only names the barrel re-exports from another module (a name
the barrel defines itself stays on the barrel); a barrel that runs code of its own
(including a decorator), carries a directive, or cannot be analysed is left untouched.

**Listing a package asserts its modules are side-effect free** (Next.js's contract too):
the modules beside the one a name comes from are never loaded, so a top-level side effect
in one of them no longer runs. Next's `experimental.optimizePackageImports` spelling is
honored, with a dev warning, when this field is absent.

Packages whose own `package.json` declares them side-effect free (`"sideEffects": false`, or
an array naming none of the modules the barrel loads) are looked through automatically,
unlisted: the barrel must be the file the build resolves the specifier to, a name it
re-exports from another package stays on the barrel, and every module the barrel would have
loaded must be side-effect free. That also keeps a lazy route's modules out of the startup
chunks when the startup graph imports other names from the same barrel. `"!pkg"` excludes a
package from the automatic mode too, and `"!*"` turns the automatic mode off.

members.name: nextScriptWorkers
members.doc:
Run `<Script strategy="worker">` in a web worker through Partytown, as Next.js does (its
`experimental.nextScriptWorkers`, honored with a dev warning when this field is absent).
The app installs Partytown itself — `@qwik.dev/partytown`, or Next's
`@builder.io/partytown`, in `node_modules` — and `denext dev` / `build` / `export` serve its
files from the app's own origin under `/_denext/~partytown/`, so the strict default CSP
needs no opt-in. Off (the default), or with no Partytown installed, worker scripts run on
the main thread as `afterInteractive`, with a dev warning naming the fix.

members.name: resolveAlias
members.doc:
Module aliases for the esbuild bundles, optionally sensitive to the importing file, as
Metro's `resolveRequest` and Vite's `resolve.alias` express them. A key is an import
specifier, matched exactly; its value is where that import goes: a package or package
subpath (`"uniwind/components/web"`), or a `./` file of the project. The object form's
`except` lists packages whose OWN imports of the key keep the original module, the shape a
library that wraps the module it replaces needs (uniwind's `react-native`).

```ts
resolveAlias: {
  "react-native": { to: "uniwind/components/web", except: ["uniwind"] },
  "legacy-sdk": "./src/web/legacy-sdk.ts",
}
```

Applied ahead of every other resolver in SPA and React Native mode, the next-compat App
Router's client and server bundles, and `denext dev`'s dependency bundles; the target is
resolved through the same build, so its own resolution rules apply. The native App
Router path (`deno bundle`) resolves through the import map instead: use `deno.json`
`imports`, and `scopes` for an importer-sensitive entry.

members.name: momentumSafeScroll
members.doc:
Keep iOS momentum scrolling alive while scroll-anchoring code corrects the scroll offset —
default ON. In iOS WebKit (Safari, WKWebView, Capacitor) any programmatic scroll write
during a touch fling (`scrollBy`, `scrollTo`, assigning `scrollTop`) stops the fling dead,
and virtualized lists (LegendList, react-virtuoso, TanStack Virtual) issue exactly such
writes to compensate for rows measured taller or shorter than estimated. The client
runtime therefore defers those writes during a gesture (see `installMomentumSafeScroll`
in `denext/mobile`) and applies them in one step once the scroller comes to rest.

It installs only on iOS/iPadOS WebKit, loaded as its own chunk, so other platforms pay a
user-agent check and nothing more. Set `false` to opt out.

members.name: lists
members.doc:
Which engine runs the DOM list packages. `"denext"`: `@legendapp/list/react` (LegendList's
DOM build), imported by the app or by its packages, runs on denext's `VirtualList` with
LegendList's props, ref methods (`scrollToEnd`, `scrollToIndex`, `getState`, …) and cell
hooks, in SPA mode and on the App Router (server render included); the app's source stays
unchanged. `"library"` (the default): the real package. Applies to apps that use npm React
(the esbuild build path). React Native mode's own list packages are `reactNative.lists`.

members.name: platformExtensions
members.doc:
Platform-specific files: an import of `./BigButton` (or `./BigButton.tsx`) resolves to
`BigButton.ios.tsx` in the iOS export, `BigButton.desktop.tsx` in a desktop package,
`BigButton.web.tsx` on the web, and to the plain file where a target has no variant. The
probe order per target (most specific first): web `.web`; ios `.ios` → `.mobile` → `.web`;
android `.android` → `.mobile` → `.web`; macos / windows / linux the OS → `.desktop` →
`.web`. Applies to the app's own modules (packages in `node_modules` keep their own
resolution). `{ native: true }` also probes React Native's `.native` after the OS on ios and
android (off by default: `.native` files are usually native code, which a WebView cannot
run). In React Native mode the app's `.ios` / `.android` files are native code too, so they
are not probed unless `{ osFiles: true }`. `false` turns platform files off. See
{@link https://denext.dev/docs/platform-files}.

members.name: mobile
members.doc:
Capacitor shell settings for `denext mobile build` and `denext mobile assets`: build flavors
(per-flavor app id, name, server URL, icon and splash). See
{@link https://denext.dev/docs/mobile-build}.

members.name: desktop
members.doc:
Deno Desktop native capabilities: the allowlist the desktop runtime's capability bridge
serves (default deny) and the source the package scripts derive least-privilege `--allow-*`
from. Written by `denext desktop add <cap>`. Distinct from {@link SpaConfig.desktop} (packaging
settings such as the icon); the two may be unified in a later release. Docs:
https://denext.dev/docs/desktop

members.name: compile
members.doc:
`denext build --compile`: the single-executable server build (`deno compile` on denext's
Deno toolchain). What the binary embeds beyond what denext finds itself, and the `--allow-*`
baked into it beyond the least-privilege baseline. See
{@link https://denext.dev/docs/deployment-targets#a-single-binary-with-denext-build---compile}.

members.name: start
members.doc:
The production server (`denext start`, the `build --compile` executable, the generated Docker
image and systemd unit): its idle memory trim and its resource limits. See
{@link https://denext.dev/docs/deployment-targets#idle-memory-trim}.

members.name: deploy
members.doc:
Deploy adapter: `denext build` runs its `prepare` with the typed deploy manifest
(`.denext/deploy-manifest.json`) after every build, and `denext deploy` pushes with it. A
preset from `denext/deploy` (`docker()`, `fly()`, `denoDeploy()`, `genericHost()`,
`staticHost()`) or your own adapter. See {@link https://denext.dev/docs/deploy#deploy-adapters}.

members.name: reactNative
members.doc:
Build a React Native / Expo app's source for the web through `react-native-web`, in SPA
mode (`mode: "spa"`) or on the App Router. `true` turns on the defaults; an object sets
options.

- `react-native` (and every `react-native/…` subpath) resolves to the installed
  `react-native-web`, for every importer, even when a real `react-native` is installed.
  A deep `react-native/Libraries/…` import maps to react-native-web's equivalent where one
  exists, else to a stub that throws, naming the import, when it is called.
- Web platform files win: `.web.tsx`, `.web.ts`, `.web.jsx` and `.web.js` are probed
  before the plain extensions, for relative and alias imports and for package subpaths.
- `.js` files are parsed as JSX (React Native libraries ship JSX in `.js`).
- `__DEV__` (true in dev, false in a production build), `global` → `globalThis` and
  `process.env.EXPO_OS` → `"web"` are defined at build time.
- The SPA shell gets Expo web's root style (see {@link ReactNativeConfig.rootStyle}).

The build always takes the esbuild (compat) path. Install `react-native-web` in the
project; native-only modules still need web shims of your own.

On the App Router, the server bundle, the client islands and the hydrated routes all
resolve this way, so Server Components and `"use client"` components can both import
`react-native`; react-native-web's style sheet is written into each server-rendered
`<head>` (`<style id="react-native-stylesheet">`). `expo-router` imports fail there (`app/`
is the App Router's), `dev` uses the bundled loop, and `fonts` and
`compatibilityMode: false` are refused.

members.name: classComponents
members.doc:
How the client bundle gets the React class-component runtime (`class X extends
React.Component`: lifecycle, setState batching, class error boundaries). It is a
code-split chunk (`denext/class-runtime`), so the default needs no configuration.
Unset, `denext build` scans your sources and installs it eagerly when a class is found,
otherwise a page loads it on demand; `true` always installs it eagerly; `false` never
ships it — the runtime is dead-code-eliminated and a class used anyway throws a guided
error.

- **unset** (default): loaded **on demand**. `denext build` scans your app's own sources
  (and sibling workspace packages) for `Component`/`PureComponent` and, when it finds
  one, installs the runtime eagerly; otherwise the generated entry fetches the chunk
  only for a page whose server render produced a class component — so a class that
  lives in an npm dependency you never name still works in production, and a
  function-only page never downloads it.
- **`true`**: always install it eagerly (skips the scan and the on-demand round trip).
- **`false`**: never ship it. In the next-compat (esbuild) build the flag is a `define`,
  so the entire runtime is dead-code-eliminated — zero bytes — and a class used anyway
  throws a guided error.

members.name: compatibilityMode
members.doc:
Run the app through the **next-compat** SSR/client pipeline, which rewrites
every `react`/`react-dom`/`next/*` import (including those inside npm React
libraries) to denext at bundle time so the whole app runs on one denext React
— the drop-in path for real Next.js App Router projects. `true`/`false` force
it; the default `"auto"` enables it when `node_modules/react` exists or
`package.json` lists `react`/`next`. A pure denext-native app keeps the
zero-overhead source-load path.

(Renamed from `nextCompat`; the old key is no longer accepted.)

members.name: plugins
members.doc:
denext plugins (e.g. a Pages Router). Each is set up once before routes are
scanned and may contribute routes, claim requests, and emit build assets — see
{@linkcode DenextPlugin}. Apps with no plugins pay nothing.

members.name: commands
members.doc:
Project-local CLI verbs: `denext <name>` runs the entry's `run`, with the same
flag parsing, `--help` rendering, and "did you mean" suggestions a built-in verb
gets. The shorthand for a one-off project script — a plugin (`addCommand`) is
only needed when the verb ships as a reusable package.

They are listed under "Project commands" by `denext commands` and included in
`denext completions <shell>` (`denext --help` deliberately imports nothing and
points at `denext commands`). A **built-in verb always wins a name collision**:
an entry named `dev` or `build` is ignored, never shadowing the core verb.
Loading them costs one config read, paid only when the CLI must enumerate every
verb (`commands`, `completions`) or hits a verb it doesn't recognize — never for
a script (`denext main.ts`) or a Deno verb, which run without importing the config.

An entry may not take the name of a Deno verb that runs or installs code (`run`,
`x`, `eval`, `serve`, `compile`, `install`, `uninstall`, `upgrade`, `task`): the
config is refused. One named after another Deno verb (`bench`, `doc`, …) runs in
its place only once `denext commands` has listed it (the listing in
`.denext/commands.json` must match the current config, `deno.json` and
`deno.lock`); until then `denext <name>` runs Deno's.

symbols.name: DenextPlugin
symbols.doc: A denext plugin. Declared in denext.config.ts as plugins: [myPlugin()]; its setup runs once per process, before the first route scan.
symbols.docFull:
A denext plugin. Declared in `denext.config.ts` as `plugins: [myPlugin()]`; its
{@linkcode setup} runs once per process, before the first route scan.

members.name: name
members.doc: Unique plugin name (used to de-duplicate registration across a process).

members.name: setup
members.doc: Wire the plugin into denext's seams. Runs once, before routes are scanned.

symbols.name: denoKvCacheStore
symbols.doc: A CacheStore on Deno KV, shared by every isolate using the database.
symbols.docFull: A {@link CacheStore} on Deno KV, shared by every isolate using the database.

params.name: options

symbols.docFull: {@link DesktopConfig.app}'s `icons`: the app icon file per OS, relative to the project.

members.name: macos
members.doc: macOS: an `.icns`, or a 1024² `.png`.

members.name: windows
members.doc: Windows: an `.ico`.

members.name: linux
members.doc: Linux: a `.png` (512² or larger).

symbols.name: DesktopCapabilitiesConfig
symbols.doc: desktop.capabilities: which native capabilities the page may reach, keyed by the name denext desktop add <name> writes. true enables a capability with its defaults; an object scopes it. Anything absent is denied. An unknown key is allowed (a newer desktop add) and the validator warns on it.
symbols.docFull:
`desktop.capabilities`: which native capabilities the page may reach, keyed by the name
`denext desktop add <name>` writes. `true` enables a capability with its defaults; an object
scopes it. Anything absent is denied. An unknown key is allowed (a newer `desktop add`) and the
validator warns on it.

members.name: secureStore
members.doc:
OS keychain: macOS Keychain / Linux libsecret / Windows WinRT PasswordVault (the Windows
backend is verified by the Windows CI round-trip).

members.name: fs
members.doc: App files under the OS app-support / cache folders.

members.name: sqlite
members.doc: An app SQLite database under the app-support folder.

members.name: contextMenu
members.doc:
`showContextMenu` / `useContextMenu` as the OS's native menu (submenus, disabled and checked
items, a real dismissal) through denext's pinned runtime; under the stock runtime the page keeps
its in-page menu.

members.name: shell
members.doc: Open external URLs / paths / reveal / trash (scoped).

members.name: authSession
members.doc:
System-browser OAuth via `openAuthSession` (loopback redirect). The runtime's auth-session
endpoint is default-deny unless this is enabled; the packaged app then bakes the browser
opener's `--allow-run`.

members.name: dialogs
members.doc: Native open/save/folder dialogs returning paths.

members.name: notifications
members.doc:
Local notifications as the OS's own through denext's pinned runtime: shown now or scheduled
(repeating triggers too), cancelled and listed, with action buttons, the permission status, and
clicks routed to `onLocalNotificationTapped` (including the one that launched the app). Under the
stock runtime the page keeps the WebView's Notification API (immediate only).

members.name: globalShortcuts
members.doc:
System-wide keyboard shortcuts (`registerShortcut` in `denext/desktop/app`) through denext's
pinned runtime: macOS hot keys, Windows `RegisterHotKey`, X11 key grabs, the Wayland
GlobalShortcuts portal (the user approves each).

members.name: launchAtLogin
members.doc:
Start the app at login (`getLaunchAtLogin` / `setLaunchAtLogin` in `denext/desktop/app`)
through denext's pinned runtime: a macOS login item, a Windows `Run` value, a Linux XDG
autostart entry, named after `desktop.app.identifier`.

members.name: updates
members.doc:
The page drives the app's own updates (`checkForUpdates` / `applyUpdates` from
`denext/updates`): the signed UI overlay ({@link DesktopUpdateConfig.ui}) and the whole app
({@link DesktopUpdateConfig.manifestUrl}, denext's pinned runtime), with download progress.

members.name: keepAwake
members.doc: Prevent the machine from sleeping while held.

members.name: clipboard
members.doc:
The OS clipboard — text, HTML and PNG images (`readClipboard` / `writeClipboard` /
`clipboardFormats`) — through denext's pinned runtime; under the stock runtime the page keeps
the WebView's `navigator.clipboard` (text).

members.name: device
members.doc: Device info (`os`, `osVersion`, `model?`).

members.name: passkeys
members.doc:
Native passkeys (macOS Touch ID / iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello; none on Linux) through
denext's pinned runtime, for a page whose custom-scheme origin the webview's own WebAuthn cannot
use (the bridge behind `denext/desktop/clerk`). `{ rpIds }` pins the relying-party IDs the app
may request and is required; anything else answers `invalid_rp` without reaching the OS.
The list is also written to the packaged app's `laufey-launch.json` (`"passkeyRpIds"`), so the
webview backend enforces it natively; from runtime 3.0.0-denext.1 (`"strictPolicy"`) a launch
file without it refuses every ceremony. `false` (or leaving it out) disables it.

members.name: microphone
members.doc:
The page's `getUserMedia({ audio })` gets the microphone, for the app's own origin only (never
another origin the window navigates to, nor a sub-frame of another origin). The packaged app's
`laufey-launch.json` carries the grant (`"mediaCapture"`, Deno Desktop runtime 3.0.0-denext.9+;
an older runtime refuses every request), macOS's `Info.plist` its
`NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`, and a signed macOS build the
`com.apple.security.device.audio-input` entitlement. macOS still asks the user once.

members.name: camera
members.doc:
The page's `getUserMedia({ video })` gets the camera, as {@link microphone} the microphone
(`NSCameraUsageDescription`, `com.apple.security.device.camera`).

members.name: echo
members.doc: The `echo` diagnostic capability (bridge connectivity check).

members.name: extensions
members.doc: User extension module paths (`defineDesktopExtension`); each module's `name` is its cap name.

symbols.name: DesktopConfig
symbols.doc: The desktop block of denext.config.ts: Deno Desktop native capabilities. The allowlist the desktop runtime's capability bridge serves (default deny), and the source the package scripts derive least-privilege --allow-* from. Written by denext desktop add <cap>. Distinct from SpaDesktopConfig (spa.desktop, packaging settings such as the icon); the two may be unified later. Docs: https://denext.dev/docs/desktop
symbols.docFull:
The `desktop` block of `denext.config.ts`: Deno Desktop native capabilities. The allowlist the
desktop runtime's capability bridge serves (default deny), and the source the package scripts
derive least-privilege `--allow-*` from. Written by `denext desktop add <cap>`. Distinct from
{@link SpaDesktopConfig} (`spa.desktop`, packaging settings such as the icon); the two may be
unified later. Docs: https://denext.dev/docs/desktop

members.name: app
members.signature: app?: { identifier?: string; name?: string; icons?: DesktopAppIcons; origin?: string; deepLinks?: string[]; singleInstance?: boolean; bridgeOrigins?: string[]; allowedNavigationOrigins?: string[]; keepAlive?: boolean; dock?: boolean; activationPolicy?: "regular" | "accessory" }
members.doc:
App identity for the RUNTIME. Its `identifier` keys the OS app-support/cache/documents folders
and the `secureStore` keychain SERVICE, so it MUST be unique per app — a reverse-DNS id such as
`"com.example.myapp"`. Without it, `secureStore`/`fs`/`sqlite` refuse to start (they would
otherwise share one folder and one keychain service across every denext desktop app, letting
one app read another's data and secrets). Keep it equal to `deno.json`'s `desktop.app.identifier`
(which `deno desktop` uses for the bundle id); the scaffold writes both.

members.name: tray
members.doc:
A tray icon (macOS menu bar extra, Windows notification area, Linux StatusNotifierItem /
AppIndicator) the app's backend owns: created by `runDesktop` before any page loads, kept
across page reloads, and reachable from every window (`getTray()` in `denext/desktop/app`) and
from `desktop.ts` (`DesktopRuntime.tray`, with `runDesktop({ tray })` handlers). Setting it
keeps the app alive with no window ({@link DesktopConfig.app}`.keepAlive`). Where the session
has no tray host (stock GNOME without the AppIndicator extension) no icon is shown and the
first window is shown instead.

members.name: capabilities
members.doc: The capability allowlist (default deny).

members.name: sidecars
members.doc:
Backends the app runs and supervises next to its window, as an Electron app spawns its server:
`{ name, run: { module } }` runs a module in a worker of the app's own Deno runtime (no second
binary; a Node backend with `nodeModules` is bundled at packaging, its native addons copied),
`{ name, run: { exec } }` spawns a program. Each gets a loopback port (`port: "auto"`), is
started once the window's server is up, checked for readiness (`ready`), restarted with backoff
after a crash (`restart`), stopped with a grace period (`shutdown`) and ended with the app.
`proxy: true` points `spa.proxy` at one. Functions (`ready.probe`, a computed `bootstrap` or
`secrets`) go in `runDesktop({ sidecars })` instead. `denext desktop add sidecar` writes one.

members.name: inspectable
members.doc:
Whether the web inspector (DevTools) can be opened in the window: F12, the context menu,
Safari's Develop menu and remote debugging. Default: on in `denext desktop dev` (always) and
`denext desktop run`, OFF in a packaged app — set `true` to ship an inspectable build. The
package scripts write it to the app's `laufey-launch.json` (`"inspectable"`); `run` passes it as
`LAUFEY_INSPECTABLE`. Needs denext's pinned runtime (the stock runtime ignores it).

members.name: preload
members.doc:
A module run in the window before the page's scripts (Electron's preload), e.g.
`"./desktop/preload.ts"` (relative to the project). A desktop export (`macos` / `windows` /
`linux`: `denext desktop run`, the package scripts) bundles it into one classic script
(`out/_denext/desktop-preload.js`; a web, iOS or Android export does not carry it), and the
desktop runtime inlines it as the first page
script of every top-level document it serves over the memory transport (the denext-pinned
runtime), right after the `__denext` global, with its own CSP hash. Never in an iframe, and not
under the stock runtime (loopback). It runs in the page's world with the page's privileges
(trusted app code, no isolated world): use it to expose bridges such as `window.desktopBridge`
or Clerk's (`installClerkDesktopBridge` from `denext/desktop/clerk`) before the app reads them.

members.name: window
members.doc:
The initial window: size, title and resizability, applied by the desktop runtime when it
adopts the window (on every runtime). Under denext's pinned runtime the size is capped at the
work area of the display the window opens on, and the window is moved inside it. The page
changes it later with `denext/desktop/window`.

members.name: titleBar
members.doc:
The title bar style (macOS): `"hidden"` draws the page under a transparent title bar,
`"hiddenInset"` also insets the traffic lights. Give the page a drag region
(`makeWindowDraggable` from `denext/desktop/window`). Needs denext's pinned runtime.

members.name: backdrop
members.doc:
The window backdrop, showing where the page's background is transparent: `"mica"` /
`"acrylic"` on Windows 11, `"vibrancy"` (the `under-window` material) on macOS. Ignored on
other OSes and on the CEF backend. Needs denext's pinned runtime.

members.name: minSize
members.doc: The smallest window size the user can resize to. Needs denext's pinned runtime.

members.name: maxSize
members.doc: The largest window size the user can resize to. Needs denext's pinned runtime.

members.name: extraPermissions
members.doc:
Extra Deno permissions the packaging scripts bake into the `deno desktop` binary beyond what
the enabled {@link DesktopCapabilitiesConfig capabilities} imply — the escape hatch for what
the capability catalog can't see: the desktop updater's feed host (`net`) and data dir
(`write`), a `defineDesktopExtension` module's own `run`/`ffi`, or any custom need.
`denext desktop package --regenerate-scripts` preserves it (it lives here, not in the script).

members.name: update
members.doc:
Full-app self-update (`checkForAppUpdate` … from `denext/desktop/updater`): the whole signed
app is replaced by a newer signed build. Needs denext's pinned Deno Desktop runtime.

members.name: installers
members.doc:
The installers `denext desktop package` (the `scripts/package-*.ts`) builds, per OS. Unset,
an OS builds its defaults: `.dmg` on macOS (beside the `.app`), `.tar.gz` + `.deb` on Linux,
`.msi` on Windows. `--format` overrides the list for one run.

members.name: macos
members.doc:
macOS code-signing extras for `scripts/package-macos.ts`: a provisioning profile embedded as
`Contents/embedded.provisionprofile`, and entitlements signed into the app. What an app needs
for a restricted entitlement such as `com.apple.developer.associated-domains` (native passkeys,
universal links), which macOS honours only with a profile that grants it. Applied when the
bundle is signed with a real identity (`DENEXT_CODESIGN_IDENTITY`).

members.name: linux
members.doc: Linux launch settings the package scripts write to the app's `laufey-launch.json`.

members.name: windows
members.doc: Windows launch settings the package scripts write to the app's `laufey-launch.json`.

members.name: denoFlags
members.doc:
Extra `deno desktop` flags, passed before the entry by `denext desktop run` / `dev` and the
package scripts: for a project that needs them to build at all. npm resolution needs none:
a project with a package.json or node_modules (a pnpm workspace member included) is built
with `--node-modules-dir=none --exclude-unused-npm` already.
One flag per entry, `--flag` or `--flag=value`, from an allow-list: `--node-modules-dir`,
`--node-modules-linker`, `--exclude-unused-npm`, `--no-check`, `--check`, `--no-lock`,
`--lock`, `--frozen-lockfile`, `--cached-only`, `--no-remote`, `--no-npm`, `--no-code-cache`,
`--conditions` and `--unstable-*`. Permission flags are refused: they come from
{@link capabilities} and {@link extraPermissions}.

symbols.name: DesktopEntitlementValue
symbols.signature: type DesktopEntitlementValue = string | number | boolean | string[]
symbols.doc: One entitlement's value in DesktopMacosConfig.entitlements.
symbols.docFull: One entitlement's value in {@link DesktopMacosConfig.entitlements}.

symbols.name: DesktopExtraPermissions
symbols.doc: Extra --allow-* for the desktop packaging scripts (see DesktopConfig.extraPermissions). Each field is a list of Deno permission values, unioned into the derived flags.
symbols.docFull:
Extra `--allow-*` for the desktop packaging scripts (see {@link DesktopConfig.extraPermissions}).
Each field is a list of Deno permission values, unioned into the derived flags.

members.name: read
members.doc: `--allow-read` paths (usually unnecessary — the baseline is already broad read).

members.name: write
members.doc: `--allow-write` paths; ANY entry bakes a broad `--allow-write` (a per-user path can't be scoped).

members.name: net
netConnect
members.doc:
Outbound hosts only (`--allow-net-connect` under the pinned runtime; folded into `--allow-net`
under the stock one). The loopback baseline is always there.

members.name: netListen
members.doc:
Listen addresses only (`--allow-net-listen` under the pinned runtime; folded into
`--allow-net` under the stock one). The baseline listens on loopback (`127.0.0.1`,
`localhost`, any port).

members.name: run
members.doc: `--allow-run` programs; `["*"]` bakes an unscoped `--allow-run`.

members.name: ffi
members.doc:
`--allow-ffi` libraries; `["*"]` bakes an unscoped `--allow-ffi`, which a Node-API addon (an
npm package's prebuilt `.node`) needs: the packaged app loads it from its embedded file system,
whose path cannot be named at package time.

members.name: env
members.doc: `--allow-env` variable names.

members.name: sys
members.doc: `--allow-sys` kinds; `["*"]` bakes an unscoped `--allow-sys`.

symbols.name: DesktopFsConfig
symbols.doc: The fs desktop capability's scoped roots (path tokens $APPDATA / $CACHE / $DOCUMENTS, plus the per-session $PICKED set the user grows through native dialogs).
symbols.docFull:
The `fs` desktop capability's scoped roots (path tokens `$APPDATA` / `$CACHE` / `$DOCUMENTS`,
plus the per-session `$PICKED` set the user grows through native dialogs).

members.name: read
members.doc: Roots the app may read.

members.name: write
members.doc: Roots the app may write.

symbols.name: DesktopInstallersConfig
symbols.doc: DesktopConfig.installers: the installer formats per OS, and what they say about the app.
symbols.docFull: {@link DesktopConfig.installers}: the installer formats per OS, and what they say about the app.

members.name: macos
members.doc:
macOS installers built beside the `.app`: `"dmg"` (a drag-to-Applications disk image) and
`"pkg"` (a `productbuild` installer package for MDM / `installer -pkg`; signed with
`DENEXT_INSTALLER_IDENTITY`, a "Developer ID Installer" identity). Default `["dmg"]`.

members.name: linux
members.doc:
Linux installers: `"tar.gz"` (the bundle directory), `"deb"` (built by denext, no tool),
`"rpm"` (needs `rpmbuild`), `"appimage"` (needs `appimagetool`). Default `["tar.gz", "deb"]`.

members.name: windows
members.doc:
Windows installers: `"msi"` (per-user by default, per-machine with `ALLUSERS=1`; needs WiX 5,
`wix`, on a Windows host) and `"zip"` (the bundle directory). Default `["msi"]`.

members.name: publisher
members.doc:
Who publishes the app: the MSI Manufacturer (Add/Remove Programs), the `.deb` Maintainer
(`"Name <email>"` there) and the `.rpm` Vendor. Default: the app name.

members.name: description
members.doc: One line describing the app, for the package managers. Default `"<name> desktop application"`.

symbols.name: DesktopLinuxConfig
symbols.doc: DesktopConfig.linux: Linux launch settings of the packaged app.
symbols.docFull: {@link DesktopConfig.linux}: Linux launch settings of the packaged app.

members.name: requireSandbox
members.doc:
Refuse to start where the CEF backend would run web content without Chromium's sandbox: no
unprivileged user namespaces and no usable `chrome-sandbox` helper, as for a tarball or an
AppImage on Ubuntu 23.10 and later (the `.deb` / `.rpm` install the helper setuid root). The
app then prints one line (`laufey: this app requires the Chromium sandbox (requireSandbox),
…`) and exits with status 78 before the runtime loads. Default `false`: the app starts
unsandboxed there and `appCapabilities().sandbox` reads `"off"`. The package scripts write it
to the Linux bundle's `laufey-launch.json` (`"requireSandbox": true`), where
`LAUFEY_REQUIRE_SANDBOX=0` cannot turn it off. The WebView backend ignores it. Needs denext's
pinned runtime. `denext desktop doctor --linux` says which sandbox this machine allows.

symbols.name: DesktopMacosConfig
symbols.doc: DesktopConfig.macos: the macOS provisioning profile and entitlements.
symbols.docFull: {@link DesktopConfig.macos}: the macOS provisioning profile and entitlements.

members.name: provisioningProfile
members.doc:
The provisioning profile (`.provisionprofile`) to embed, relative to the project or absolute:
a Developer ID profile for the App ID `<TeamID>.<desktop.app.identifier>` that grants every
restricted entitlement in {@link entitlements}. `DENEXT_PROVISIONING_PROFILE` overrides it for
one run (a profile is account-specific: keep it out of the repository). The package script
checks it before building (its App ID, team, expiry, and that it grants each restricted
entitlement), embeds it as `Contents/embedded.provisionprofile`, and adds the
`com.apple.application-identifier` / `com.apple.developer.team-identifier` entitlements macOS
matches it by. Needs a real signing identity (`DENEXT_CODESIGN_IDENTITY`) of the same team.

members.name: entitlements
members.doc:
Entitlements signed into the app, e.g.
`{ "com.apple.developer.associated-domains": ["webcredentials:example.com"] }`. Merged over
the `DENEXT_ENTITLEMENTS` plist when both are set (these win). A restricted entitlement
(`com.apple.developer.*`, `com.apple.application-identifier`, `keychain-access-groups`) needs
{@link provisioningProfile}.

members.name: userActivityTypes
members.doc:
The user activity types the app continues (Handoff from another device, a Spotlight result):
reverse-DNS names, written to the bundle's `NSUserActivityTypes` by the package script. A type
`setUserActivity` (in `denext/desktop/app`) sets must be listed here for
`onUserActivityContinued` to receive it.

symbols.name: DesktopMediaCaptureConfig
symbols.doc: desktop.capabilities.microphone / camera options.
symbols.docFull: `desktop.capabilities.microphone` / `camera` options.

members.name: usageDescription
members.doc:
What macOS shows when it asks the user for the device (`NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` /
`NSCameraUsageDescription`). Default: "<app name> uses your microphone." / "… camera.".

symbols.name: DesktopPasskeysConfig
symbols.doc: desktop.capabilities.passkeys options.
symbols.docFull: `desktop.capabilities.passkeys` options.

members.name: rpIds
members.doc:
The relying-party IDs (`"example.com"`) the app may request. Required: an empty list allows
none (enforced natively and failing closed; `denext doctor` flags it), and no default allows
any.

symbols.name: DesktopShellConfig
symbols.doc: The shell desktop capability's scoped options (an allowlist per action).
symbols.docFull: The `shell` desktop capability's scoped options (an allowlist per action).

members.name: openExternal
members.doc: URL schemes `openExternal` may hand to the system browser (e.g. `["https:", "mailto:"]`).

members.name: openPath
members.doc: Allow `openPath` (open a path with its default app).

members.name: reveal
members.doc: Allow `reveal` (show a path in the file manager).

members.name: trash
members.doc: Allow `trash` (move a path to the OS trash).

members.name: openPathAllowExtensions
members.doc:
File extensions `openPath` may open despite its executable/script denylist — bare, no
leading dot, case-insensitive (e.g. `["py", "sh"]`). By default `openPath` refuses
programs, scripts and launchers, because the OS default handler would RUN them; list an
extension to opt back in when you trust the handler for that type. Ignored unless
`openPath` is true; `reveal` and `trash` never execute, so they are unaffected.

symbols.name: DesktopSidecarConfig
symbols.doc: One DesktopConfig.sidecars entry: a backend the app runs and supervises (the data form of defineSidecar from denext/desktop, whose runDesktop({ sidecars }) also takes functions and a bootstrap value).
symbols.docFull:
One {@link DesktopConfig.sidecars} entry: a backend the app runs and supervises (the data form of
`defineSidecar` from `denext/desktop`, whose `runDesktop({ sidecars })` also takes functions and a
`bootstrap` value).

members.name: name
members.doc: A unique name: lower-case letters, digits and `-` (`"server"`).

members.name: run
members.doc: What runs: a module in a worker of the app's runtime, or a program (exactly one of them).

members.name: args
members.doc: Arguments (`process.argv.slice(2)`, or the program's argv); `{port}` becomes the port.

members.name: env
members.doc: Environment variables (a module sidecar's own `process.env` copy; a program's environment).

members.name: loginShellEnv
members.doc:
Start it with the user's login-shell environment (macOS, Linux): `$SHELL` runs once per launch
as a login + interactive shell and its `PATH` (ahead of the inherited one) and any `keys` are
laid under {@link env}, so a backend opened from the Dock finds Homebrew / nvm / asdf tools. A
failure or a shell slower than `timeoutMs` (default 3 000 ms) logs a warning and keeps the
inherited environment. Only this sidecar sees them; never `DENO_*` / `DENEXT_*`.

members.name: cwd
members.doc: A program's working directory (relative to the app's data folder, or absolute).

members.name: port
members.doc: A loopback port: `"auto"` picks a free one at launch (kept across restarts), or a number.

members.name: portEnv
members.doc: The environment variable the port is published under (default `PORT`).

members.name: secrets
members.doc:
Values only the sidecar sees (`denextSidecar.secrets`, or a program's first stdin line), never
in its environment or argv; `"$random"` is 32 random bytes, new each launch.

members.name: ready
members.doc: When it counts as ready; every check given must pass (none: once started).

members.name: restart
members.doc: When an ended sidecar is started again, and how fast.

members.name: shutdown

joins every Space on macOS, and stays off the taskbar and Alt-Tab on Windows and Linux.

members.doc:

members.name: visibleOnAllWorkspaces
overlay
members.doc:
Make the window a desktop overlay surface on Linux Wayland: where the compositor has
wlr-layer-shell (KDE Plasma, wlroots compositors such as Sway and Hyprland, COSMIC; not GNOME)
the window is a layer surface above every other window, on every workspace, with no taskbar
entry, placeable, and with `focusable: false` never focused; that is the only way to get those
on Wayland, where an ordinary window can't ask for them. An ordinary window elsewhere (every
other OS, GNOME, X11, a missing `libgtk-layer-shell`; `windowCapabilities().layerShell` says).
Creation-time (written to `.deno-desktop/app.json` `initialWindow.overlay`); needs denext's Deno
Desktop runtime 3.0.0-denext.7 or later (ignored with a warning before). Default `false`.

members.name: proxy
members.doc:
How the CEF window reaches the network (runtime 2.9.7-denext.20): `"system"` (the default) uses
the OS proxy configuration, WPAD and PAC files included, and the runtime starts resolving it as
the window is created; `"direct"` uses no proxy at all, so a slow WPAD / PAC lookup never holds
the page's requests (its Live WebSocket to the loopback relay included) at startup. Choose
`"direct"` only for an app whose users never need a proxy. The package scripts write it to the
Windows bundle's `laufey-launch.json` (`"proxy"`); `denext desktop run` / `dev` pass it as
`LAUFEY_PROXY`. A proxy switch on the app's own command line wins. The WebView2 backend and
macOS / Linux ignore it.

symbols.name: disableTotp
symbols.doc: Remove a user's TOTP factors — and their backup codes when no other verified factor remains. A no-op for a user without one. Callers must have proved a fresh factor first — see the /mfa/disable endpoint.
symbols.docFull:
Remove a user's TOTP factors — and their backup codes when no other verified factor remains.
A no-op for a user without one. Callers must have proved a fresh factor first — see the
`/mfa/disable` endpoint.

It is also the **administrator's recovery** for a factor no configured `secret` opens any
more (a `secret` replaced rather than rotated, or an altered row): such a user can't pass a
TOTP check, so without a backup code or a passkey with user verification they can't reach
`/mfa/disable` themselves, and `enrollTotp` keeps answering `already_enrolled` — by design,
since a pending (password-only) session may enroll and must not be able to replace a factor.
Verify the user's identity out of band, call this, and they enroll again.
