symbols.name: sqliteAuthAdapter
symbols.doc: Build the durable AuthAdapter on Deno's built-in node:sqlite: every method group (users, accounts, verification tokens, credentials, API tokens, MFA, native app sessions, passkeys, account deletion) plus a sessions store over the **same** database handle and an idempotent close().
symbols.docFull:
Build the durable {@link ./adapter.ts | AuthAdapter} on Deno's built-in `node:sqlite`:
every method group (users, accounts, verification tokens, credentials, API tokens, MFA,
native app sessions, passkeys, account deletion)
plus a `sessions` store over the **same** database handle and an idempotent `close()`.

Ids are `crypto.randomUUID()` unless the caller supplies one; emails are matched
case-insensitively and whitespace-trimmed, and a unique index refuses a second user on
one address. The schema is created on first use and evolved additively on every open
(see the module doc). Single-node; TOTP secrets are stored as the MFA layer seals them.

members.name: idleTrim
members.doc:
Hand the memory a load burst leaves behind back to the OS once the server goes idle: after
the event loop has gone a second without work, a full V8 GC and then `malloc_trim(0)` (at most
once per idle period, 10 s apart, and after the first only when the resident memory grew by
16 MB). On by default for `denext start`, the `build --compile` executable, and the Docker
image and systemd unit the generators write, when they run on denext's Deno from runtime
3.0.0-rc.5 — never for `dev`, tests or jobs. It does anything on glibc Linux only. `false`
turns it off, as does `DENEXT_IDLE_TRIM=0` in the environment. See
{@link https://denext.dev/docs/deployment-targets#idle-memory-trim}.

members.name: limits
members.doc:
Process resource limits for the production server, enforced by denext's Deno from runtime
3.0.0-rc.2 (`--max-memory`, `--max-cpu-time`, `--max-time`). Applied where the production
server starts: `denext start` (on the process it starts), baked into the `build --compile`
executable, and written into the Docker image's command and the systemd unit's `ExecStart` —
never for `dev`, tests or `denext job` (a compiled executable enforces them on whatever it
runs, `./app job` included). Each limit ends the whole process with its own exit code, for
a supervisor (Docker's restart policy, systemd's `Restart=`) to start it again. Best-effort
guardrails, not a security boundary: subprocesses are not counted. On stock Deno they are not
applied (a warning says so). See
{@link https://denext.dev/docs/deployment-targets#resource-limits}.

members.name: tls
members.doc:
Serve HTTPS directly, without a proxy in front: the certificates and the host names each
serves. The certificate and key files' paths come from the environment variables each entry
names (`certFileEnv`, `keyFileEnv`), never from the config, and are read when the server
starts. One certificate serves every name, on any Deno. Several pick one per connection by
the name the client asks for (SNI), which needs denext's Deno from runtime 3.0.0-denext.3 and
`"unstable": ["net"]` in `deno.json`; elsewhere the server refuses to start and says why.
Applies to `denext start` and a `build --compile` server, never to `dev`. See
{@link https://denext.dev/docs/deployment-targets#https-without-a-proxy}.

members.name: memory
members.doc:
The main thread's JavaScript heap limit: a number of megabytes, or a size string with a
binary `k` / `m` / `g` unit (`"512m"`, `"2g"`); at least 32 MB. Over it the process exits
with code 137 (`Memory limit exceeded`). Workers have their own heaps, and memory outside the
heap (`ArrayBuffer`s, native code) is not counted.

members.name: cpuSeconds
members.doc:
The process's CPU time budget, user + system across every thread, in whole seconds (at least
1), counted from the server's start: once spent the process exits with code 152 (`CPU time
limit exceeded`). A long-running server spends it over its whole life.

members.name: deadlineSeconds
members.doc:
Wall-clock lifetime in whole seconds (at least 1), idle time included: the process exits with
code 124 (`Time limit exceeded`) when it is reached — a scheduled restart under a supervisor.

symbols.doc: Create a supervisor: it starts its children in order, restarts a crashed one with exponential backoff (and, per strategy, the siblings that depend on it), gives up after more than intensity restarts within period — failing to its own supervisor, or at the top to the app's error reporting — and stops them in reverse order on shutdown.

Create a supervisor: it starts its children in order, restarts a crashed one with exponential
backoff (and, per `strategy`, the siblings that depend on it), gives up after more than
`intensity` restarts within `period` — failing to its own supervisor, or at the top to the
app's error reporting — and stops them in reverse order on shutdown.

Restart semantics, not isolation: children share the process, the heap and the event loop.

symbols.doc: Observe a channel's publishes on the SERVER: every payload published to key on any instance — through the installed transport, decoded, in seq order per instance — until the returned disposer runs. The seam a plugin uses to bridge channel pushes into another protocol (a GraphQL subscription in @denext/graphql, an SSE stream, a queue) without a second event bus. Survives setChannelTransport (re-binds to the new transport).

Observe a channel's publishes on the SERVER: every payload published to `key` on any
instance — through the installed transport, decoded, in `seq` order per instance — until
the returned disposer runs. The seam a plugin uses to bridge channel pushes into another
protocol (a GraphQL subscription in `@denext/graphql`, an SSE stream, a queue) without a
second event bus. Survives `setChannelTransport` (re-binds to the new transport).

Not authorization: `authorize` gates socket SUBSCRIBERS; a server-side tap sees every
publish to the key. A tap that serves a viewer goes through `tapChannelAuthorized` (from
`denext/server`), which runs the channel's `authorize` for that viewer first.

Dependency-free: the symbol comes from denext's own ISO/IEC 18004 encoder (byte mode, Reed–Solomon error correction, the smallest version that fits, the lowest-penalty mask), and the markup is a single <path> with no script and no external reference, safe to inline under a strict CSP.
symbols.docFull:
Render the `otpauth://` provisioning URI {@linkcode totpAuthUri} (or `enrollTotp`) returns as
a QR code, as SVG markup — for an authenticator app to scan. Dependency-free: the symbol comes
from denext's own ISO/IEC 18004 encoder (byte mode, Reed–Solomon error correction, the
smallest version that fits, the lowest-penalty mask), and the markup is a single `<path>` with
no script and no external reference, safe to inline under a strict CSP.

The URI carries the TOTP secret: render it only on the page that enrolls the factor, never in
a cached response, a log or a URL.

symbols.name: unstable_cache
symbols.signature: unstable_cache<A, R>(fn: (...args: A) => Promise<R> | R, keyParts?: string[], options?: CacheOptions): (...args: A) => Promise<R>
symbols.doc: Wrap an async data-loading function in a cross-request cache with an optional TTL and tags (Next.js unstable_cache). Results are keyed by keyParts plus the call arguments. Tags propagate to the enclosing page render, so revalidateTag purges both the data and any page that read it.
symbols.docFull:
Wrap an async data-loading function in a cross-request cache with an optional
TTL and tags (Next.js `unstable_cache`). Results are keyed by `keyParts` plus
the call arguments. Tags propagate to the enclosing page render, so
{@link revalidateTag} purges both the data and any page that read it.

Nesting follows Next.js 16. Called inside a `"use cache"` (or `"use cache: private"`)
function, the call's `tags` reach the outer entry — `revalidateTag` on one of them drops the
outer entry too — and its `revalidate` caps the outer entry's revalidate (the minimum wins,
unless the outer body sets `cacheLife()` itself); a stale hit is refreshed in the foreground
there, so the outer entry never stores a stale value. Called inside another `unstable_cache`
loader the cache is bypassed (the outer entry holds the result). A `"use cache"` function
called inside a loader keeps its tags and lifetime to itself.

params.name: keyParts
params.doc: Extra key segments distinguishing this cache from others.

symbols.returns: A wrapper returning cached (or freshly computed) results.

symbols.name: updateAuthSession
symbols.doc: Read the session **and** slide its expiry forward when session.updateAge has elapsed — the explicit version of what GET {basePath}/session, requireAuth and requireSession() do for you. Call it from a Server Action or a route.ts handler (anywhere the response has not been sent yet); the refreshed cookie rides that response. In a streamed Server Component use auth instead — a Set-Cookie written after the headers flush is dropped silently. A session due to slide whose user is an SSO user is ended instead (its identity provider is that user's only way in).
symbols.docFull:
Read the session **and** slide its expiry forward when `session.updateAge` has elapsed
— the explicit version of what `GET {basePath}/session`, {@link requireAuth} and
`requireSession()` do for you. Call it from a Server Action or a `route.ts` handler

symbols.name: updateTag
symbols.doc: **Read-your-writes** tag invalidation for use inside a Server Action (Next.js 16 updateTag). Unlike revalidateTag, it expires the tag **immediately and synchronously for the rest of this request**: a later cache read in the same action whose entry carries tag recomputes, so the acting user sees their own write right away. It also hard-purges the store (for other requests/replicas) and records the tag so the client router can refresh the affected content.
symbols.docFull:
**Read-your-writes** tag invalidation for use inside a Server Action (Next.js 16
`updateTag`). Unlike {@link revalidateTag}, it expires the tag **immediately and
synchronously for the rest of this request**: a later cache read in the same
action whose entry carries `tag` recomputes, so the acting user sees their own
write right away. It also hard-purges the store (for other requests/replicas) and
records the tag so the client router can refresh the affected content.

Outside a request context it degrades to a plain {@link revalidateTag} purge.

symbols.name: verifyEmail
symbols.signature: verifyEmail(config: AuthConfig, input: { email: string; token: string }): Promise<VerifyEmailResult>
symbols.doc: Redeem an email-verification token and mark the address verified (emailVerified, epoch seconds, through adapter.updateUser). Fires emailVerified.
symbols.docFull:
Redeem an email-verification token and mark the address verified (`emailVerified`,
epoch seconds, through `adapter.updateUser`). Fires `emailVerified`.

Unlike a first magic-link / one-time-code sign-in, this does **not** retire the
account's password or revoke its sessions. In the normal register → verify → sign-in
flow the password was set by the very person now proving the mailbox, so wiping it
would break that flow; and verifying signs nobody in, so the mailbox owner gains no
access here. The residual risk is a victim confirming an account someone else
registered with their address — it then counts as verified (a later OAuth sign-in with
that address links to it) — so word the mail to say that ignoring it is safe.

params.name: input
params.doc: The address and the presented token.

symbols.returns: { ok: true, user } with the verified user, or { ok: false, error: "invalid_token" } for any failure (a wrong, spent or expired token; an address whose account is gone). Throws only when the adapter lacks the token group.

symbols.name: verifyPassword
symbols.signature: verifyPassword(password: string, stored: string, options?: HashPasswordOptions): Promise<boolean>
symbols.doc: Verify a password against a hash produced by hashPassword. The comparison is constant-time (timingSafeEqual), and a malformed/unsupported stored value — an empty column, a legacy format, a corrupted row — returns false rather than throwing, so an authorize callback can't leak a stack trace or a 500. That rejection still runs a full scrypt derivation, so an unknown account takes as long to reject as a wrong password for a known one (no user-enumeration timing oracle).
symbols.docFull:
Verify a password against a hash produced by {@linkcode hashPassword}. The comparison
is constant-time (`timingSafeEqual`), and a malformed/unsupported `stored` value —
an empty column, a legacy format, a corrupted row — returns `false` rather than
throwing, so an `authorize` callback can't leak a stack trace or a 500. That rejection
still runs a full scrypt derivation, so an unknown account takes as long to reject as
a wrong password for a known one (no user-enumeration timing oracle).

params.name: options
params.doc: The cost this deployment hashes at — pass the SAME options hashPassword was given (scryptHasher does). It is used only for the equal-work rejection of a missing/malformed stored value: a real comparison always uses the parameters embedded in the stored string. Omitting it on a deployment that raised the cost makes an unknown account reject measurably faster than a known one.

symbols.returns: true only when the password matches.

symbols.name: verifyRevenueCatWebhook
symbols.doc: Verify a RevenueCat webhook request and parse its event.
symbols.docFull:
Verify a RevenueCat webhook request and parse its event.

It compares the request's `Authorization` header with `options.authorization` in constant
time, then reads (at most `maxBodyBytes`) and parses the JSON body, checking that the event
has an `id`, a `type` and an `app_user_id`. It rejects with a {@linkcode RevenueCatWebhookError}
whose `status` is the answer to give (401, 400, 413).

RevenueCat retries a delivery that does not get a 200 within 60 seconds: answer quickly,
deduplicate on `event.id`, and fetch the subscriber from RevenueCat's REST API when you need
the full current state rather than the event's snapshot.

params.name: options
params.doc: The expected Authorization value and the body limit.

symbols.returns: The parsed body (api_version and the typed event).

symbols.docFull:
Verify an HTTP-POST-binding SAML 2.0 Response and return its Assertion's claims.

Checks, in order: well-formed strict XML (no DOCTYPE); a samlp:Response root with status
Success; exactly one Assertion or EncryptedAssertion in the whole document, a direct child of
the Response, and an EncryptedID only as its Subject's identifier; unique IDs; the Response signature, when present, BEFORE
anything is decrypted (so it covers the cipher text); an EncryptedAssertion decrypted with
`sp.encryptionKey` and its content parsed by the same strict parser (no DOCTYPE, exactly one
Assertion, IDs unique across the outer document and the decrypted one); every signature
present verifies with a configured certificate and at least one is present (the Assertion's
when `requireSignedAssertion`); Destination; Issuers; a bearer SubjectConfirmation for this
ACS URL; the Subject's one NameID or EncryptedID (decrypted only now, after the signature
over it verified, by the same rules as an EncryptedAssertion); Conditions and
AudienceRestriction; the AuthnStatement session window; InResponseTo; and finally the replay
cache. Claims are read only from the verified element objects.

symbols.name: verifyTotp
symbols.signature: verifyTotp(secret: string, code: string, options?: TotpVerifyOptions): Promise<TotpVerifyResult>
symbols.doc: Verify a TOTP code (RFC 6238 over RFC 4226 HOTP, HMAC-SHA-1) against a base32 secret, accepting any step within ±window of the current one. Whitespace in the code is stripped ("123 456"); anything else malformed — non-digits, the wrong length, a secret that isn't base32 — is { ok: false }, never a throw. Every candidate step is computed and compared in constant time; the loop never exits early on a match.
symbols.docFull:
Verify a TOTP code (RFC 6238 over RFC 4226 HOTP, HMAC-SHA-1) against a base32 secret,
accepting any step within ±`window` of the current one. Whitespace in the code is
stripped (`"123 456"`); anything else malformed — non-digits, the wrong length, a
secret that isn't base32 — is `{ ok: false }`, never a throw. Every candidate step is
computed and compared in constant time; the loop never exits early on a match.

This does NOT stop replay: pass the returned `step` to the adapter's `claimTotpStep`.

symbols.name: withDirectConnection
symbols.signature: withDirectConnection(pooled: SqlClient, direct: SqlClient, owns: { pooled?: boolean; direct?: boolean }): DirectPairedClient
symbols.doc: Pair a pooled client (a PgBouncer in transaction mode, say) with a direct connection to the same database — Prisma's directUrl. Queries and transactions go to pooled; what needs a session of its own goes to direct: listen() (LISTEN / NOTIFY), reserve() (a session-level advisory lock, a temporary replication slot), and denext's migrations and their locks (sessionClient). close() closes the ones owns names.
symbols.docFull:
Pair a pooled client (a PgBouncer in transaction mode, say) with a direct connection to the
same database — Prisma's `directUrl`. Queries and transactions go to `pooled`; what needs a
session of its own goes to `direct`: `listen()` (LISTEN / NOTIFY), `reserve()` (a session-level
advisory lock, a temporary replication slot), and denext's migrations and their locks
({@linkcode sessionClient}). `close()` closes the ones `owns` names.

```ts
const sql = withDirectConnection(
  postgresClient(Deno.env.get("DATABASE_URL")), // the pooler
  postgresClient(Deno.env.get("DATABASE_DIRECT_URL")), // the server itself
);
```

symbols.name: act
symbols.doc: act(callback) — the React test helper. Runs callback, flushes all pending state updates and effects synchronously, and returns a thenable so both sync and async usage work.
symbols.docFull:
`act(callback)` — the React test helper. Runs `callback`, flushes all pending
state updates and effects synchronously, and returns a thenable so both sync
and async usage work.

Like React's, the returned promise settles only once the work the callback set off
has gone quiet: after the callback (and its promise) it yields a macrotask and flushes
again, repeating while that turn rendered, committed or queued effects. So an
un-awaited promise chain started inside `act` — an async click handler whose
`.then` sets state — has committed by the time `await act(...)` returns.

members.name: dedupe
members.doc:
Share one in-flight fetch between concurrent GET/HEAD calls with equal path, params,
query, body, and headers (default true). Mutations are never deduped. In the browser the
in-flight table is per client instance; during SSR it is per request (never shared across
requests), and off outside a request.

members.name: batch
members.signature: batch?: boolean | { maxItems?: number; mutations?: boolean; forwardHeaders?: readonly string[] }
members.doc:
Coalesce the calls made in one tick into a single `POST /_denext/api-batch` (default true;
`{ maxItems }` caps a batch, default 20). Reads (GET/HEAD) run concurrently on the server;
mutations (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) each run alone, in the order they were called, with their
route's CSRF checks — `{ mutations: false }` sends them as their own requests.
`{ forwardHeaders: ["x-tenant"] }` lets calls carrying those headers ride too, each item with
its own value (the server must list the same names in `apiBatch.forwardHeaders`; credential,
framing and proxy headers never ride). A read with any other custom header or a body, a
mutation with a header other than `x-csrf-token` or a forwarded one, or a call with
`batch: false` always goes alone; a single pending call skips the batch framing entirely.

members.name: fetch
members.doc: The `fetch` to use (default: the global; a seam for tests and custom transports).

members.name: auth
members.doc:
Bearer authentication for a client pointed at a remote `base` (a Capacitor shell calling its
server): every call carries `Authorization: Bearer <getToken()>`, and a `401` is retried
ONCE after `refresh()` — concurrent 401s share a single refresh. Pass `nativeSession(…)`
(native session mode) or your own provider. Batching is off for an authenticated client
(the batch endpoint is same-origin only).

symbols.doc: Run callback as a low-priority "transition": the callback runs synchronously (like React), but any state updates it triggers are scheduled at transition priority — flushed after the reconciler yields to the browser, so urgent updates and paint/input happen first. Without the client scheduler it just runs the callback. The transition render is time-sliced and interruptible: a higher-priority (sync) update abandons the in-flight transition and restarts it (see the Async transitions guide: /docs/rendering#async-transitions).
symbols.docFull:
Run `callback` as a low-priority "transition": the callback runs synchronously
(like React), but any state updates it triggers are scheduled at transition
priority — flushed after the reconciler yields to the browser, so urgent updates
and paint/input happen first. Without the client scheduler it just runs the callback. The transition render is time-sliced and interruptible: a
higher-priority (sync) update abandons the in-flight transition and restarts it
(see the Async transitions guide: /docs/rendering#async-transitions).

An **async** callback (`startTransition(async () => { await x; setState() })`) is
supported: the transition stays active across the `await`, so updates scheduled
after it still land at transition priority. By default denext entangles by a time
window while the returned promise is pending; enable `asyncContext` in
`denext.config.ts` to scope by transition identity instead, so an unrelated urgent
update in that window keeps its priority (see the Async transitions guide /
KNOWN-LIMITATIONS).

With revealOrder="forwards" a boundary stays in its fallback until every boundary before it has revealed ("backwards" reverses; "together" holds all until the last resolves). tail="collapsed" shows only the next boundary's fallback, "hidden" shows none.
symbols.docFull:
`React.SuspenseList` — coordinates the reveal order of sibling `<Suspense>`
boundaries. With `revealOrder="forwards"` a boundary stays in its fallback until
every boundary before it has revealed (`"backwards"` reverses; `"together"` holds
all until the last resolves). `tail="collapsed"` shows only the next boundary's
fallback, `"hidden"` shows none.

Reveal ordering is enforced on the **client** (and in streaming SSR). During
buffered server rendering every boundary has already resolved, so order is moot.

Return a callback that always sees the latest committed props/state — React 19.2's
`useEffectEvent`. Use it for the "event" part of an Effect that should not itself be a
dependency (so the Effect doesn't re-run when the handler's closure changes).

As in React, the handler it forwards to is swapped in when the render commits (before any
layout or passive effect runs), not while rendering, so a render that never commits leaves
the previous one in place; and calling it during a render throws. Its identity is stable
(React's is not guaranteed to be — don't list it as an Effect dependency either way).

symbols.name: dispatchReducer
symbols.signature: dispatchReducer(fiberId: number, hookIndex: number, action: unknown): boolean
symbols.doc: Dispatch an action to a useReducer cell live, driving the component's own dispatch (so the reducer runs and a re-render schedules exactly as the app would). Distinct from setHookState: a reducer's updater expects an *action*, not the next value. Returns whether the cell was found and is a reducer.
symbols.docFull:
Dispatch an action to a `useReducer` cell live, driving the component's own dispatch
(so the reducer runs and a re-render schedules exactly as the app would). Distinct
from {@link setHookState}: a reducer's updater expects an *action*, not the next value.
Returns whether the cell was found and is a reducer.

symbols.name: enableRenderReasons
symbols.doc: Begin tracking why each component renders — install the commit hook and, when tracking was off, clear any prior data. The panel enables this when its "why did this render" view is on; the first commit after enabling seeds the baseline (so reasons appear from the next render onward). No-op in production.
symbols.docFull:
Begin tracking why each component renders — install the commit hook and, when tracking
was off, clear any prior data. The panel enables this when its "why did this render"
view is on; the first commit after enabling seeds the baseline (so reasons appear from
the next render onward). No-op in production.

**Refcounted.** Each caller takes one hold and releases it with exactly one
{@link disableRenderReasons}. Enabling while another holder is already tracking keeps
the accrued history instead of clearing it — otherwise opening and closing the DevTools
panel would wipe what the MCP bridge's `denext_why_render` reports.

symbols.name: getBoundaryTimings
symbols.doc: The per-Suspense-boundary timeline — a LIVE merge of two sources: the swap runtime's real-time reveal marks (window.__denextBoundaries, populated as each hole lands, in dev) and the end-of-stream #__denext_boundary_timing island (authoritative server resolve times, present once the stream finishes). So the panel shows a boundary the instant it reveals (client reveal + the template's data-dnx-ms server time), then settles to the island's rounded server time. Empty in production / on a non-streamed page / before any boundary reveals.

members.doc:
The variable the hook call was bound to (`count`), breadcrumbed through custom-hook
expansions (`useAuth › count`) — a hook declared in the same module or bound by a static
relative import, up to three levels deep. Present only when the dev metadata
resolved (see {@link InspectNode.hooksNamed}), this cell's call is knowable, and the call
was bound to something.

members.name: hook
members.doc:
The hook that produced this cell (`useState`), breadcrumbed likewise
(`useAuth › useState`). Present only when the dev metadata resolved and this cell's call
is knowable. A composite's extra cells (e.g. the memo behind `useTransition`) carry the
hook without a name, as do the cells an opaque custom hook (a package's) took.

members.name: debug
members.doc:
The `useDebugValue` label recorded after this cell during the last render — its
`format` applied now, lazily (a throwing formatter reads `"<format threw>"`). A call
takes no cell, so it rides the row of the cell it FOLLOWS: for the idiomatic call at
the end of a custom hook, that hook's last cell. Several calls there read as an array.
Absent when none was recorded (always, in production).

symbols.name: setPropOverride

symbols.doc: Override a component's prop live — pin key to value and re-render it (the live companion to setHookState). The override persists across the component's own re-renders until clearPropOverrides. fiberId comes from the most recent getInspectorTree. Returns whether the fiber was found.

Override a component's prop live — pin `key` to `value` and re-render it (the live

symbols.name: setRefValue
symbols.signature: setRefValue(fiberId: number, hookIndex: number, value: unknown): boolean

symbols.name: act
symbols.doc: act(callback) — the React test helper. Runs callback, flushes all pending state updates and effects synchronously, and returns a thenable so both sync and async usage work.
symbols.docFull:
`act(callback)` — the React test helper. Runs `callback`, flushes all pending
state updates and effects synchronously, and returns a thenable so both sync
and async usage work.

Like React's, the returned promise settles only once the work the callback set off
has gone quiet: after the callback (and its promise) it yields a macrotask and flushes
again, repeating while that turn rendered, committed or queued effects. So an
un-awaited promise chain started inside `act` — an async click handler whose
`.then` sets state — has committed by the time `await act(...)` returns.

symbols.name: createTestApp
symbols.doc: Build an in-process request handler for a real project directory — **no build step, no socket**. It renders Server Components, runs Server Actions and middleware.ts, and reads cookies/sessions, exactly as production does, but it ships no client bundle — so it drives the **JavaScript-disabled** path your app must support. The handler keeps one PageCache, so revalidate-based ISR is exercised across successive requests. Pair it with createTestClient.
symbols.docFull:
Build an in-process request handler for a real project directory — **no build
step, no socket**. It renders Server Components, runs Server Actions and
`middleware.ts`, and reads cookies/sessions, exactly as production does, but it
ships no client bundle — so it drives the **JavaScript-disabled** path your app
must support. The handler keeps one `PageCache`, so `revalidate`-based ISR is
exercised across successive requests. Pair it with {@linkcode createTestClient}.

The `plugins` in the project's `denext.config.ts` run as they do under `denext dev`: their
prepare steps once, their route synthesizers over the scanned routes, and their request
handlers for what the App Router does not match — so a Pages Router app
(`@denext/pages-router`) or a plugin-served route answers here too. Their build steps run as
well, and the files they emit are served. `jobs/` is registered (`runJob` works) and
`services/` is started, as `denext start` does ({@linkcode TestAppOptions} turns each off).
Call `close()` (or `await using`) to stop the services and run the plugins' teardowns; it
also cancels the response bodies the test never read, as a server does when the client goes
away (an unread body keeps the request's deadline timer running). Each call gets its own
plugin set.

```ts
import { createTestApp, createTestClient } from "@denext/denext/testing";
import { runJob } from "@denext/denext/server";
await using app = await createTestApp("./");
const client = createTestClient(app);
await runJob("cleanup");
```

reconnect — unless the channel keeps a `history`: then `since` replays what was missed, each
payload reaches `onMessage`, and a reconnect resumes from the last cursor.

symbols.doc: Boot the deferred half of resumability: install delegated qrl dispatch (so serialized data-dnx-h handlers run without hydration), then register every island wrapper for deferred per-island hydration. Boot the deferred half of resumability: install delegated qrl dispatch (so
serialized `data-dnx-h` handlers run without hydration), then register every
island wrapper for deferred per-island hydration. The generated Flight entry
dynamically imports and calls this only when a page carries lazy islands or
resumable handlers, so non-resumable apps bundle none of it.

params.name: eager
params.doc: Soft-navigation re-boot. On the initial load islands are *deferred* (server HTML adopted, hydration runs per strategy). After a soft nav the retained root reconciled each island wrapper **empty** (it is a foreign host in the route Flight), so there is no server DOM to adopt and no benefit to deferring — each island is mounted immediately from its own Flight, rendering its content and wiring it up.

params.name: islandsIn
params.doc: Soft-nav islands (from the Flight-nav payload). When given, used directly instead of re-reading #__denext_islands from the DOM.

The desktop request handler: the `onRequest` escape hatch, the token-gated local endpoints,
then — when `devProxy` is set (`denext desktop dev` only) — the reverse proxy to `denext dev`
for EVERYTHING else; otherwise the backend proxy, the export's static assets (`no-store`), the

it to `Deno.serve`.

forwarded to the dev server, even in live-reload mode.

The permissions every packaged desktop binary needs regardless of capabilities, and which the
per-capability flags widen rather than replace:
- `--allow-net=127.0.0.1,localhost`: `runDesktop` binds loopback and any `spa.proxy` targets a
  loopback backend, so the distributed binary can't reach the wider network.
- `--allow-read` (broad): serve the embedded `out/` AND the per-user OS app-support directory —
  a path only known on the end-user's machine, so it can't be baked; the runtime's fs/sqlite
  caps confine what the page can actually reach.
- `--allow-env` (broad): `PORT` plus the app's own environment.

symbols.name: desktopBuildFlags
symbols.signature: desktopBuildFlags(config: unknown, os: DesktopOs, options?: DesktopBuildFlagOptions): string[]
symbols.doc: The full --allow-* flag list to bake into the deno desktop binary for os — the least-privilege replacement for -A in the package scripts — derived from the WHOLE project config, not just desktop.capabilities (deriving from capabilities alone would starve the non-capability runtime features: an audit found the updater, openAuthSession and a non-loopback proxy all broke). On top of DESKTOP_BASELINE_FLAGS it adds: - the enabled capabilities' run / ffi / sys exactly (the real least-privilege wins), and a single broad --allow-write when any capability writes (a per-user path can't be baked; the runtime cap layer confines it); an unscoped --allow-sys when a capability needs it (clipboard, global shortcuts, launch at login, notifications) or desktop.app.deepLinks declares a scheme (claiming it back needs it): the pinned runtime refuses those with NotCapable under a partial --allow-sys=<names>; - a non-loopback spa.proxy target's host, MERGED into the single --allow-net (Deno keeps only the last --allow-net, so every host is one flag), and so are full-app self-update's hosts (desktop.update.manifestUrl's, desktop.update.ui.feedUrl's and desktop.update.hosts), and desktop.update.ui adds the broad --allow-write its overlay needs. With netSplit (the pinned runtime, 3.0.0-rc.2 or later) the network grant is baked by direction instead: --allow-net-connect takes those outbound hosts, loopback and extraPermissions.netConnect, --allow-net-listen only loopback and extraPermissions.netListen (any port: the app's server picks one at launch), and extraPermissions.net / a sidecar's net go to both; - desktop.extraPermissions — the escape hatch for what the catalog can't see: the updater's feed host (net) and data dir (write), an extension's own run/ffi, etc. It is UNIONED in, and --regenerate-scripts preserves it because it lives in the config, not the script. symbols.docFull:
The full `--allow-*` flag list to bake into the `deno desktop` binary for `os` — the
least-privilege replacement for `-A` in the package scripts — derived from the WHOLE project
config, not just `desktop.capabilities` (deriving from capabilities alone would starve the
non-capability runtime features: an audit found the updater, `openAuthSession` and a non-loopback
proxy all broke). On top of {@linkcode DESKTOP_BASELINE_FLAGS} it adds:
- the enabled capabilities' `run` / `ffi` / `sys` exactly (the real least-privilege wins), and a
  single broad `--allow-write` when any capability writes (a per-user path can't be baked; the
  runtime cap layer confines it); an unscoped `--allow-sys` when a capability needs it
  (clipboard, global shortcuts, launch at login, notifications) or `desktop.app.deepLinks`
  declares a scheme (claiming it back needs it): the pinned runtime refuses those with
  `NotCapable` under a partial `--allow-sys=<names>`;
- a non-loopback `spa.proxy` target's host, MERGED into the single `--allow-net` (Deno keeps only
  the last `--allow-net`, so every host is one flag), and so are full-app self-update's hosts
  (`desktop.update.manifestUrl`'s, `desktop.update.ui.feedUrl`'s and `desktop.update.hosts`), and
  `desktop.update.ui` adds the broad `--allow-write` its overlay needs. With `netSplit` (the
  pinned runtime, 3.0.0-rc.2 or later) the network grant is baked by direction instead:
  `--allow-net-connect` takes those outbound hosts, loopback and `extraPermissions.netConnect`,
  `--allow-net-listen` only loopback and `extraPermissions.netListen` (any port: the app's server
  picks one at launch), and `extraPermissions.net` / a sidecar's `net` go to both;
- `desktop.extraPermissions` — the escape hatch for what the catalog can't see: the updater's
  feed host (`net`) and data dir (`write`), an extension's own `run`/`ffi`, etc. It is UNIONED
  in, and `--regenerate-scripts` preserves it because it lives in the config, not the script.
A capability's `read`/`env` is dropped (already broad in the baseline); a capability's `net`
(only `downloadToFile`'s `*`) is dropped too — per-host download access is an `extraPermissions`
grant, never `*` baked in.

members.name: onPageLoad

Called when a window starts a NEW top-level page load (a reload or a navigation): the page
that owned any per-page state is gone, so release it (keep-awake holds, open handles). Errors
are logged, never surfaced. The same idea as the mobile native views' teardown on navigation.
It is called for the main window's page loads, with `"main"`, and — only when
{@linkcode DesktopCapability.perWindow} is set — for every other window's too, with its id.

symbols.name: DesktopCapabilityMethod
symbols.doc: One capability method: an optional input schema (validated before the handler), an optional output schema (strips the result before it reaches the page, in production too), the Deno permissions it needs, an optional per-method timeout, and the handler that runs in the Deno process.
symbols.docFull:
One capability method: an optional input schema (validated before the handler), an optional
output schema (strips the result before it reaches the page, in production too), the Deno
permissions it needs, an optional per-method timeout, and the handler that runs in the Deno
process.

Input inference for the PAGE flows from `input`/`output` (read by `denext/desktop/client`'s
typed proxy). The HANDLER receives `args` typed as `unknown` (the bridge has already validated it
against `input`); read fields off it or cast it to the input schema's output type INSIDE the
handler — do not annotate the `args` parameter with a narrower type, as a handler assigned to
`(args: unknown) => …` cannot narrow it (parameter contravariance).

members.name: input
members.doc: Validates the page's arguments; a mismatch is a `validation` error before the handler runs.

members.name: output
members.doc: Strips the handler's result to the declared shape before it reaches the page.

members.name: permissions
members.doc: The Deno permissions this method needs (drives least-privilege packaging + `doctor`).

members.name: timeoutMs
members.doc:
How long the handler may run before the bridge answers `timeout` and aborts `ctx.signal`.
A number of ms, or `false` to wait as long as it takes (a native dialog the user is reading).
Defaults to the bridge's default (30 s).

members.name: runOnMainThread
members.doc:
Call a native function on the app's UI thread (the thread AppKit, Win32 windows and GTK objects
belong to) and resolve with its pointer-sized return value as an unsigned `bigint`
(meaningless for a `void` function). `fn` is a C function `void* fn(void* context)`: a
`Deno.UnsafeFnPointer`, a `Deno.UnsafeCallback`, or a pointer (from `Deno.dlopen(...)` through
`Deno.UnsafePointer.of`); it is called with `context` (default `null`). The call is queued
behind the UI work already posted and never runs on the calling thread.

**Full trust**: this is FFI. The app needs `--allow-ffi` (grant it in
`desktop.extraPermissions`), and a wrong pointer or signature crashes the app. A
`Deno.UnsafeCallback` runs on the JavaScript thread while the UI thread waits for it, so it must
not wait for the UI thread itself.

Over `Deno.desktop.runOnMainThread`, so it needs denext's pinned Deno Desktop runtime
(2.9.7-denext.6 or later): elsewhere it rejects with a {@linkcode DesktopCapError} whose code is
`unsupported`. It also rejects, without calling `fn`, once the app is quitting.

params.name: fn
params.doc: The native function to call on the UI thread.

params.name: context
params.doc: The pointer passed to fn (default null).

members.returns: fn's return value as an unsigned bigint.

symbols.doc: Throw this from a capability handler to answer the page with a specific error code and a SAFE message. The bridge puts code, the message and any data into the { ok: false, error } envelope at status (default 400). Never encode an absolute path, environment value or stack into the message — it crosses to the page. The code "unavailable" is RESERVED (it means the capability/method is not enabled, which makes the page fall back to its web path); use another code for a real failure.

symbols.name: desktopDevProxyDecision
symbols.signature: desktopDevProxyDecision(devUrl: string | undefined, lan: boolean, execPath: string, devBuild?: boolean): DesktopDevProxyDecision
symbols.doc: Decide whether runDesktop enters live-reload PROXY mode, enforcing the loopback rule at RUNTIME rather than trusting the env (invariant: a release build never proxies to a remote origin). Pure + testable. Proxy mode requires ALL of: - a devUrl (the DESKTOP_DEV_URL_ENV value); - execPath being the deno CLI (isDenoCliExecPath), or devBuild (the mark only a denext desktop dev build compiles in) — a packaged app IGNORES the env, so an inherited/hostile env cannot turn a shipped window into a proxy; - a parseable URL whose host is loopback — OR non-loopback WITH lan (the DESKTOP_DEV_LAN_ENV opt-in that only desktop dev --lan sets). allowNonLoopback is true only in that LAN case, and injectToken there requires the dev server's per-run session token on the URL (desktop dev --lan puts it there), so the window's page gets its bridge only from a dev server that gates its other peers. A blocked case returns { proxy: false, refused } so the caller can log why and serve static.
symbols.docFull:
Decide whether `runDesktop` enters live-reload PROXY mode, enforcing the loopback rule at
RUNTIME rather than trusting the env (invariant: a release build never proxies to a remote
origin). Pure + testable. Proxy mode requires ALL of:
- a `devUrl` (the {@linkcode DESKTOP_DEV_URL_ENV} value);
- `execPath` being the `deno` CLI ({@linkcode isDenoCliExecPath}), or `devBuild` (the mark only a
  `denext desktop dev` build compiles in) — a packaged app IGNORES the env, so an
  inherited/hostile env cannot turn a shipped window into a proxy;
- a parseable URL whose host is loopback — OR non-loopback WITH `lan` (the
  {@linkcode DESKTOP_DEV_LAN_ENV} opt-in that only `desktop dev --lan` sets). `allowNonLoopback`
  is true only in that LAN case, and `injectToken` there requires the dev server's per-run
  session token on the URL (`desktop dev --lan` puts it there), so the window's page gets its
  bridge only from a dev server that gates its other peers.
A blocked case returns `{ proxy: false, refused }` so the caller can log why and serve static.

symbols.signature: type DesktopDevProxyDecision = { readonly proxy: false; readonly refused?: string } | { readonly proxy: true; readonly target: string; readonly allowNonLoopback: boolean; readonly injectToken: boolean }
symbols.doc: The live-reload proxy decision from the env + the running binary — see desktopDevProxyDecision.
symbols.docFull: The live-reload proxy decision from the env + the running binary — see {@linkcode desktopDevProxyDecision}.

symbols.name: desktopIncludeArgs
symbols.doc: The extra args a scaffolded packaging script must add so the packaged binary embeds every module the app loads at runtime, and loads each one from the binary, never from the build machine's disk:
symbols.docFull:
The extra args a scaffolded packaging script must add so the packaged binary embeds every module
the app loads at runtime, and loads each one from the binary, never from the build machine's
disk:

- `--include <path>` per `desktop.capabilities.extensions` module — otherwise the app launches
  but the runtime fails to load the extension ("Module not found"), since `--include out` only
  bundles the export;
- `--import-map <.deno-desktop/import-map.json>` when deno.json's import map has an absolute
  local target (`"denext/desktop": "file:///…"`): a compiled binary resolves such a target to the
  build machine's path, so a relocatable copy of the map is written and used instead.

Reads the project's `denext.config.ts` and deno.json next to `entryUrl` (a `scripts/` script →
`../`), like {@linkcode desktopPackageFlags}; a project with neither gets `[]`.
symbols.returns: ["--include", path, …, "--import-map", file], ready to splice into the deno desktop argv.

symbols.doc: The deno desktop flags a build on denext's pinned Deno Desktop runtime (or a local runtime build) gets, given the env resolveDesktopRuntimeEnv resolved for it. A runtime before 3.0.0-rc.5 gets --unstable-no-legacy-abort, which it keeps from the compiled app's metadata (from 2.9.7-denext.21), so the app's server aborts request.signal only when a response is not delivered and prints no Deno.serve legacy-behavior notice on its first request, as under denext start and a build --compile binary. From 3.0.0-rc.5 that is the runtime's default, so it gets none. The stock runtime (an empty env) gets none either: it ignores the setting. A flag already in denoFlags (desktop.denoFlags) is not repeated.
symbols.docFull:
The `deno desktop` flags a build on denext's pinned Deno Desktop runtime (or a local runtime
build) gets, given the env {@linkcode resolveDesktopRuntimeEnv} resolved for it. A runtime before
`3.0.0-rc.5` gets `--unstable-no-legacy-abort`, which it keeps from the compiled app's metadata
(from 2.9.7-denext.21), so the app's server aborts `request.signal` only when a response is not
delivered and prints no `Deno.serve` legacy-behavior notice on its first request, as under
`denext start` and a `build --compile` binary. From `3.0.0-rc.5` that is the runtime's default,
so it gets none. The stock runtime (an empty env) gets none either: it ignores the setting. A
flag already in `denoFlags` (`desktop.denoFlags`) is not repeated.

symbols.name: desktopSignWindows
symbols.signature: desktopSignWindows(files: readonly string[], deps?: DesktopSignWindowsDeps): Promise<boolean>
symbols.doc: Authenticode-sign files with the certificate in DENEXT_WINDOWS_CERT (password DENEXT_WINDOWS_CERT_PASSWORD), else the certificate store's DENEXT_WINDOWS_CERT_THUMBPRINT, timestamped by DENEXT_SIGN_TIMESTAMP_URL, batched a few dozen files per signtool sign call. Without a certificate nothing is signed and a warning says so. With one but without signtool (off Windows, or no Windows SDK) it throws instead of letting the run ship an unsigned app: the script's --no-sign builds unsigned on purpose. The password, which signtool takes only as /p, never reaches its command line: a password-protected .pfx is imported into the user's certificate store for the run and signed with by thumbprint (withSigntoolCertificate).
symbols.docFull:
Authenticode-sign `files` with the certificate in `DENEXT_WINDOWS_CERT` (password
`DENEXT_WINDOWS_CERT_PASSWORD`), else the certificate store's `DENEXT_WINDOWS_CERT_THUMBPRINT`,
timestamped by `DENEXT_SIGN_TIMESTAMP_URL`, batched a few dozen files per `signtool sign` call.
Without a certificate nothing is signed and a warning says so. With one but without `signtool`
(off Windows, or no Windows SDK) it throws instead of letting the run ship an unsigned app: the
script's `--no-sign` builds unsigned on purpose. The password, which signtool takes only as
`/p`, never reaches its command line: a password-protected `.pfx` is imported into the user's
certificate store for the run and signed with by thumbprint ({@linkcode withSigntoolCertificate}).

symbols.name: injectDesktopGlobal
symbols.signature: injectDesktopGlobal(html: string, token: string | null, beacon?: boolean, preload?: string, preloadKey?: string, page?: DesktopPageGlobals): Promise<string>
symbols.doc: Inject globalThis.__denext = { desktop: true, token } as an inline <script> immediately after the opening <head> (falling back to after <body>, then to a prepend). The value is JSON.stringify-escaped. When beacon is set, the boot-confirm beacon (BOOT_BEACON_JS) is appended to the SAME script so one CSP hash covers both. When the shell carries a hash-based CSP meta, its script-src is extended with this script's 'sha256-…' so the script survives a strict policy.
symbols.docFull:
Inject `globalThis.__denext = { desktop: true, token }` as an inline `<script>` immediately
after the opening `<head>` (falling back to after `<body>`, then to a prepend). The value is
`JSON.stringify`-escaped. When `beacon` is set, the boot-confirm beacon ({@linkcode
BOOT_BEACON_JS}) is appended to the SAME script so one CSP hash covers both. When the shell
carries a hash-based CSP meta, its `script-src` is extended with this script's `'sha256-…'` so
the script survives a strict policy.

`preload` (the bundled `desktop.preload`, already inline-safe) is injected as a SECOND inline
script right after the global — so it runs after `__denext` exists and before any page script —
with its own hash. It is injected only together with the token (a top-level document); the
caller additionally limits it to the memory world. With a `preloadKey`, the preload is framed by
two more scripts that set `globalThis.__denextPreloadKey` before it and delete it after (even
when the preload throws), so only code the preload runs synchronously can read the key — the
proof `denext/desktop/clerk` presents for its Clerk-only session binding. The setting script
removes its own element as it runs, so the key cannot be read back from `document.scripts`.

`page` adds what the page needs from the runtime ({@linkcode DesktopPageGlobals}): the
WebSocket relay URL and — both only with the token — the web `Notification` shim, appended to the
same script (one CSP hash) so it is in place before any page script runs.

A package run's setup: the app name, the installer plan (`--format`, else
`desktop.installers.<os>`, else the defaults), `dist/`, unless `--no-export` the static export
(`deno task export`), then the `.deno-desktop/app.json` + `compile.include` + deno.json

deno.json; a made-up version or identifier is warned about).

The sync runs AFTER the export, right before `deno desktop` reads deno.json: under
`denext desktop package` the CLI's CSS re-exec keeps a backup of the project's deno.json while the
script runs, and the export's own CLI restores that backup when it starts, which undid a sync
done before it (the bundle then took deno.json's identifier, not `denext.config.ts`'s).

symbols.name: resolveDesktopCapabilities

symbols.doc: Resolve config.desktop.capabilities into the capability objects the bridge serves, plus the app-support directory the runtime hands to handlers.
symbols.docFull:
Resolve `config.desktop.capabilities` into the capability objects the bridge serves, plus the
app-support directory the runtime hands to handlers.

The built-in bridge capabilities are mapped (`device`, `fs`, `sqlite`, `shell`, `keepAwake`,
`secureStore`, `dialogs`, `clipboard`, `passkeys`, `notifications`, `contextMenu`,
`globalShortcuts`, `launchAtLogin`, `updates`, and the `echo` diagnostic), plus any `extensions` module
paths; `auth-session` is a runtime endpoint (not a bridge cap) so it only sets
`authSessionEnabled`. A capability the running Deno Desktop runtime cannot serve answers
`unavailable` per call (the page uses its web path), never an error. A bad extension path IS an
error, and so is enabling a data-storing cap (`secureStore`/`fs`/`sqlite`) without a
`desktop.app.identifier` — both fail fast at launch.

params.doc: The project config, or .deno-desktop/config.json (its runtime slice, see DesktopRuntimeConfig); undefined yields no capabilities.

params.doc: The app id (for storage dirs) and the entry's import.meta.url (for extensions).

The deep-link schemes (`desktop.app.deepLinks`, lower-case; from {@link
resolveDesktopCapabilities}). Under denext's pinned runtime, links with these schemes reach the
page's `onDeepLink`, and they are the only schemes `openAuthSession` accepts as a callback.

members.name: pickedPaths
members.doc:
The per-launch picked-path set the `dialogs`/`fs`/`shell` capabilities share (from {@link
resolveDesktopCapabilities}); files the OS opens with the app become read-only handles in it.

members.name: window
members.doc:
The initial-window settings from `desktop.window` / `desktop.titleBar` / `desktop.backdrop` /
`desktop.minSize` / `desktop.maxSize` (from {@link resolveDesktopCapabilities}), applied to the
adopted window at launch. The size limits, title bar style and backdrop need denext's pinned
runtime; the stock runtime skips them with a warning.

members.name: app
members.doc:
`desktop.app`'s launch settings (from {@link resolveDesktopCapabilities}): `keepAlive` (the
app stays up with no window; default on with a tray) and `dock` (`false`: no macOS Dock icon).

members.name: configTray
members.doc: `desktop.tray` from the config (from {@link resolveDesktopCapabilities}); {@link tray} is laid over it.

members.name: tray
members.doc:
The tray icon the backend owns: created before the first page needs it, kept across page
reloads, reachable from every window (`getTray()` in `denext/desktop/app`) and from
{@linkcode DesktopRuntime.tray}. Its keys replace `desktop.tray`'s; the handlers run in the
backend, before the pages hear of a click. Setting a tray keeps the app alive with no window
unless `desktop.app.keepAlive` is `false`.

members.name: appDirs
members.doc:
The app's own folders (from {@link resolveDesktopCapabilities}): besides picked handles, the
only files the page may drag out of the window (`startFileDrag` in `denext/desktop/window`).

members.name: autoConfirmAppUpdate
sidecars
members.doc:
Backends the app runs and supervises next to its window ({@linkcode defineSidecar}): a module in
a worker of the app's own runtime, or a program. Laid over {@link configSidecars} by name (a
field set here replaces the config's), so `probe`, `bootstrap` and `secrets` can be functions.
They start once the window's server is up; {@linkcode DesktopRuntime.sidecar} controls one.

members.name: configSidecars
members.doc:
`desktop.sidecars` from the config (from {@link resolveDesktopCapabilities}); {@link sidecars}
is laid over it.

symbols.name: shouldInjectDesktopToken
symbols.signature: shouldInjectDesktopToken(request: Request, url: URL, trust: DesktopTrust, info?: DesktopServeInfo): boolean
symbols.doc: Whether the per-launch token may be injected into the document this request fetches: never on a request the runtime relayed from its loopback WebSocket relay (any local process can dial it, so its missing Origin / Sec-Fetch-Dest prove nothing); otherwise a TOP-LEVEL document only (Sec-Fetch-Dest, document when absent), so a subframe that declares itself gets the desktop global without the token. Absent stays document on purpose: engines send no Sec-Fetch-* to a scheme they don't treat as secure (WKWebView has no API to register one; the Fetch spec sends them only to potentially trustworthy URLs), so failing closed would strip the token from the page itself there. Where it is absent, a same-origin frame cannot be told from the page; the per-world rules below still refuse a request that names another origin. Then, per world: loopback — a LOOPBACK Host, so a DNS-rebinding Host gets no token; memory — the in-process memory transport and an Origin that is absent or exactly the app origin; refuse — never.
symbols.docFull:
Whether the per-launch token may be injected into the document this request fetches: never on
a request the runtime relayed from its loopback WebSocket relay (any local process can dial it,
so its missing `Origin` / `Sec-Fetch-Dest` prove nothing); otherwise a TOP-LEVEL document only
(`Sec-Fetch-Dest`, `document` when absent), so a subframe that declares itself gets the desktop
global without the token. Absent stays `document` on purpose: engines send no `Sec-Fetch-*` to a
scheme they don't treat as secure (WKWebView has no API to register one; the Fetch spec sends
them only to potentially trustworthy URLs), so failing closed would strip the token from the
page itself there. Where it is absent, a same-origin frame cannot be told from the page; the
per-world rules below still refuse a request that names another origin. Then, per world: loopback — a LOOPBACK `Host`, so a DNS-rebinding Host gets no token;
memory — the in-process memory transport and an `Origin` that is absent or exactly the app
origin; refuse — never.

symbols.name: SidecarDefinition
symbols.doc: One sidecar. Data-only fields can live in desktop.sidecars (denext.config.ts); probe, bootstrap and secrets as functions only in runDesktop({ sidecars }), which also overrides a config entry of the same name field by field.

members.name: name
members.doc: A unique name: lower-case letters, digits and `-` (`"server"`).

members.name: run
members.doc: What runs.

members.name: args
members.doc:
Arguments: the module's `process.argv.slice(2)`, or the program's argv. `{port}` is replaced
with the sidecar's port.

members.name: env
members.doc:
Environment variables. A module sidecar sees them in `process.env` (its own copy: the app's
environment is not changed); a program gets them on top of the app's environment.

members.name: loginShellEnv
members.doc:
Start it with the user's login-shell environment (macOS and Linux; nothing on Windows): an app
opened from the Dock or a desktop launcher inherits a minimal `PATH`, so a backend would not
find what Homebrew, nvm, asdf or mise installed (`git`, `node`, `codex`). Once per launch of the
app, when the first sidecar that sets it starts, the user's `$SHELL` runs as a login and
interactive shell and its `PATH` (ahead of the inherited one) and the `keys` asked for are laid
under this sidecar's {@linkcode env}. A shell that fails or takes longer than `timeoutMs`
(default 3 000 ms) logs a warning and the sidecar starts with the inherited environment. The
variables reach only the sidecars that set this, never the page or the app's own environment.
A module sidecar sees them in `process.env` (and so `node:child_process`); a program in its
environment, and a bare `run.exec` name is looked up on that `PATH`.

members.name: cwd
members.doc: A program's working directory (relative to the app's data folder, or absolute).

members.name: port
members.doc:
A loopback port for the sidecar: `"auto"` picks a free one at launch (kept across restarts), a
number is fixed. Published as `PORT` (see {@linkcode portEnv}), `{port}` in {@linkcode args},
`denextSidecar.port`, and to the page through `sidecarInfo`.

members.name: portEnv
members.doc: The environment variable the port is published under (default `PORT`).

members.name: secrets
members.signature: readonly secrets?: Readonly<Record<string, string>> | (() => Record<string, string> | Promise<Record<string, string>>)
members.doc:
Values the sidecar needs and nothing else may see: never in its environment or argv. A module
sidecar reads them from `denextSidecar.secrets`; a program from the first line of its stdin
(`{"name","port","bootstrap","secrets"}`). A value `"$random"` is replaced with 32 random bytes
(base64url), new on every launch of the app; a function (code only) computes them.

members.name: bootstrap
members.signature: readonly bootstrap?: unknown | ((info: SidecarInfo) => unknown | Promise<unknown>)
members.doc:
A JSON value handed to the sidecar at every start (`denextSidecar.bootstrap`, or the program's
first stdin line): what an Electron app passes on an extra file descriptor. A function (code
only) computes it per start.

symbols.name: SidecarRun
symbols.signature: type SidecarRun = { readonly module: string; readonly nodeModules?: string; readonly external?: readonly string[]; readonly entries?: readonly string[] } | { readonly exec: string }
symbols.doc: What runs: a module in the app's runtime, or a program.
symbols.docFull:
What runs: a module in the app's runtime, or a program.

`module` is relative to the project (`"./server/main.ts"`). Without `nodeModules` it is part of
the app's own module graph (resolved through the app's `deno.json`) and embedded as it is. With
`nodeModules` (a Node backend, e.g. `"apps/server/dist/bin.mjs"` and its package's
`node_modules`) denext bundles it at packaging, every npm import inlined, except the packages
with a native addon (`.node`) and those listed in `external`, which are copied whole beside the
bundle and loaded with `require`.

`exec` is a program path: absolute, a bare name found on `PATH`, or relative to the project
(`"./bin/server"`), which the package scripts copy into the app.

symbols.name: stripDesktopCredentials
symbols.doc: The request to forward to the dev server with the desktop credential removed: the per-launch x-denext-desktop-token header is dropped so it never reaches the dev server (invariant: the token gates the LOCAL endpoints only). A WebSocket upgrade is returned untouched — it cannot be reconstructed (Deno.upgradeWebSocket needs the original connection), a browser cannot set a custom header on a WS handshake, and proxyToBackend's WS bridge forwards only host/origin/cookie upstream, never the token. denext injects no desktop-specific cookie (the token lives in globalThis.__denext and this header only), so there is none to strip.
symbols.docFull:
The request to forward to the dev server with the desktop credential removed: the per-launch
`x-denext-desktop-token` header is dropped so it never reaches the dev server (invariant: the
token gates the LOCAL endpoints only). A WebSocket upgrade is returned untouched — it cannot be
reconstructed (`Deno.upgradeWebSocket` needs the original connection), a browser cannot set a
custom header on a WS handshake, and {@link proxyToBackend}'s WS bridge forwards only
`host`/`origin`/`cookie` upstream, never the token. denext injects no desktop-specific cookie
(the token lives in `globalThis.__denext` and this header only), so there is none to strip.

symbols.name: applyDesktopUpdate
symbols.doc: Promote the staged version to the active overlay and flip the "current" pointer atomically. Re-verifies the staged manifest (version + signature, the downgrade floor and the expiry) and re-hashes every staged file BEFORE the swap. The previous version dir is kept for rollback, the accepted sequence is recorded, every other staging folder is deleted, and the new version starts PENDING — desktopBooted must confirm it or the next resolveDesktopUiDir rolls it back.
symbols.docFull:
Promote the staged `version` to the active overlay and flip the "current" pointer atomically.
Re-verifies the staged manifest (version + signature, the downgrade floor and the expiry) and
re-hashes every staged file BEFORE the swap. The previous version dir is kept for rollback, the
accepted `sequence` is recorded, every other staging folder is deleted, and the new version
starts PENDING — {@linkcode desktopBooted} must confirm it or the next
{@linkcode resolveDesktopUiDir} rolls it back.

symbols.name: checkForDesktopUpdate
symbols.doc: Check the feed for a newer, fully-verified UI. Fetches ${feedUrl}/_denext/ota.json, validates its shape, RECOMPUTES the version and refuses a mismatch, VERIFIES the ECDSA signature, and refuses a non-monotonic sequence — all BEFORE reporting anything as available. symbols.name: confirmAppUpdate
symbols.doc: Confirm the running version after an update, once the app has shown it is healthy (its window loaded, its backend answered): the update is final, and the previous app is moved aside and deleted in the background (the call does not wait for the deletion). A no-op (false) when no update is pending, so it is safe to call on every launch. runDesktop calls it once the window has loaded unless desktop.update.autoConfirm is false.

symbols.docFull:
Install the staged update: start the swap helper and quit the app (Electron's
`quitAndInstall`). The helper waits for this process to exit, swaps the install, and relaunches
the new version, which `runDesktop` confirms once its window has loaded (or, with
`desktop.update.autoConfirm: false`, the app's own {@linkcode confirmAppUpdate} call).

The app's sidecars (`desktop.sidecars`) are ended first, so none holds the install open; to give
them their graceful shutdown, `await stopSidecars()` (from `denext/desktop`) before calling it.

symbols.name: openDesktopUi
symbols.doc: The UI the desktop runtime should serve this launch: the active overlay, re-verified, or only the bundled export (overlay: null). Serve the overlay's files through DesktopUiOverlay.read, which checks each one against the signed manifest when it is served, never straight from its folder; runDesktop({ updater }) does.
symbols.docFull:
The UI the desktop runtime should serve this launch: the active overlay, re-verified, or only
the bundled export (`overlay: null`). Serve the overlay's files through
{@linkcode DesktopUiOverlay.read}, which checks each one against the signed manifest when it is
served, never straight from its folder; `runDesktop({ updater })` does.

This is also the BOOT WATCHDOG. If the pointer is PENDING and a boot marker for the same
version already exists, the previous launch applied that version and never confirmed it (it
failed to boot), so it is ROLLED BACK — its sequence refused so it is not retried in a loop —
and the previous good version (or the bundle) is served. A pending version on its FIRST launch
is served with a fresh marker armed; {@linkcode desktopBooted} clears it. An overlay that fails
re-verification (a file changed, missing or added, a symbolic link, a manifest that no longer
verifies) is rolled back the same way and reported as `rejected`; one that cannot be read right
now (a permission or I/O error) is skipped for this launch only.

An overlay is tied to the bundled export it was installed over (`bundle.json`: the export's
stamped version, else its `index.html` hash). When the app itself was replaced — a full-app
update or a reinstall brings a different bundle — every overlay is dropped and the new bundle is
served, so a UI built for the old app never runs on the new one.

params.doc: The bundled export (the app's own UI).

members.name: version
members.doc: Lowercase hex SHA-256 over the sorted `"<path>\t<sha256>\n"` lines.

members.name: required
members.doc:
Whether the app should not let the user decline this UI (`denext ota manifest --required`).
A hint for the app's own update prompt; absent means `false`. Not part of the version.

members.name: notes
members.doc:
Release notes for the app's update prompt (`denext ota manifest --notes <text>`), at most
{@linkcode OTA_NOTES_MAX_LENGTH} characters. Not part of the version.

members.name: sequence
members.doc:
A release counter that only grows (`denext ota manifest --sign` stamps the current Unix time
in seconds; `--sequence <n>` sets it). The native plugin remembers the highest one it accepted
and refuses a lower one, or a manifest without one after that (code `downgrade`). A
non-negative integer no larger than `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. Not part of the version;
signed in the v2 payload.

members.name: minNative
members.doc:
The lowest native build number (iOS `CFBundleVersion`, Android `versionCode`) this UI runs on
(`denext ota manifest --min-native <n>`). An older app binary refuses it before downloading
(code `native_too_old`). A non-negative safe integer. Not part of the version; signed in the
v2 payload.

members.name: nativeFingerprint
members.doc:
The native fingerprint of the app binary this UI was built for (`denext ota manifest
--native-fingerprint <fp|auto>`, the value `denext mobile fingerprint` prints): 64 lowercase
hex digits. A binary that embeds a fingerprint (`denext mobile fingerprint --write`) refuses
a manifest carrying a different one before downloading (code `native_mismatch`); when either
side has none, the check is skipped. Not part of the version; signed in the v3 payload.

members.name: expiresAt
members.doc:
When the release stops being accepted, in Unix seconds (`denext ota manifest --expires-in
<days>` / `--expires-at <RFC 3339>`; a signed manifest gets 30 days unless one is given). At
or after it the native plugin, `checkForUiUpdate` and the desktop updater refuse the manifest
(code `expired`): re-sign it before then. Only with a `sequence`. Not part of the version;
signed in the v4 payload. A UI already installed keeps running past it: the expiry gates
installing (and reporting "current"), not serving.

members.name: platform
members.doc:
The target the export was built for (`ios`, `android`, `macos`, `windows`, `linux`): a shell
of another target refuses it (code `platform_mismatch`). Must match the export's
{@linkcode OTA_PLATFORM_PATH} stamp, which the version covers; the field is not signed, so a
shell also checks the stamp itself. Absent with no stamp: a `web` export every shell accepts
(`web` names no stamp, so it is never written here).

members.name: appId
members.doc:
The app the release is for (`denext ota manifest --app-id <id>`; a signed `spa.ota` export
and `denext ota manifest --sign` stamp the Capacitor `appId` on an `ios` / `android` export,
and `spa.ota` stamps `desktop.app.identifier` on a desktop one): the iOS bundle id, the
Android application id, or the Deno Desktop app identifier ({@linkcode isOtaAppId}). A shell
that knows its own id refuses another (code `app_mismatch`); an app that embeds a public key,
and a desktop overlay configured with `desktop.app.identifier`, also refuse a manifest
without one. Only with a `sequence`. Not part of the version; signed by `appSignature`.

members.name: signature
members.doc:
Standard (padded) base64 of the raw 64-byte `r‖s` ECDSA P-256 / SHA-256 signature over
{@linkcode otaSignaturePayload} (`denext ota manifest --sign <keyfile>`). An app whose binary
embeds a public key refuses a manifest without a valid one.

members.name: appSignature
members.doc:
Standard (padded) base64 of the raw 64-byte `r‖s` ECDSA P-256 / SHA-256 signature over
{@linkcode otaAppSignaturePayload} (the v5 format, which adds `appId` to what `signature`
covers), made with the same key. Written beside `signature` whenever a signed manifest has an
`appId`; a shell that requires the `appId` refuses a manifest without a valid one (code
`signature`).

symbols.name: DesktopErrorCode
symbols.doc: Why a desktop call failed:
symbols.docFull:
Why a desktop call failed:

- `unavailable`: not inside a Deno Desktop window, or the capability / method is not enabled
  in `desktop.capabilities` (the runtime's allowlist), or no runtime answered.
- `forbidden`: the runtime's gate refused the request (token, origin or content type).
- `validation`: the arguments did not match the method's input schema.
- `timeout`: no answer in time.
- `too_large`: the request body is over {@linkcode MAX_RPC_BODY_BYTES}.
- `bridge_error`: the runtime answered without the bridge envelope.

A capability may fail with its own codes too (`not_found`, `cancelled`, …).

symbols.name: DesktopErrorCode
symbols.doc: Why a desktop call failed:
symbols.docFull:
Why a desktop call failed:

- `unavailable`: not inside a Deno Desktop window, or the capability / method is not enabled
  in `desktop.capabilities` (the runtime's allowlist), or no runtime answered.
- `forbidden`: the runtime's gate refused the request (token, origin or content type).
- `validation`: the arguments did not match the method's input schema.
- `timeout`: no answer in time.
- `too_large`: the request body is over {@linkcode MAX_RPC_BODY_BYTES}.
- `bridge_error`: the runtime answered without the bridge envelope.

A capability may fail with its own codes too (`not_found`, `cancelled`, …).

symbols.name: onCloseRequested
symbols.doc: Ask before the window closes: its close button, Cmd+W / Alt+F4, or the app quitting (quitApp, Deno.desktop.quit(), the Quit item of a Windows tray menu). The handler gets a CloseRequestEvent whose reason says which ("close" or "quit"), like Electron's before-quit + close pair: a close-to-tray window hides on a close and lets a quit through. While a handler is registered the runtime holds every close and calls the handlers; the window closes (or the quit goes on) unless one returns (or resolves) false. A page that stops answering cannot keep the window open: a close requested again after 5 seconds without an answer goes through. Quitting from the macOS app menu (Cmd+Q) or a macOS tray menu's quit role ends the app at once and is not asked. Needs denext's pinned runtime (closeGuard in windowCapabilities); elsewhere the handler is never called and the window closes.

({@linkcode quitApp}, `Deno.desktop.quit()`, the Quit item of a Windows tray menu). The handler
gets a {@linkcode CloseRequestEvent} whose `reason` says which (`"close"` or `"quit"`), like
Electron's `before-quit` + `close` pair: a close-to-tray window hides on a close and lets a quit
through. While a handler is registered the runtime holds every close and calls the handlers; the
window closes (or the quit goes on) unless one returns (or resolves) `false`. A page that stops
answering cannot keep the window open: a close requested again after 5 seconds without an answer
goes through. Quitting from the macOS app menu (Cmd+Q) or a macOS tray menu's quit role ends the
app at once and is not asked. Needs denext's pinned runtime (`closeGuard` in

members.doc:
A desktop overlay surface (runtime 3.0.0-denext.6): on a Wayland compositor with
wlr-layer-shell (wlroots compositors, KDE Plasma, COSMIC) a layer above every window, on every

members.name: show
members.doc:
Show it once created (default `true`). With `false` it opens hidden (its page loads), to be
shown with the handle's `show()`; a runtime before 3.0.0-denext.6 may flash it first.

members.name: capabilities
members.doc:
The desktop capabilities its pages may call (default: all the app has; `window` always). Least
privilege for a trusted page that needs little, not a security boundary: every window shares
the app's origin, storage and launch token, so script in this window can still reach every
capability the app has (for example by calling the bridge as the main window). Never open
untrusted content in an app window because of a subset.

symbols.name: quitApp
symbols.doc: Quit the app, like Electron's app.quit(): the onBeforeQuit handlers and then the onCloseRequested ones (with reason: "quit") of every guarded window are asked first, so a handler that answers false keeps it running.
symbols.docFull:
Quit the app, like Electron's `app.quit()`: the {@linkcode onBeforeQuit} handlers and then the
{@linkcode onCloseRequested} ones (with `reason: "quit"`) of every guarded window are asked

symbols.returns: true when the app is quitting at once, false when a guarded window holds the quit (its handlers decide; the app quits once they let it go).

symbols.name: setIgnoreMouseEvents
symbols.signature: setIgnoreMouseEvents(ignore: boolean, options: { readonly forward?: boolean }): Promise<void>
symbols.doc: Let clicks go through the window to what is under it (Electron's setIgnoreMouseEvents). With forward, pointer moves still reach the page where the runtime can (clickThroughForward), so it can turn clicks back on over its own content. Without forward the window can never be clicked again, so that is refused (validation) unless the app has a tray icon to come back through. Needs a runtime with it (clickThrough in windowCapabilities).
symbols.docFull:
Let clicks go through the window to what is under it (Electron's `setIgnoreMouseEvents`). With
`forward`, pointer moves still reach the page where the runtime can (`clickThroughForward`), so
it can turn clicks back on over its own content. Without `forward` the window can never be
clicked again, so that is refused (`validation`) unless the app has a tray icon to come back
through. Needs a runtime with it (`clickThrough` in {@linkcode windowCapabilities}).

params.name: ignore

members.name: cookieEncryption
members.doc:
CEF's cookie store: `"os"` (encrypted with a key the OS keeps: Windows' DPAPI, the Linux
keyring, and from runtime 2.9.7-denext.20 a team-signed macOS app's own
`"<app id> Safe Storage"` keychain item) or `"basic"` (obfuscated with a fixed key, not
protected by the OS): an ad-hoc signed or unsigned macOS build, where CEF runs with Chromium's
mock keychain and its constant key, and Linux when the login keyring was locked with no one to
unlock it. `null` on the WebView backends.

members.name: badgeShows
members.doc:
Where the badge shows: `"dock"` (the macOS Dock tile), `"launcher-entry"` (Linux: a count on
the app's launcher, where a dock reads it: Ubuntu's dock, Dash to Dock, Plasma's task manager)
or `"title"` (a `"(N) "` prefix on the window titles: Windows, Linux without such a dock, and a
badge that isn't a number), as the runtime probed it (runtime 2.9.7-denext.11 and later).

members.doc: Linux, when `badgeShows` is `"title"`: why no launcher shows the count (the runtime's).

members.name: sandbox
members.doc:
CEF on Linux: the Chromium sandbox the window's web content runs in: `"namespace"`
(unprivileged user namespaces), `"setuid"` (the `chrome-sandbox` helper the `.deb` / `.rpm`
installs), `"chromium"` (on; the runtime's probe could not run, so Chromium picked the layer) or
`"off"` (neither: a tarball or AppImage on Ubuntu 23.10 and later, or root; see
`desktop.linux.requireSandbox`). `null` on other platforms and backends; `"unknown"` before
runtime 2.9.7-denext.12.

runtime 3.0.0-rc.1, where a Linux window signs in with a passkey through the browser.

members.signature: onClick(handler: (event: "click" | "doubleClick", detail: TrayMouseDetail | null) => void): () => void
members.doc:
Call `handler` on each click of the primary button (`"click"`) and each double click
(`"doubleClick"`), with the runtime's detail (button, modifiers, position, `double`; runtime
3.0.0-denext.6, else `null`). A right click is a `contextmenu` event ({@linkcode AppTray.on}).
Returns the unsubscribe.

members.name: on
members.signature: on(type: TrayEventType, handler: (detail: TrayMouseDetail | null) => void): () => void
members.doc:
Call `handler` on each `type` event, by its DOM name: `click` (the primary button), `dblclick`,
`contextmenu` (a right click), `auxclick` (a middle click), `mouseenter` / `mouseleave` (hover;
macOS, Windows). All but `click` / `dblclick` need runtime 3.0.0-denext.6 (`trayRightClick`,
`trayMiddleClick`, `trayHover` in {@linkcode appCapabilities}). Returns the unsubscribe.

symbols.name: DesktopErrorCode
symbols.doc: Why a desktop call failed:
symbols.docFull:
Why a desktop call failed:

- `unavailable`: not inside a Deno Desktop window, or the capability / method is not enabled
  in `desktop.capabilities` (the runtime's allowlist), or no runtime answered.
- `forbidden`: the runtime's gate refused the request (token, origin or content type).
- `validation`: the arguments did not match the method's input schema.
- `timeout`: no answer in time.
- `too_large`: the request body is over {@linkcode MAX_RPC_BODY_BYTES}.
- `bridge_error`: the runtime answered without the bridge envelope.

A capability may fail with its own codes too (`not_found`, `cancelled`, …).
