symbols.name: setActivationPolicy
symbols.doc: Set the app's macOS activation policy (Electron's app.setActivationPolicy): "regular" (a Dock icon and a menu bar), "accessory" (neither: a menu-bar app or a desktop companion) or "prohibited". Switching to regular also brings the app to the front, so a tray app can show a Dock icon only while it has a full window open. desktop.app.activationPolicy (or desktop.app.dock: false) sets the one the app starts in. Needs runtime 3.0.0-denext.6 (activationPolicy in appCapabilities); on an older runtime "regular" / "accessory" show / hide the Dock icon as setDockVisible does.
symbols.docFull:
Set the app's macOS activation policy (Electron's `app.setActivationPolicy`): `"regular"` (a
Dock icon and a menu bar), `"accessory"` (neither: a menu-bar app or a desktop companion) or
`"prohibited"`. Switching to regular also brings the app to the front, so a tray app can show a
Dock icon only while it has a full window open. `desktop.app.activationPolicy` (or
`desktop.app.dock: false`) sets the one the app starts in. Needs runtime 3.0.0-denext.6
(`activationPolicy` in {@linkcode appCapabilities}); on an older runtime `"regular"` /
`"accessory"` show / hide the Dock icon as {@linkcode setDockVisible} does.

Windows and Linux have no policy: there `"regular"` shows the main window's taskbar entry and the
others hide it, as `desktop.app.activationPolicy: "accessory"` hides it at launch.
symbols.returns: Whether it applied (false where the runtime can't hide a taskbar entry).

members.doc:
Also run the clerk-js instance any other Clerk React SDK creates in native mode — the one
`@clerk/nextjs`'s or `@clerk/react`'s `ClerkProvider` loads from the Frontend API and keeps at
`globalThis.Clerk` — the way `@clerk/electron/react`'s provider runs its bundled one: Frontend

`_is_native=1`), the JWT the API returns is saved, and `load()` gets `standardBrowser: false`
plus this bridge's OAuth transport. So the app's own `<ClerkProvider>` signs in on desktop
unchanged. `{ passkeys }` attaches a WebAuthn adapter (`passkeys` from
`@clerk/electron/passkeys`, over `window.__clerk_internal_electron_passkeys`, so with
`passkeys: true`). Leave it off with `@clerk/electron/react`'s provider, which does this itself.

social providers Clerk offers (Google, GitHub, Apple, Microsoft, Facebook, Discord, GitLab,

symbols.name: startClerkBrowserSignIn
symbols.signature: startClerkBrowserSignIn(clerk: ClerkLike, options: ClerkBrowserSignInOptions): Promise<{ createdSessionId: string }>
symbols.doc: Sign in through Clerk's hosted pages in the system browser and activate the session here: the protocol of @clerk/expo's useHostedAuth, over openAuthSession's custom-scheme flow. A fresh state and PKCE pair are made per call; the hosted-auth record is created with the S256 challenge, the callback must come back to redirectUrl with the same state, and its rotating_token_nonce is redeemed ONLY together with the verifier, which never leaves this page — so a callback intercepted by another app is useless to it.
symbols.docFull:
Sign in through Clerk's hosted pages in the system browser and activate the session here: the
protocol of `@clerk/expo`'s `useHostedAuth`, over `openAuthSession`'s custom-scheme flow. A
fresh `state` and PKCE pair are made per call; the hosted-auth record is created with the S256
challenge, the callback must come back to `redirectUrl` with the same `state`, and its
`rotating_token_nonce` is redeemed ONLY together with the verifier, which never leaves this
page — so a callback intercepted by another app is useless to it.

This is the passkey fallback when native passkeys answer `invalid_rp` (the RP's own domain in
the browser has its passkeys), and works for any sign-in method Clerk's hosted pages offer.

symbols.docFull:
Switch to the UI {@linkcode prepareUiUpdate} staged: the native side starts its trial,
arms the rollback watchdog (15 s of foreground time by default), points the webview at it
and reloads. The new page must
call {@linkcode otaBooted}, exactly as after {@linkcode checkForUiUpdate}.

On success the page reloads, so the returned promise does not settle; it resolves only
with a failure: `unsupported` off native (or with a plugin that predates staged updates),
or `error` when the native side refuses (`version` is not the staged one, a download or
trial is in progress, or the version was rolled back). It never throws.

Ask the user to authenticate with Face ID / Touch ID / a fingerprint (or, with

It resolves once the user is verified and rejects with a {@linkcode BiometricError}

`passcode-not-set`, `failed`, or `unsupported` outside the shell (there is no web fallback:
gate a web build's flow on {@linkcode isBiometricAvailable} first).

owner is here, and the app decides what that unlocks. See `secureStore.set(key, value,

members.name: callbackScheme
members.doc:
The custom URL scheme the provider redirects back to, without `://` (e.g. `"myapp"` for a
`myapp://auth/callback` redirect URI): lower-case letters, digits, `+`, `-` or `.` after a
letter. iOS catches it inside the sheet; Android receives it through the app's intent
filter for it (`denext mobile add auth-session --scheme myapp`). Ignored by the web popup,
whose redirect is an https page of this origin that calls {@linkcode completeAuthSession}.

members.name: preferEphemeral
members.doc:
Do not share cookies with the browser (`prefersEphemeralWebBrowserSession`), so no existing
provider login is reused and none is kept: iOS, and Deno Desktop on macOS when a custom-scheme
callback runs in the OS's auth session (which then also skips the "Wants to Use … to Sign In"
prompt). Ignored by the system browser (Android, Windows, Linux, the loopback flow). Default
`false`.

members.name: timeoutMs
members.doc:
Give up after this many ms with code `timeout`. Default: no limit (Deno Desktop: 5 minutes for
the loopback flow, 10 for a custom-scheme callback).

members.name: callbackPrefix
members.doc:
Custom-scheme callback (Deno Desktop, and the iOS / Android shell): where the callback lands
(`"myapp://auth/callback"`) when the URL's own `redirect_uri` is not a `callbackScheme` URL (a
provider that redirects through its own server first). It is matched exactly on scheme, host
and path; a callback elsewhere is refused.

members.name: pkce
members.doc:
PKCE (S256) is mandatory (the iOS / Android shell, the web popup, and Deno Desktop's
loopback and custom-scheme callbacks) unless this is `"not-applicable"`, for a provider that
binds the callback to the initiating client another way; then
{@linkcode AuthSessionOptions.reason} says how. Without PKCE another app that registers the
same callback scheme, or another local process that answers the loopback redirect, could take
the `code` and redeem it.

members.name: reason
members.doc: Why PKCE does not apply (required with `pkce: "not-applicable"`; kept with the session).

members.name: state
members.doc:
Custom-scheme callback (Deno Desktop, and the iOS / Android shell): the `state` the callback
must carry. When the URL itself carries a `state`, it is checked automatically (in the
callback's query or, on mobile, its fragment).

members.name: signal
members.doc:
Deno Desktop: aborting it cancels the session (`cancelled`). The system browser on Windows and
Linux reports no cancellation, so denext shows a Cancel button there (see
{@linkcode AuthSessionOptions.cancelOverlay}); wire your own to this instead if you hide it.

members.name: cancelOverlay
members.doc:
Deno Desktop, when the sign-in runs in the system browser (Windows and Linux, the loopback flow
everywhere, and runtimes without an OS auth session): while it waits, a small modal over the
app says "Finish signing in in your browser." with a Cancel button (Escape too), which ends the
session with `cancelled`, because the browser reports no cancellation and otherwise only
`timeoutMs` would. `false` hides it (render your own, wired to
{@linkcode AuthSessionOptions.signal}); `{ message, cancelLabel }` changes its text. Not shown
where the OS's auth session has its own Cancel (macOS), nor on iOS, Android or the web.

members.name: loopbackPort
members.doc:
Deno Desktop, loopback flow (an `http://127.0.0.1` / `localhost` / `[::1]` `redirect_uri`):
listen for the redirect on this fixed port instead of one the OS picks, for a provider that
only accepts its registered loopback redirect (`http://localhost:1455/auth/callback`). The
`redirect_uri` then keeps its host as written and must name this port or none. A port another
program holds rejects `port_in_use`. RFC 8252 §7.3 allows a fixed port; an ephemeral one is
still the better default, because a fixed port is easier for another local program to take
first. Ignored elsewhere.

symbols.name: checkForUiUpdate
symbols.doc: Check a server for a newer UI and, when it offers a different version, install it.
symbols.docFull:
Check a server for a newer UI and, when it offers a different version, install it.

1. Fetches `${baseUrl}/_denext/ota.json` (with `headers`, `cache: "no-store"` and a
   timeout) and validates its shape.
2. Asks the native `DenextOta` plugin for its {@linkcode OtaStatus}; if the manifest's
   version equals the running UI (`pending`, else `current`, else `bundled`), it returns
   `current` (as it does when the native side finds nothing to switch).
3. Otherwise the plugin downloads `${baseUrl}/<path>` for every file (copying files it
   already has by SHA-256), verifies each SHA-256 and size, switches the webview's web
   root to the new directory and reloads. The new page must call {@linkcode otaBooted}
   within the boot timeout (15 s of foreground time by default) or it is rolled back.

It never throws. Outside the native shell it resolves `{ kind: "unsupported" }` without
touching the network. One check runs at a time: a call made while another is in flight
gets that call's promise (and its options).

params.name: options
params.doc: Where the UI is served, plus headers, timeout and fetch.

symbols.name: checkPermission
symbols.doc: The current status of a permission, without prompting (see PermissionState for what each status means).
symbols.docFull:
The current status of a permission, without prompting (see {@linkcode PermissionState} for
what each status means).

In the iOS/Android shell it asks the plugin behind the permission (`Camera` for `camera` and
`photos`, `Geolocation` for `location`, `LocalNotifications` / `PushNotifications` for
`notifications`, `Contacts`, `Calendar`, and the biometric plugin for `biometrics`); on the
web (and for `microphone`, which the WebView itself asks for) the browser's Permissions /
Notifications API. In a Deno Desktop window with the `notifications` capability,
`notifications` is the OS's own setting. It rejects with a {@linkcode PermissionError} (`unsupported`) when nothing
here can answer: a plugin that is not installed and no browser API.

  local-notifications` or `push`, generation 3 of denext's `DenextSettings` plugin; it rejects in

  OS's notification centre still shows (runtime 2.9.7-denext.20), local ones the app scheduled
  through denext. On Linux, whose notification servers keep no list, the ones denext posted
  during this run whose time has come and that were not removed through denext: one the user
  dismissed is still listed, and one from an earlier run is not.
- Web: the open notifications `scheduleNotification` showed from this page, plus the service
  worker registration's (a web push's thread is its `data.threadId`).

symbols.name: downloadToFile
symbols.signature: downloadToFile(url: string, path: string, options?: DownloadToFileOptions): Promise<{ path: string }>
symbols.doc: Download a URL straight into a file (missing parent folders are created), with progress.
symbols.docFull:
Download a URL straight into a file (missing parent folders are created), with progress.

- Inside the native shell with denext's `DenextTransfer` plugin (`denext mobile add
  file-transfer`), the OS's background transfer service downloads it (a `URLSession`
  background session on iOS, WorkManager on Android): it carries on while the app is in the
  background, and {@linkcode pauseFileTransfer} / {@linkcode resumeFileTransfer} continue it
  where it stopped when the server allows a range. The body never passes through the WebView,
  and CORS does not apply.
- Inside the shell with only `@capacitor/filesystem` (`denext mobile add filesystem`), the
  plugin's native download (`downloadFile`), without progress. (A plugin without
  `downloadFile`, which it deprecates, gets `fetch(url)` and the plugin's `writeFile`.)
- In a Deno Desktop window with the `fs` capability (`denext desktop add fs`), the runtime
  fetches in the Deno process (with the request `headers`; CORS does not apply) and writes
  under the app's folder, with progress. {@linkcode fileTransfers} lists it and
  {@linkcode onFileTransfer} reports it; {@linkcode pauseFileTransfer} keeps the bytes so far
  and {@linkcode resumeFileTransfer} asks for the rest with a range request (a server that
  answers 200 starts it over); {@linkcode cancelFileTransfer} or aborting `signal` cancels it
  and drops the partial file. The runtime keeps the download's record across restarts, so
  {@linkcode fileTransfers} lists it after one and {@linkcode resumeFileTransfer} continues it
  from its partial file (one running at quit is listed as failed, resumable).
- Otherwise `fetch(url)` (CORS applies), its body streamed into the Origin Private File System
  with progress; a pause keeps the bytes so far, and a resume asks for the rest with a range
  request (a server that answers 200 starts it over). The bytes go to a part file in OPFS's
  `cache/.denext-part/` folder (hidden from `listDir`) that replaces the file only once the
  download is done, so a file already at `path` keeps its contents until then.
  {@linkcode cancelFileTransfer}, aborting `signal` or a failure ends it and deletes the part
  file, never the file it would have replaced. A reload forgets the transfer: downloading to
  the same file again starts over in the same part file. Without OPFS (no secure context), a
  download into a picked file or folder writes through the picked file's own writable stream,
  which swaps the bytes in only when the download is done (a cancel or a failure leaves the
  file as it was); such a download cannot pause ({@linkcode pauseFileTransfer} resolves
  `false`). An app-folder download needs OPFS.

params.doc: The file's path inside directory; no .. segments.

symbols.name: installKeyboardInset
symbols.doc: Keep a CSS custom property on document.documentElement (default --denext-keyboard-inset) equal to the px of the page the on-screen keyboard covers, so layout can lift a docked text field or a bottom bar above it: padding-bottom: var(--denext-keyboard-inset).
symbols.docFull:
Keep a CSS custom property on `document.documentElement` (default
`--denext-keyboard-inset`) equal to the px of the page the on-screen keyboard covers, so
layout can lift a docked text field or a bottom bar above it: `padding-bottom:
var(--denext-keyboard-inset)`.

In a browser and on Android it is
derived from `window.visualViewport` (`innerHeight - visualViewport.height -
visualViewport.offsetTop`, clamped at ≥ 0) and updated at most once per animation frame; it
stays `0px` where `visualViewport` is unavailable. In the iOS shell with `@capacitor/keyboard`
it follows the plugin's will-show / will-hide: the keyboard's height while it slides in over
the page, then `0` once the shell has resized the WebView (`resize: "native"`, the default),
`<body>` (`"body"`) or `ion-app` (`"ionic"`) around it, which the plugin does only after the
keyboard's animation; with `resize: "none"` it stays the keyboard's height. It is set to `0px`
immediately.

Pass it as `VirtualList`'s `keyboardInset` and a bottom-anchored list (`anchor="end"`) keeps
its last row above the keyboard from the moment the keyboard starts to open, in every resize
mode, with no jump when the shell's resize lands.

Several installs of the same property may coexist (e.g. two {@linkcode useKeyboardInset}
components); the property is removed when the last one is disposed. SSR-safe: without a
`document` it installs nothing.

params.name: opts
params.doc: { property }, the custom property to maintain.

symbols.returns: A dispose function that stops listening and, for the last install, removes the property.

symbols.name: installMomentumSafeScroll
symbols.doc: Keep iOS momentum scrolling alive while scroll-anchoring code corrects the scroll offset.
symbols.docFull:
Keep iOS momentum scrolling alive while scroll-anchoring code corrects the scroll offset.

In iOS WebKit (Safari, WKWebView, Capacitor) any programmatic scroll write during a touch
fling cancels the momentum instantly. Virtualized lists (LegendList, react-virtuoso,
TanStack Virtual) issue such writes while the user scrolls, to compensate for rows measured
taller or shorter than estimated, so a flick toward older content stops hard.

While a finger is down, and while a scroller is still flinging after it lifts,
`Element.prototype.scrollBy` / `scrollTo` / `scroll` and the `scrollTop` / `scrollLeft`
setters record the write as a pending delta instead of scrolling. The scroller's element
children get a CSS `translate` of minus that delta, so the picture is what the write would
have shown, and the getters return the real offset plus the delta, so a library reading back
the offset sees what it wrote. When the fling settles (`scrollend`, or `settleMs` without a
`scroll` event) or a new touch starts, the translate is removed and the real offset moves by
the delta in one synchronous step. Deferred targets are clamped to the scroll range, so
`el.scrollTop = el.scrollHeight` shows the bottom rather than blank space (`scrollHeight` /
`scrollWidth` read as if the children were not shifted). Outside a gesture every call goes
straight through; so do `behavior: "smooth"` calls (a smooth `scrollBy` applies the pending
delta first; a smooth `scrollTo` drops it, as its target is absolute) and `scrollIntoView`
(which first drops the pending delta of every scroller it moves).

Only element scrollers are deferred. The document scroller (`document.scrollingElement`,
`<html>`, `<body>`) is never shifted, and its writes, including `window.scrollTo`, always go
straight through. While a list is shifted, its children carry the `translate` composed with
their own computed `translate` (so Tailwind's `translate-*` classes keep their offset), and a
transformed child becomes the containing block of its `position: fixed` descendants and moves
its `position: sticky` headers with it until the fling settles. Documents inside iframes are
not covered: each has its own `Element.prototype`.

**denext's client runtime already installs it on iOS WebKit** (opt out with
`momentumSafeScroll: false` in `denext.config.ts`), so call this only from a page that does
not run on denext's runtime. By default it installs only on iOS/iPadOS WebKit, where the bug
exists; elsewhere, and without a DOM, it is a no-op. It is idempotent: while installed,
another call (whatever its options) returns the same uninstaller. Uninstalling applies any
pending delta and restores every patched `Element.prototype` member exactly.

params.name: options
params.doc: { force, settleMs }: install on every platform; the quiet period, in ms, that ends a fling where scrollend is unsupported (default 250; where scrollend is supported it ends the fling, with a 1 s idle fallback).

examples:
```ts
import { installMomentumSafeScroll } from "denext/mobile";
installMomentumSafeScroll(); // once, at client startup
```

symbols.doc: A <div> that makes room for the on-screen keyboard, like React Native's KeyboardAvoidingView: with behavior="padding" (the default) it adds the covered height to its bottom padding, with "height" it shrinks its height by it (from style.height, else 100%), and with "position" it moves up by it. keyboardVerticalOffset subtracts a fixed amount (a bottom bar the keyboard hides anyway).
symbols.docFull:
A `<div>` that makes room for the on-screen keyboard, like React Native's
`KeyboardAvoidingView`: with `behavior="padding"` (the default) it adds the covered height to
its bottom padding, with `"height"` it shrinks its height by it (from `style.height`, else
`100%`), and with `"position"` it moves up by it. `keyboardVerticalOffset` subtracts a fixed
amount (a bottom bar the keyboard hides anyway).

"Covered" is the part of the keyboard over the page's layout viewport, which is 0 where the
WebView has resized around the keyboard; the view then leaves layout alone. In the iOS shell
with `@capacitor/keyboard` it follows the keyboard's will-show / will-hide, animated over the
keyboard's own duration, so it lifts as the keyboard slides in; with `resize: "native"` (the
default), `"body"` or `"ionic"` the shell resizes the app only after the animation, and the
lift drops at once as that resize lands (no double lift), while with `resize: "none"` it
stays. On Android (the WebView resizes itself) and the web it follows the visual viewport
(see {@linkcode onKeyboardChange}). It renders without any avoidance during SSR.

symbols.docFull:
A `<div>` that rides on top of the on-screen keyboard: while the keyboard covers the page it
moves up by the covered height (a compositor-only `translateY`), and back down when the
keyboard hides. Place it at the bottom of the screen yourself (`position: fixed` /
`sticky`, `bottom: 0`); the view only adds the transform. This is a text field docked above
the keyboard: see the text-field recipe on /docs/mobile.

Like {@linkcode KeyboardAvoidingView} it follows only the part of the keyboard that covers the
page, so once the WebView has resized around the keyboard it stays put (the resize already
moved it); in the iOS shell it rides the keyboard while it slides in, before the shell's
resize lands. `offset` adds a fixed shift in each state.

How a call's arguments reach the native method and how its result comes back.

A typed client for your own native plugin `name`: the Capacitor plugin of that name inside
the iOS/Android shell, the desktop extension of that name in a Deno Desktop window, else
`null` (on the web, during SSR, or when the shell has no such plugin).

the plugin's events (`notifyListeners` natively, `emit` from a desktop extension). The
bridge is asynchronous, so always `await` a call. Calls pass one options object and resolve
with the plugin's result object (Capacitor's convention); pass `{ calls: "positional" }` for
React Native's positional arguments and `{ value }` unwrapping ({@linkcode NativeCallConvention}).

error (`unavailable` when the extension is not enabled).

symbols.name: NativeViewPlacement
symbols.doc: Where a native view is drawn relative to the WebView.
symbols.docFull:
Where a native view is drawn relative to the WebView.

- `"embed"` (iOS): inside the page's own layer tree, in the native scroll view WebKit makes for
  an `overflow: scroll` element (what `@capacitor/google-maps` does). The compositor moves,
  clips and transforms it with the page, and DOM overlays draw above it.
- `"under"`: behind a transparent WebView, seen through a transparent hole in the page. DOM
  drawn over the slot shows above it; every ancestor of the slot must be transparent there.
- `"over"`: above the WebView, clipped to the slot's visible part. Needs nothing from the page,
  but no DOM can draw over it: it hides while page content covers any part of it.

symbols.name: onAppResume
symbols.doc: Call cb each time the page returns to the foreground, with how long it was away in milliseconds.
symbols.docFull:
Call `cb` each time the page returns to the foreground, with how long it was away in
milliseconds.

It listens for `visibilitychange` (every browser and webview), `pagehide`/`pageshow`
(a back-forward-cache restore) and the `pause`/`resume` document events that Capacitor's
iOS shell fires on scene background/foreground. Whichever signal arrives first counts; the
others are deduplicated, so `cb` runs once per return. A subscription made while the page is
already hidden measures from the moment of subscribing.

The time away is wall-clock (`Date.now()`), not `performance.now()`: iOS's monotonic clock
stops while the device sleeps, which would under-report a phone left locked for an hour.
A backwards clock jump reads as `0`.

**The intended pattern** (the rule native apps commonly use): under 10 s away, the
connection is probably intact, so probe it (a ping, a cheap refetch); 10 s or more, assume
the OS froze the page and its sockets, so reconnect and refetch.

SSR-safe: without a `document` it subscribes to nothing and returns a no-op.

params.name: cb
params.doc: Called with awayMs, the time since the page was hidden.

symbols.name: onBack
symbols.doc: Register handler for the system back action, on top of the handlers already registered (a LIFO stack, like React Native's BackHandler). On a back action the newest handler runs first; returning true consumes it. When no handler consumes it, the default runs: history back when there is somewhere to go back to, else the app leaves the foreground (@capacitor/app's minimizeApp, exitApp where that is missing).
symbols.docFull:
Register `handler` for the system back action, on top of the handlers already registered
(a LIFO stack, like React Native's `BackHandler`). On a back action the newest handler runs
first; returning `true` consumes it. When no handler consumes it, the default runs: history
back when there is somewhere to go back to, else the app leaves the foreground
(`@capacitor/app`'s `minimizeApp`, `exitApp` where that is missing).

Where it applies:
- **Android shell**: the back button and back gesture. With `denext mobile add back` (the
  `DenextBack` plugin) the native callback is enabled only while a handler is registered, so
  without one the system's own predictive back-to-home animation plays. With only
  `@capacitor/app` it listens to its `backButton` event.
- **iOS shell**: nothing; there is no back button.
- **Web**: the browser's back button. While a handler is registered, a same-URL history
  entry sits on top of the page's, so back pops it and the handlers run. An unconsumed back
  then goes back for real. After a soft navigation the entry is re-added where the browser
  has the Navigation API; elsewhere register handlers on the page that uses them.

SSR-safe: without a `window` it registers nothing.

params.name: handler
params.doc: Returns true to consume the back action.

symbols.name: onBackProgress
symbols.doc: Call cb with each predictive-back event: the back gesture's start, its progress (0…1, with the edge it started from), then cancel or commit. Only the Android shell with denext mobile add back reports them (Android 14+ animates the gesture; earlier versions report only the commit). Elsewhere cb never runs.
symbols.docFull:
Call `cb` with each predictive-back event: the back gesture's `start`, its `progress` (0…1,
with the edge it started from), then `cancel` or `commit`. Only the Android shell with
`denext mobile add back` reports them (Android 14+ animates the gesture; earlier versions
report only the `commit`). Elsewhere `cb` never runs.

On Android a listener enables the native back callback like a handler does, so the system's
back-to-home animation gives way to yours; a committed back with no handler consuming it
still runs the default (history back, else leave the app).

symbols.name: onDeepLink
symbols.signature: onDeepLink(callback: (event: DeepLinkEvent) => void, options?: DeepLinkOptions): () => void
symbols.doc: Call callback for every link that opens the app, and (by default) navigate to it.
symbols.docFull:
Call `callback` for every link that opens the app, and (by default) navigate to it.

- **Cold start:** the link that launched the app is delivered once per page, with
  `launch: true`, to every subscriber registered before the shell answers (so subscribe
  early: a root layout or the app shell). A subscriber that registers after that, say on a
  component that remounts after a navigation, never sees it again, and neither does the
  page after a reload in the same session (e.g. an OTA update).
- **Warm:** every link opened while the app runs, with `launch: false`. A link that arrives
  while nobody is subscribed waits in the shell for the next subscriber.
- **Filter:** only links that pass `options.accept` (default: the app's custom schemes, no
  `https` host) reach `callback`. An unfiltered deep link is an injection vector: anyone
  can craft one, so treat its path and query as untrusted input.
- **Route:** an accepted link's in-app path is navigated (see
  {@linkcode DeepLinkOptions.route}), once per link however many subscribers see it.
- **Auth callbacks:** while {@linkcode openAuthSession} waits in the shell, links with its
  callback scheme (and, for a few seconds after, the callback it received) are its own and
  are not delivered here.

On the web (and during SSR) there is no native plugin and this does nothing: the browser
already loaded the linked URL. Needs `@capacitor/app` in the shell (`denext mobile add
deep-links --scheme myapp`).

**Deno Desktop** (denext's pinned runtime): links with a scheme declared in
`desktop.app.deepLinks` — a cold start, a link opened while the app runs (macOS), or one a
second launch forwards (`desktop.app.singleInstance`, Windows and Linux) — arrive here with the
same filter and once-only routing. The runtime hands each link over once: a link that came
before anyone subscribed goes to the first subscriber, and none is replayed after a reload. A
callback a pending `openAuthSession` is waiting for never arrives here. The stock runtime
delivers no links.

params.name: options
params.doc: Which links to accept, and how to navigate.

symbols.doc: Call callback when the user taps a local notification (or one of its actions), and by default navigate to its data.path (an in-app path) or data.url (under the deep-link acceptance rules), exactly as onPushTapped does for a push. A tap that cold-started the app is kept by the shell (or the Deno Desktop runtime) for the first listener, so subscribe early. In a Deno Desktop window it needs the notifications capability. Elsewhere it does nothing.
symbols.docFull:
Call `callback` when the user taps a local notification (or one of its actions), and by
default navigate to its `data.path` (an in-app path) or `data.url` (under the deep-link
acceptance rules), exactly as `onPushTapped` does for a push. A tap that
cold-started the app is kept by the shell (or the Deno Desktop runtime) for the first
listener, so subscribe early. In a Deno Desktop window it needs the `notifications`
capability. Elsewhere it does nothing.

Treat a tap's `data` (and its action) as untrusted input: on Linux a click arrives as a D-Bus
call on the app's name, which any process of the same user can make with any `data` (as a
Windows toast activation can be forged by the user's own processes). Validate it before acting
on it; the default navigation already applies the deep-link acceptance rules.

params.name: options
params.doc: Which links to accept, and how to navigate.

symbols.docFull:
Call `handler` with each command the OS sends for the now-playing item (lock screen, Control

symbols.name: onOpenFile
symbols.doc: Call callback for every file the OS opens with the app (Deno Desktop).
symbols.docFull:
Call `callback` for every file the OS opens with the app (Deno Desktop).

Each file is delivered once: one that arrived before anyone subscribed (the file the app was
launched with) goes to the first subscriber, so subscribe early (the root layout or app shell);
none is replayed after a reload. The OS hands the app a file it was asked to open, which any
program of the same user can ask for, so the handle is read-only and the content is untrusted
input.

symbols.name: onOtaRejected
symbols.doc: Call listener when the native side refuses a downloaded UI that no longer matches its signed manifest. The shell re-verifies a downloaded UI whenever it serves it: at every launch it checks the manifest stored with the files (its signature with the embedded key, and its version), and it hashes each file the first time it serves it. A file changed, added or removed on the device after the download (another app on a rooted or jailbroken device, malware with storage access, or corruption) is never served: the version is quarantined, the webview switches to the bundled UI (or the confirmed one), and this fires there. The event is kept until a listener is added, so register early (in the root layout); otaStatus reports the same version as tampered. The version may be downloaded again.
symbols.docFull:
Call `listener` when the native side refuses a downloaded UI that no longer matches its signed
manifest. The shell re-verifies a downloaded UI whenever it serves it: at every launch it
checks the manifest stored with the files (its signature with the embedded key, and its
version), and it hashes each file the first time it serves it. A file changed, added or
removed on the device after the download (another app on a rooted or jailbroken device,
malware with storage access, or corruption) is never served: the version is quarantined, the
webview switches to the bundled UI (or the confirmed one), and this fires there. The event is
kept until a listener is added, so register early (in the root layout); {@linkcode otaStatus}
reports the same version as `tampered`. The version may be downloaded again.

It also fires, with `code: "guard_unavailable"`, when the iOS shell did not serve a downloaded
UI because it could not install its check on Capacitor's `/_capacitor_file_` requests (the web
view's asset handler is the app's own class): the bundled UI runs instead, nothing is
quarantined, and updates are refused with that code in this process.

On the web, and in a shell whose `DenextOta` plugin predates this check, it never fires and
the returned function does nothing.

params.name: listener
params.doc: Called with the quarantined version and the reason.

symbols.returns: A function that removes the listener.

Outside the native shell, or without the plugin, it does nothing.
symbols.docFull:
Call `callback` with each share other apps send to this one, including the one that opened
the app: shares wait natively until the first subscriber arrives, so subscribe early (a root

symbols.name: openAppSettings
symbols.doc: Open the app's own page in the system settings, where the user can change a permission they refused (a blocked one can only be changed there).
symbols.docFull:
Open the app's own page in the system settings, where the user can change a permission they
refused (a `blocked` one can only be changed there).

- In the shell with denext's `DenextSettings` plugin (`denext mobile add permissions`; the
  local-notifications, biometrics and geolocation capabilities install it too): iOS opens
  `UIApplication.openSettingsURLString`, Android the app's "App info" screen
  (`ACTION_APPLICATION_DETAILS_SETTINGS`).
- iOS without the plugin: it hands `app-settings:` to the OS, which opens the same page.
- Android without the plugin, and the web: it rejects with a {@linkcode PermissionError}
  (`unsupported`); a browser has no way to open its site settings.
symbols.returns: A promise that settles once the settings were opened.

symbols.name: openAppStore
symbols.doc: Open the app's store page (the App Store on iOS, Play on Android) so the user can update. Without the plugin, natively or on the web, it opens the store URL instead (the App Store when appStoreId is given, else Play when androidPackage is).
symbols.docFull:
Open the app's store page (the App Store on iOS, Play on Android) so the user can update.
Without the plugin, natively or on the web, it opens the store URL instead (the App Store
when `appStoreId` is given, else Play when `androidPackage` is).

params.name: options
params.doc: The App Store id (required on iOS) and the Android package (optional).

symbols.returns: A promise that settles once the store was opened. It rejects with a TypeError on iOS without appStoreId, or when no plugin is there and neither id is given.

symbols.name: openAuthSession
symbols.doc: Sign in with an OAuth 2 / OpenID Connect provider in a system browser sheet, and get the callback URL the provider redirected to.
symbols.docFull:
Sign in with an OAuth 2 / OpenID Connect provider in a system browser sheet, and get the
callback URL the provider redirected to.

- **iOS** (inside the Capacitor shell): an `ASWebAuthenticationSession` sheet. It shares
  Safari's cookies unless `preferEphemeral`, and catches the redirect to
  `<callbackScheme>:` itself.
- **Android** (inside the shell): a Custom Tab. The redirect reaches the app through its
  intent filter for `callbackScheme` (`denext mobile add auth-session --scheme <scheme>`)
  and resolves the call. Coming back without a callback (back button, closing the tab)
  rejects `cancelled`. While a session is open, a link with that scheme is not routed by
  {@linkcode onDeepLink}.
- **Web**: a popup window. Register an https page of this origin as the redirect URI and
  call {@linkcode completeAuthSession} there; the popup posts its URL back and closes. A
  blocked popup rejects `unsupported` (call this from a click handler), and a popup closed
  without a callback rejects `cancelled`. A provider page served with
  `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` cuts the popup off from this page, which then
  reads as `cancelled`: use a full-page redirect for such providers.

- **Deno Desktop**: with a loopback `redirect_uri` (`http://127.0.0.1/cb`) the system browser,
  and the runtime catches the redirect on an ephemeral loopback port (RFC 8252), or on
  `loopbackPort` for a provider with a fixed registered redirect. Otherwise a
  custom-scheme callback: on macOS it runs in the OS's auth session (`ASWebAuthenticationSession`,
  a sheet on the app's window with a real `cancelled`, private with `preferEphemeral`); on Windows
  and Linux the system browser, and the callback comes back as a deep link. While the system
  browser has the sign-in, a Cancel overlay covers the app (`cancelOverlay`), since the browser
  reports no cancellation. Both flows require PKCE S256 in the URL (unless
  `pkce: "not-applicable"` with a `reason`; `pkce_required` otherwise). With a custom scheme,
  `callbackScheme` must be declared in `desktop.app.deepLinks`, the callback must match the
  `redirect_uri` (or `callbackPrefix`) exactly and carry the same `state`, and another app
  handling the scheme is refused (`scheme_owned_by_other_app`) rather than handed the callback.
  The callback never reaches {@linkcode onDeepLink}. Needs `denext desktop add auth-session`
  (and, for a custom scheme, denext's pinned runtime).

Only one session is open at a time (`busy` otherwise). The URL must carry PKCE S256 (a
`code_challenge` and `code_challenge_method=S256`; `pkce_required` otherwise) unless
`pkce: "not-applicable"` with a `reason`. Generate `state` and the PKCE verifier before the
call, compare `state` after it, and exchange the `code` (with the verifier) on your server.

params.name: options
params.doc: The callback scheme, and the iOS ephemeral and timeout options.

symbols.returns: The callback URL. It rejects with an AuthSessionError whose code is one of AuthSessionErrorCode.

symbols.name: openExternal
symbols.doc: Open a URL outside the app.
symbols.docFull:
Open a URL outside the app.

- Inside the native shell, an http(s) URL opens in the in-app browser of the
  `@capacitor/browser` plugin when it is installed natively (read from
  `Capacitor.Plugins.Browser`; no JS import of the plugin is needed).
- In a Deno Desktop window (`denext desktop add shell`), the OS opens it (the system
  browser, mail or phone app), never the app's own webview; the runtime re-checks the
  scheme against `desktop.capabilities.shell.openExternal`.
- Otherwise, including `mailto:`/`tel:` and on the web, it calls
  `window.open(url, "_blank", "noopener,noreferrer")`. The iOS shell hands a
  `window.open` to the OS (Safari, Mail, Phone); Android routes it to an intent.

Only `http:`, `https:`, `mailto:` and `tel:` URLs are accepted. Anything else, including
`javascript:`, `data:`, `file:` and relative URLs, is refused before anything opens: the
promise rejects with a `TypeError`. The vetted, normalized `URL.href` is what gets opened.

params.name: url
params.doc: An absolute http:, https:, mailto: or tel: URL.

symbols.returns: A promise that settles once the URL has been handed off. It rejects with a TypeError for a relative URL or a disallowed scheme, if the Browser plugin rejects, or when there is no window (SSR).

symbols.name: openKeyValueStore
symbols.doc: Open the durable key-value store name (default "default"). Nothing is opened until the first call; every store shares one backing, and each has its own keys.
symbols.docFull:
Open the durable key-value store `name` (default `"default"`). Nothing is opened until the
first call; every store shares one backing, and each has its own keys.

Inside the iOS / Android shell the data is written to a SQLite file in the app's data folder
by denext's `DenextStorage` plugin (`denext mobile add storage`), which the OS does not evict
the way it may evict a WebView's `localStorage` and IndexedDB under storage pressure.
`backend()` says where it went; see the module docs for the fallbacks.

With `{ encrypted: true }` the store is encrypted at rest (SQLCipher, `denext mobile add
storage --encrypted`), its key kept in secureStore; anywhere that cannot encrypt it, every call
rejects with a {@linkcode KeyValueStoreError} (`ENCRYPTION_UNAVAILABLE`) and nothing is written.

symbols.doc: Open a file or folder with the OS default app (Finder / Explorer for a folder).
symbols.docFull: Open a file or folder with the OS default app (Finder / Explorer for a folder).

symbols.signature: type OtaApplyResult = { readonly kind: "unsupported" } | { readonly kind: "error"; readonly reason: string; readonly code?: OtaErrorCode }
symbols.doc: The outcome of applyUiUpdate when it settles. On success the webview reloads into the new UI, so the promise does not settle at all.
symbols.docFull:
The outcome of {@linkcode applyUiUpdate} when it settles. On success the webview reloads
into the new UI, so the promise does not settle at all.

symbols.name: otaAppSignaturePayload
symbols.doc: The bytes a manifest's appSignature covers: the v5 format, UTF-8 with \n separators and no trailing newline,
symbols.docFull:
The bytes a manifest's `appSignature` covers: the v5 format, UTF-8 with `\n` separators and no
trailing newline,

`"denext-ota-v5\n" + version + "\n" + ("1" | "0") + "\n" + sha256hex(notes ?? "") + "\n" +
sequence + "\n" + (minNative ?? "") + "\n" + (nativeFingerprint ?? "") + "\n" + (expiresAt ??
"") + "\n" + appId`

with each value encoded as in {@linkcode otaSignaturePayload} (an absent `nativeFingerprint` or
`expiresAt` is the empty string). It is every field the v4 format covers plus the app id, under
its own first line, so an `appSignature` never verifies as a `signature` or the reverse. The
native `DenextOta` plugin and the desktop updater build the same bytes.

params.name: manifest
params.doc: The version and the signed metadata, with an appId and a sequence.

symbols.name: otaBooted
symbols.doc: Confirm to the native side that the running UI booted. Call it once after the app's first render: a UI on its trial launch that never calls it is rolled back by the native watchdog (after 15 s of foreground time by default), and on the next launch if the app died twice before confirming. Harmless on the bundled UI or a confirmed one.
symbols.docFull:
Confirm to the native side that the running UI booted. Call it once after the app's
first render: a UI on its trial launch that never calls it is rolled back by the
native watchdog (after 15 s of foreground time by default), and on the next launch if the
app died twice before confirming. Harmless on the bundled UI or a confirmed one.

It sends this page's own UI version, read from the `_denext/ota.json` the page was served
with (its web root), and the native side confirms only when that is the version on trial.
A late call from the page being replaced therefore cannot confirm the new UI. A page with no
readable manifest sends no version, and a current shell (OTA template generation 11 on) then
confirms nothing: every downloaded UI carries its manifest, so only a page that is not the
trial UI lacks one. (A shell older than that confirms a version-less call.) The manifest
is read at the first call, before the page could have been switched away from; reading
`otaStatus().pending` instead would name the new version as soon as the switch starts.

Resolves on the web and when the plugin is missing, and never rejects: a failure here
must not break the app that just booted.
symbols.returns: A promise that settles once the native side has recorded the boot.

symbols.name: OtaCheckOptions
symbols.doc: Options for checkForUiUpdate and prepareUiUpdate.
symbols.docFull: Options for {@linkcode checkForUiUpdate} and {@linkcode prepareUiUpdate}.

members.name: baseUrl
members.doc:
The web root the UI is served from, e.g. `"https://api.example.com/mobile-ui"`. The
manifest is fetched from `${baseUrl}/_denext/ota.json` and each file from
`${baseUrl}/<path>`. A trailing slash is ignored.

members.name: headers
members.doc:
Headers sent with the manifest request AND with every native file download, e.g.
`{ authorization: "Bearer …" }`. Serve the UI behind the same auth as your API.

members.name: timeoutMs
members.doc: Timeout for the manifest request, in ms. Default 15 000.

members.name: fetch
members.doc: The `fetch` to use for the manifest (default: the global `fetch`).

members.name: channel
members.doc:
The OTA channel this app follows (`"production"`, `"beta"`, …), sent as the
`x-denext-ota-channel` header on the manifest request and on every native file download. A
server built with `createOtaHandler({ channels })` serves that channel's release; without it
the server's default channel. Setting it turns on `installId: "auto"`.

members.name: installId
members.doc:
The install id sent as `x-denext-ota-install-id`, which a channels server hashes into the
device's staged-rollout bucket (a request without one always gets the stable release).
`"auto"` (the default when `channel` is set) uses {@linkcode otaInstallId}, a random id kept
in `localStorage`; a string is sent as given (8–128 characters of `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`, or the
server ignores it). Omitted without `channel`: no header.

members.name: platform
members.doc:
This shell's target, which a manifest naming another one is refused against (code
`platform_mismatch`) and which is sent as the `x-denext-ota-platform` header (a
`createOtaHandler({ platforms })` server serves each target its own export). Default:
`runtimePlatform()` in the iOS / Android shell.

members.name: appId
members.doc:
This app's id (the iOS bundle id / Android application id): a manifest naming another app is
refused before the native side sees it (code `app_mismatch`). Default: the id the shell's
status reports. The native side checks it either way.

members.name: onNativeUpdateRequired
members.signature: onNativeUpdateRequired?: (refusal: { code: "native_too_old" | "native_mismatch"; reason: string }) => unknown | Promise<unknown>
members.doc:
Called when the server's UI needs a newer app binary: a check or prepare that ends in an
`error` result with code `native_too_old` (the manifest's `minNative` is above this build) or
`native_mismatch` (it was built for another native fingerprint). The usual answer is a
store-update prompt. It is fired once per call after the result is known, not awaited into
it; what it returns (such as `promptStoreUpdate`'s promise) is ignored, and a throw or
rejection is swallowed and the result is returned unchanged.

symbols.name: OtaCheckResult
symbols.signature: type OtaCheckResult = { readonly kind: "unsupported" } | { readonly kind: "current" } | { readonly kind: "applied"; readonly version: string } | { readonly kind: "skipped"; readonly reason: "rejected" | "busy" } | { readonly kind: "error"; readonly reason: string; readonly code?: OtaErrorCode }
symbols.doc: The outcome of checkForUiUpdate. It never throws; every failure is a value.
symbols.docFull: The outcome of {@linkcode checkForUiUpdate}. It never throws; every failure is a value.

symbols.name: OtaErrorCode
symbols.doc: The code of a native DenextOta refusal, carried on an error result:
symbols.docFull:
The `code` of a native `DenextOta` refusal, carried on an `error` result:

- `invalid`: a malformed request or manifest; `busy`, `rejected`: see the results;
- `download`: a file could not be fetched; `integrity`: a file, or the manifest's `version`
  (the native side recomputes it from the file list), does not match;
- `not_staged`: {@linkcode applyUiUpdate} named a version that is not staged;
- `signature`: the app binary embeds a public key (`denext mobile add-ota --public-key`) and the
  manifest's `signature` is missing or does not verify;
- `insecure`: the binary pins origins (`denext mobile add-ota --ota-origin`) and `baseUrl` is on
  none of them, or it embeds no key and `baseUrl` is not a pinned https origin. A loopback
  `baseUrl` (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, and `10.0.2.2` on Android) passes both checks
  only in a debug build (iOS: compiled with `DEBUG`, Xcode's Debug configuration; Android: a
  debuggable build); a release build treats it as any other origin;
- `expired`: the manifest's signed `expiresAt` has passed (re-sign it: `denext ota manifest
  --sign`), or it carries none while the app's bundled UI does (an expiry-aware app refuses an
  unexpiring release). Checked here too, before the running version is reported `current`, so
  a feed stuck on an old release shows up as an error;
- `downgrade`: the manifest's `sequence` is lower than the highest this device has accepted or
  the bundled UI's own manifest carries, or it has none once there is such a floor;
- `native_too_old`: the manifest's `minNative` is above the app binary's build number (iOS
  `CFBundleVersion`, Android `versionCode`);
- `native_mismatch`: the manifest's `nativeFingerprint` differs from the one the app binary
  embeds (`denext mobile fingerprint --write`): the UI was built for another native layer.
  Checked only when both carry one.
- `platform_mismatch`: the manifest names another target than this shell's (`ios` /
  `android`): it is that platform's export (`denext export --platform`), with that platform's
  files. Checked here, before the native side sees it. The manifest's `platform` field is not
  signed; the export's stamp file is (the version covers it), so a stamped export is refused
  by another target whether or not the field is present. A manifest with neither (a `web`
  export) fits a shell without a public key only: an app that embeds one (`denext mobile add-ota
  --public-key`) takes only its own platform's stamped export (`denext export --platform ios`,
  or `denext ota manifest --platform ios` over the export), so a web export signed with the same
  key cannot install itself on a phone. The page cannot tell whether the binary embeds a key, so
  that refusal comes from the native side.
- `app_mismatch`: the manifest's signed `appId` names another app than this one (the iOS bundle
  id / Android application id). An app that embeds a public key also refuses a manifest
  without one (re-sign it: `denext ota manifest --app-id <id> --sign`), so a feed for another
  app that shares the signing key cannot install its UI here. The page refuses another app's
  manifest before the native side sees it (with {@linkcode OtaCheckOptions.appId}, or the id the
  shell's status reports); the missing-id refusal comes from the native side.
- `guard_unavailable`: the iOS shell could not install the check on Capacitor's
  `/_capacitor_file_` requests (an app whose web view uses its own asset handler class), so it
  serves no downloaded UI in this process and refuses every update: see {@linkcode onOtaRejected}.

The trust checks (`integrity`, `signature`, `insecure`, `downgrade`, `native_too_old`,
`native_mismatch`, `app_mismatch`, `expired`, and
`invalid` for a malformed or oversized manifest) run before any file is downloaded, and a
refusal leaves the running UI and any staged one as they were.

symbols.doc: This install's stable OTA id: a random base64url string made on first use and kept in localStorage (denext:ota-install-id), so a channels server (createOtaHandler({ channels })) puts the device in the same staged-rollout bucket on every check. It identifies nothing but the install; clearing the app's data makes a new one. Where storage is unavailable it lasts for the page's lifetime.

symbols.doc: The _denext/ota.json document: a version stamped over the sorted file list.
symbols.docFull: The `_denext/ota.json` document: a version stamped over the sorted file list.

members.name: version
members.doc: Lowercase hex SHA-256 over the sorted `"<path>\t<sha256>\n"` lines.

members.name: required
members.doc:
Whether the app should not let the user decline this UI (`denext ota manifest --required`).
A hint for the app's own update prompt; absent means `false`. Not part of the version.

members.name: notes
members.doc:
Release notes for the app's update prompt (`denext ota manifest --notes <text>`), at most
{@linkcode OTA_NOTES_MAX_LENGTH} characters. Not part of the version.

members.name: sequence
members.doc:
A release counter that only grows (`denext ota manifest --sign` stamps the current Unix time
in seconds; `--sequence <n>` sets it). The native plugin remembers the highest one it accepted
and refuses a lower one, or a manifest without one after that (code `downgrade`). A
non-negative integer no larger than `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. Not part of the version;
signed in the v2 payload.

members.name: minNative
members.doc:
The lowest native build number (iOS `CFBundleVersion`, Android `versionCode`) this UI runs on
(`denext ota manifest --min-native <n>`). An older app binary refuses it before downloading
(code `native_too_old`). A non-negative safe integer. Not part of the version; signed in the
v2 payload.

members.name: nativeFingerprint
members.doc:
The native fingerprint of the app binary this UI was built for (`denext ota manifest
--native-fingerprint <fp|auto>`, the value `denext mobile fingerprint` prints): 64 lowercase
hex digits. A binary that embeds a fingerprint (`denext mobile fingerprint --write`) refuses
a manifest carrying a different one before downloading (code `native_mismatch`); when either
side has none, the check is skipped. Not part of the version; signed in the v3 payload.

members.name: expiresAt
members.doc:
When the release stops being accepted, in Unix seconds (`denext ota manifest --expires-in
<days>` / `--expires-at <RFC 3339>`; a signed manifest gets 30 days unless one is given). At
or after it the native plugin, `checkForUiUpdate` and the desktop updater refuse the manifest
(code `expired`): re-sign it before then. Only with a `sequence`. Not part of the version;
signed in the v4 payload. A UI already installed keeps running past it: the expiry gates
installing (and reporting "current"), not serving.

members.name: platform
members.doc:
The target the export was built for (`ios`, `android`, `macos`, `windows`, `linux`): a shell
of another target refuses it (code `platform_mismatch`). Must match the export's
{@linkcode OTA_PLATFORM_PATH} stamp, which the version covers; the field is not signed, so a
shell also checks the stamp itself. Absent with no stamp: a `web` export every shell accepts
(`web` names no stamp, so it is never written here).

members.name: appId
members.doc:
The app the release is for (`denext ota manifest --app-id <id>`; a signed `spa.ota` export
and `denext ota manifest --sign` stamp the Capacitor `appId` on an `ios` / `android` export,
and `spa.ota` stamps `desktop.app.identifier` on a desktop one): the iOS bundle id, the
Android application id, or the Deno Desktop app identifier ({@linkcode isOtaAppId}). A shell
that knows its own id refuses another (code `app_mismatch`); an app that embeds a public key,
and a desktop overlay configured with `desktop.app.identifier`, also refuse a manifest
without one. Only with a `sequence`. Not part of the version; signed by `appSignature`.

members.name: signature
members.doc:
Standard (padded) base64 of the raw 64-byte `r‖s` ECDSA P-256 / SHA-256 signature over
{@linkcode otaSignaturePayload} (`denext ota manifest --sign <keyfile>`). An app whose binary
embeds a public key refuses a manifest without a valid one.

members.name: appSignature
members.doc:
Standard (padded) base64 of the raw 64-byte `r‖s` ECDSA P-256 / SHA-256 signature over
{@linkcode otaAppSignaturePayload} (the v5 format, which adds `appId` to what `signature`
covers), made with the same key. Written beside `signature` whenever a signed manifest has an
`appId`; a shell that requires the `appId` refuses a manifest without a valid one (code
`signature`).

symbols.name: otaSignaturePayload
symbols.doc: The bytes an OTA manifest signature covers, as UTF-8 with \n (0x0A) separators and no trailing newline. A manifest with an expiresAt (and a sequence) uses the v4 format, else one with a nativeFingerprint (and a sequence) v3, one with a sequence but neither v2, one without a sequence v1:
symbols.docFull:
The bytes an OTA manifest signature covers, as UTF-8 with `\n` (0x0A) separators and no
trailing newline. A manifest with an `expiresAt` (and a `sequence`) uses the v4 format, else one
with a `nativeFingerprint` (and a `sequence`) v3, one with a `sequence` but neither v2, one
without a `sequence` v1:

- v4: `"denext-ota-v4\n" + version + "\n" + ("1" | "0") + "\n" + sha256hex(notes ?? "") + "\n"
  + sequence + "\n" + (minNative ?? "") + "\n" + (nativeFingerprint ?? "") + "\n" + expiresAt`
- v3: `"denext-ota-v3\n" + version + "\n" + ("1" | "0") + "\n" + sha256hex(notes ?? "") + "\n"
  + sequence + "\n" + (minNative ?? "") + "\n" + nativeFingerprint`
- v2: `"denext-ota-v2\n" + version + "\n" + ("1" | "0") + "\n" + sha256hex(notes ?? "") + "\n"
  + sequence + "\n" + (minNative ?? "")`
- v1: `"denext-ota-v1\n" + version + "\n" + ("1" | "0") + "\n" + sha256hex(notes ?? "")`

`"1"` is `required === true`, anything else `"0"`; `sha256hex` is lowercase hex of the SHA-256
of the notes' UTF-8 (the empty string when absent); `sequence` and `minNative` are plain
decimal integers (no sign, no leading zeros, no exponent), and an absent `minNative` is the
empty string; `nativeFingerprint` is 64 lowercase hex digits (the empty string in v4 when
absent); `expiresAt` is a plain decimal integer (Unix seconds). The version already covers every
file, so the chain is files → version → signature, and none of the metadata can change under a
valid signature. The native `DenextOta` plugin builds the same bytes (v4 when the manifest has an
`expiresAt`, else v3 when it has a `sequence` and a `nativeFingerprint`, v2 with a `sequence`
alone, else v1). A v2 / v3 manifest (no expiry) is signed and verified exactly as before v4
existed.

symbols.docFull:
Pause a running download: the bytes so far are kept, and {@linkcode resumeFileTransfer}
continues from them where the server allows a range (else it starts over). Its
`downloadToFile` promise stays pending until then. Uploads cannot pause.

A Deno Desktop download pauses in the runtime: it keeps the partial file (and a sidecar naming
the URL and its validator) beside the destination, and a resume asks for the rest with a range
request guarded by `If-Range`.

symbols.name: PermissionState
symbols.doc: A permission's status, the same on every platform:
symbols.docFull:
A permission's status, the same on every platform:

- `granted`: allowed.
- `limited`: allowed in part (iOS: selected photos only, or limited contacts; Android:
  approximate location only; calendar: write-only access).
- `prompt`: never asked; {@linkcode requestPermission} shows the system prompt.
- `prompt-with-rationale`: Android: refused once, and a request shows the prompt again.
  Explain why the app needs it first.
- `denied`: {@linkcode requestPermission} just asked and the user said no, but the app may ask
  again later (Android's first refusal; on the web, a refusal the browser may reset).
- `blocked`: refused and the OS will not prompt again (iOS after any refusal; Android after
  "Don't allow" twice or "Don't ask again"). Only {@linkcode openAppSettings} can change it.

symbols.name: prepareUiUpdate
symbols.doc: Download and verify a newer UI WITHOUT switching to it, so the app can ask the user first.
symbols.docFull:
Download and verify a newer UI WITHOUT switching to it, so the app can ask the user first.

1. Fetches and validates `${baseUrl}/_denext/ota.json`, exactly as
   {@linkcode checkForUiUpdate} does; the running version resolves `current`.
2. Otherwise the native plugin downloads (or copies, by SHA-256) and verifies every file
   into the version's own directory and records it as **staged**. The running UI keeps
   running; a version already staged resolves at once.
3. Resolves `ready` with the manifest's `required` (default `false`) and `notes` (default
   `null`) for the app's prompt. Switch with {@linkcode applyUiUpdate}.

A staged UI is never switched to on its own, not even at the next launch; a newer prepare
replaces it, and {@linkcode otaReset} (or a new app binary) drops it. It never throws.
Outside the native shell, or with a `DenextOta` plugin that predates staged updates, it
resolves `{ kind: "unsupported" }` without touching the network. One prepare runs at a
time: a call made while another is in flight gets that call's promise (and its options).

symbols.name: PullToRefresh
symbols.doc: A scrolling <div> with pull-to-refresh: pull down from the top, past threshold, and let go to call onRefresh; the spinner then rests near the top and spins while refreshing is true. Set refreshing to true in onRefresh and back to false when the data arrives, as with React Native's RefreshControl (React Native mode's RefreshControl is this same gesture and spinner).
symbols.docFull:
A scrolling `<div>` with pull-to-refresh: pull down from the top, past `threshold`, and let
go to call `onRefresh`; the spinner then rests near the top and spins while `refreshing` is
`true`. Set `refreshing` to `true` in `onRefresh` and back to `false` when the data arrives,
as with React Native's `RefreshControl` (React Native mode's `RefreshControl` is this same
gesture and spinner).

The component is the scroll container (`overflow-y: auto`, with `overscroll-behavior-y:
contain` so the browser's own pull-to-refresh stays out of the way), so give it a height
(`style={{ height: "100dvh" }}`, or a flex parent). The gesture is touch-only; mouse and
keyboard users need another way to refresh. It works the same in the browser and in the
Capacitor shell, where arming the pull also plays a light haptic tick.

Register the device for remote notifications and resolve its token, for your server to send
to through APNs (iOS) or FCM (Android). denext ships no push relay: store the token on your
server (with the user it belongs to) and send from there.

It listens for the plugin's `registration` / `registrationError` events, calls `register()`,
and resolves the first answer, rejecting after `timeoutMs` (default 15 s). Its listeners are
removed either way. Concurrent calls share one registration. Call it on every launch: the
token can change. It does not ask for permission (see {@linkcode requestPushPermission}),
and it rejects outside the native shell or without `@capacitor/push-notifications`: there
is no web-push fallback.

symbols.name: rekeyKeyValueStore
symbols.doc: Rotate the key of the encrypted store name (openKeyValueStore(name, { encrypted: true })): a new random 256-bit key, the store's SQLCipher database re-encrypted under it (PRAGMA rekey, one transaction in SQLCipher), and the key in secureStore replaced. A store that has no key yet is given one first, as its first use would.
symbols.docFull:
Rotate the key of the encrypted store `name` (`openKeyValueStore(name, { encrypted: true })`):
a new random 256-bit key, the store's SQLCipher database re-encrypted under it (`PRAGMA
rekey`, one transaction in SQLCipher), and the key in secureStore replaced. A store that has
no key yet is given one first, as its first use would.

Crash safety: the new key is first kept in its own secureStore entry and the store's key stays
the old one until the rekey has committed; only then does the new key replace it. A process
that dies before the rekey commits leaves the store under the old key; one that dies after it
leaves the new key waiting in that entry. Either way the next use of the store tries the
current key, then the waiting one, and finishes the move — no data is lost.

Calls on the store made while it rotates wait for the new key. Refused with
{@linkcode KeyValueStoreError} `ENCRYPTION_UNAVAILABLE` wherever encrypted stores are (the
browser, Deno Desktop, the fallbacks, a build without SQLCipher, a plugin from before 4.8.1,
a secureStore that is not secret), and `WRONG_KEY` when the stored key does not open the store.
examples:

symbols.doc: Remove delivered notifications from the notification centre — local ones and remote pushes alike. Pending (scheduled) notifications are not touched: cancelNotification cancels those.
symbols.docFull:
Remove delivered notifications from the notification centre — local ones and remote pushes
alike. Pending (scheduled) notifications are not touched: `cancelNotification` cancels those.

The criteria given narrow each other: `{ threadId: "chat-7" }` removes the thread's
notifications, `{ ids: ["12"], threadId: "chat-7" }` only those of the ids in that thread. An
empty selector is a `TypeError` (so a missing argument never clears everything); pass
`{ all: true }` to remove every one. On Android, a group summary left without notifications in
its group is removed too. See {@linkcode deliveredNotifications} for what each platform can see.
symbols.returns: A promise that settles once removed.

symbols.name: requestPermission
symbols.doc: Ask for a permission when a prompt can still be shown, and report the outcome. A decided permission (granted, limited, blocked) comes back as it is, without a prompt. A refusal reads blocked on iOS (it never prompts again) and denied on Android's first refusal (a later request prompts again, after your rationale); see PermissionState.
symbols.docFull:
Ask for a permission when a prompt can still be shown, and report the outcome. A decided
permission (`granted`, `limited`, `blocked`) comes back as it is, without a prompt. A refusal
reads `blocked` on iOS (it never prompts again) and `denied` on Android's first refusal (a
later request prompts again, after your rationale); see {@linkcode PermissionState}.

`biometrics` has no separate prompt (iOS asks for Face ID the first time
`authenticateBiometric` runs), so it returns what {@linkcode checkPermission} does.
symbols.returns: Its status after the prompt, if one was shown.

symbols.name: requestPushPermission
symbols.doc: Ask for permission to show notifications, when it has not been decided yet, and report the result: "granted", "denied" (the user said no; only the system settings can change it) or "prompt" (still undecided). A decided state comes back without prompting again. Outside the native shell (or without @capacitor/push-notifications) it is "unsupported": there is no web-push fallback. In a Deno Desktop window with the notifications capability it is the OS's notification permission (the app's own notifications; there is no push service on desktop).
symbols.docFull:
Ask for permission to show notifications, when it has not been decided yet, and report the
result: `"granted"`, `"denied"` (the user said no; only the system settings can change it)
or `"prompt"` (still undecided). A decided state comes back without prompting again.
Outside the native shell (or without `@capacitor/push-notifications`) it is
`"unsupported"`: there is no web-push fallback. In a Deno Desktop window with the
`notifications` capability it is the OS's notification permission (the app's own
notifications; there is no push service on desktop).

Android before 13 needs no permission and always reads `"granted"`.

symbols.name: requestReview
symbols.doc: Ask the OS to show its in-app rating sheet (StoreKit's requestReview on iOS, the Play In-App Review flow on Android).
symbols.docFull:
Ask the OS to show its in-app rating sheet (StoreKit's `requestReview` on iOS, the Play
In-App Review flow on Android).

The OS decides whether the sheet appears: iOS shows it at most three times a year per user,
never in a TestFlight build, and Play applies its own quota (a sideloaded build never shows
it). Nothing tells the app whether it appeared or what the user chose, so ask at a natural
pause (after a completed task), never from a button labelled "Rate us": for that, use
{@linkcode openStoreReview}.
symbols.returns: "requested" natively, "unsupported" on the web or without the plugin. It rejects when the plugin fails (for example Play Services missing).

symbols.name: restoreRouteOnRelaunch
symbols.doc: Opt in to returning to the last route after the OS killed the app in the background.
symbols.docFull:
Opt in to returning to the last route after the OS killed the app in the background.

It saves the current path (with its search and hash) each time the app goes to the
background, in `@capacitor/preferences` when the app has it (`npm i @capacitor/preferences`),
else `localStorage`. When the app then cold-starts on one of `startPaths` within `maxAgeMs`,
it navigates to the saved path. Only the route comes back: component state, scroll positions
and the back stack do not (persist what matters yourself, for example a draft in
`secureStore` or `localStorage`).

Call it once, early (the client entry or the root layout's provider effect). A second call
in the same page load only restores; the saving listeners are installed once.

params.name: options
params.doc: The age limit, the start paths, the navigation, the platforms and the key.

symbols.returns: The path it navigated to, or null when there was nothing to restore.

symbols.name: RestoreRouteOptions
symbols.doc: Options for restoreRouteOnRelaunch.
symbols.docFull: Options for {@linkcode restoreRouteOnRelaunch}.

members.name: maxAgeMs
members.doc:
How old a saved route may be and still be restored, in ms. Default 30 minutes: a relaunch
much later is a fresh start, not a return.

members.name: startPaths
members.doc:
The paths a cold start lands on (the app's start page). A relaunch that lands elsewhere
(a deep link, a notification tap) is left alone. Default `["/", "/index.html"]`.

members.name: navigate
members.doc:
How to go to the saved route. Default: `history.replaceState` to it, then a `popstate`
event, which denext's router (and react-router, TanStack Router, expo-router's web
history) follow like a back/forward navigation.

members.name: platforms
members.doc: Where it runs. Default `["android", "ios"]` (the web never loses its tab this way).

members.name: key
members.doc: The storage key. Default `"denext:last-route"`.

symbols.name: resumeFileTransfer
symbols.doc: Continue a paused download from its bytes so far (a range request where the server allows one, else from the start).
symbols.docFull:
Continue a paused download from its bytes so far (a range request where the server allows one,
else from the start).

In the iOS / Android shell with the `DenextTransfer` plugin (`denext mobile add file-transfer`)
it also retries a failed transfer: a download from its bytes so far when it is `resumable`,
else anew, and an upload from the start. On the web and in a Deno Desktop window only a paused
download resumes: a failed transfer resolves `false` (start it again with `downloadToFile`; on
Deno Desktop the same URL to the same file continues from the partial file the runtime kept).
After a restart, a Deno Desktop download started with a credential header (`Authorization`,
`Cookie`, an API key) is refused here, since the runtime never writes one to disk: start it again
with `downloadToFile` and its headers (the same id, URL and file), which continues from its
partial file.
symbols.returns: Whether it resumed: false for an id with no record, a transfer that is neither paused nor (with the plugin) failed, or, outside the plugin, a failed one.

symbols.docFull:
A stylesheet fragment that defines `--denext-safe-top`, `--denext-safe-right`,
`--denext-safe-bottom` and `--denext-safe-left` on `:root` as the device's safe-area insets
(the notch, status bar, navigation bar and home indicator), `0px` where there are none. Drop
it into a stylesheet or a `<style>` tag, then pad with the variables.

Each is `var(--safe-area-inset-*, env(safe-area-inset-*, 0px))`: the value Capacitor 8's
`SystemBars` plugin injects on Android when set (Android WebView before 140 reports wrong
`env()` insets), else the browser's `env()` value. For the numbers in JavaScript, use
{@linkcode useSafeAreaInsets}.

The insets are only non-zero when the viewport meta includes `viewport-fit=cover`. In the
App Router, export `viewport = { width: "device-width", initialScale: 1, viewportFit:
"cover" }` from the root layout. In SPA mode, put the meta tag in `spa.head`; denext's SPA
shell keeps an app's own viewport meta instead of emitting its default.

symbols.docFull:
Schedule a local notification (or show it now, without a trigger). Scheduling an `id` that is
already pending replaces it.

Permission: ask first with `requestPermission("notifications")`; without it the OS drops
the notification silently. Android 12+ may deliver an exact-time trigger a few minutes late
unless the user allowed exact alarms.

On the web there is no scheduler: a notification without a trigger shows through the
Notifications API (when permission is granted), and one with a trigger rejects. On Deno Desktop
with the `notifications` capability the OS schedules it (a repeating one for its next 16
occurrences, topped up whenever the app runs; Linux delivers while the app runs).

symbols.name: secureStore
symbols.doc: A string key-value store for secrets.
symbols.docFull:
A string key-value store for secrets.

- Inside the native shell with `@aparajita/capacitor-secure-storage` installed (`denext
  mobile add secure-store`), values live in the iOS Keychain (accessible when the device is
  unlocked, not synced to iCloud) or encrypted with an Android Keystore key. Keys share the
  plugin's default prefix, so its own `SecureStorage.getItem`/`setItem` see the same
  entries.
- Inside a Deno Desktop window (`denext desktop add secure-store`), the OS credential store,
  through the desktop runtime: the macOS Keychain, the Windows `PasswordVault`, or the Secret
  Service on Linux (gnome-keyring or KWallet, through the runtime's libsecret). When that store
  is not usable (Linux without a Secret Service provider, with the keyring locked, or under a
  runtime without its own store) the call fails with `backend_unavailable` and says why: a real
  error, never `null` and never the plaintext web fallback.
- **On the web it is NOT secret.** The fallback is a plain IndexedDB database
  (`denext-secure-store`) that any script on the origin, and anyone with the device's
  browser profile, can read. It keeps a web build working; it does not protect anything.

Values are strings: `JSON.stringify` anything else.

`set(key, value, { fallback: "session" })` / `get(key, { fallback: "session" })` opt in to
`sessionStorage` when the OS store refuses (a locked or absent Linux keyring): the call warns
once and `set` resolves `{ stored: "session" }`. `get` also answers from that copy when the OS
store resolves with no value for the key (its own value, when present, wins). A successful OS
`set` clears the copy and `delete` clears both. That copy is NOT secret and ends with the tab.

`set(key, value, { accessibility: "afterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly" })` picks the iOS Keychain
class (default `"whenUnlocked"`; see {@linkcode SecureStoreSetOptions.accessibility}): a
`"…ThisDeviceOnly"` value never leaves the device in a backup.

`set(key, value, { requireBiometric: true })` gates the value: every `get` asks for Face ID /
Touch ID / a fingerprint first (`denext mobile add biometrics`) and rejects with a
`BiometricError` when the user is not verified, including always on the web. In a current
iOS / Android shell the OS enforces it (a Keychain access control, an Android Keystore key that
needs the user); in an older shell and on Deno Desktop it is denext's code in the page (see
{@linkcode SecureStoreSetOptions.requireBiometric}).

members.name: requireBiometric
members.doc:
Gate every later `get` of this value behind Face ID / Touch ID / a fingerprint (`denext mobile
add biometrics`). In an iOS / Android shell whose `DenextSettings` plugin has the biometric
secret store (generation 4: `denext mobile add biometrics` from this denext, in a new binary)
**the OS enforces it**: iOS keeps the value in a Keychain item whose access control requires
the enrolled biometrics or the device passcode ("when passcode set, this device only": not
backed up or migrated, deleted with the passcode, dropped when the enrolled biometrics change);
Android 9+ seals it under an Android Keystore key that needs the user for every use (dropped
when the enrolled biometrics change). Page script cannot read it through any bridge method
without the native prompt. In an older shell, and in a Deno Desktop window, the gate is
denext's own code in the page (the value sits in the plain secure store), and the first
`set` warns. Storing never prompts. Default `false`.

members.name: fallback
members.doc:
What to do when the OS secret store REFUSES the write (the desktop keychain answering
`backend_unavailable`: no Secret Service provider, a locked keyring nobody unlocked, or the
native plugin rejecting). Unset (the default) the call rejects, so the OS-protected contract
stays explicit. `"session"` keeps the value in the page's `sessionStorage` instead, warns
once with the reason, and reports `{ stored: "session" }`. **`sessionStorage` is NOT
secret**: any script on the origin can read it, and it ends with the tab or window (it
survives a reload). Ignored (the call still rejects) together with `requireBiometric`, which
promises a protection it cannot give.

members.name: accessibility
members.doc:
When the iOS Keychain lets the app read the value (its `kSecAttrAccessible` class), for the
shell's secure-storage plugin. The default stays `"whenUnlocked"`: readable while the device is
unlocked, and carried to a new device by an encrypted backup. `"…ThisDeviceOnly"` keeps a
value (a refresh token, say) out of every backup and off any other device;
`"afterFirstUnlock…"` keeps it readable while the device is locked again after its first
unlock (background work); `"whenPasscodeSetThisDeviceOnly"` also needs a device passcode and is
deleted when the passcode is removed. A value already stored keeps its class until it is set
again.

Android: the plugin's Android Keystore key never leaves the device and needs no unlock, so
every value there behaves as `"afterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly"`, whatever is passed. On the
web and in a Deno Desktop window the option is accepted and has no effect (the OS store there
has no such classes). A `requireBiometric` value is always `"whenPasscodeSetThisDeviceOnly"`;
another class beside it is refused. Checked on every platform: an unknown value is a
`TypeError`.
