symbols.doc: Where SecureStore.set put the value.
symbols.docFull: Where {@linkcode SecureStore.set} put the value.

members.doc:
`"keychain"`: the OS secret store (iOS Keychain, Android Keystore, the desktop keychain).
`"indexeddb"`: the web's not-secret IndexedDB database (no secret store here).
`"session"`: `sessionStorage`, because the OS store refused and `fallback: "session"` was
given; NOT secret.

symbols.name: setNotificationCategories
symbols.doc: Register the app's notification categories: the action buttons a notification shows when its categoryId names one. The call **replaces** every category registered before, so pass the full set each time.
symbols.docFull:
Register the app's notification categories: the action buttons a notification shows when its
`categoryId` names one. The call **replaces** every category registered before, so pass the
full set each time.

On iOS the categories live in the app's one `UNUserNotificationCenter`, so they apply to
remote pushes too: a push whose `aps.category` names a category shows its buttons, and the
tapped button arrives through `onPushTapped` as `actionId`. On Android they apply to local
notifications only (FCM draws its own notification without buttons). On Deno Desktop with
the `notifications` capability they are the notification's buttons (title only: no text input,
destructive or authentication options there). Elsewhere it does nothing.
symbols.returns: A promise that settles once registered.

symbols.doc: Show what is playing on the lock screen, in Control Center / the media notification, and on headsets and cars, and offer the controls in info.controls there (they reach onMediaControl). Each call merges info into the last one, so after the first a page sends what changed: { playing: false, position } on pause, a new title for the next track. Calls that only restate the clock (a timeupdate while playing) are not sent on: the OS runs the position on from the rate.
symbols.docFull:
Show what is playing on the lock screen, in Control Center / the media notification, and on
headsets and cars, and offer the controls in `info.controls` there (they reach
{@linkcode onMediaControl}). Each call merges `info` into the last one, so after the first a
page sends what changed: `{ playing: false, position }` on pause, a new title for the next
track. Calls that only restate the clock (a `timeupdate` while playing) are not sent on: the
OS runs the position on from the rate.

In the shell this needs `denext mobile add background-audio`; elsewhere it uses
`navigator.mediaSession` (nothing happens without it, or during SSR).

symbols.name: setSystemBars
symbols.doc: Style, hide or show the system bars.
symbols.docFull:
Style, hide or show the system bars.

Inside the native shell this calls Capacitor 8's `SystemBars` plugin, part of
`@capacitor/core` (no plugin to install): `style` becomes `setStyle`, `hidden` becomes
`hide` / `show` (with `animation`, iOS only), and `bar` limits both to one bar. On iOS the
app needs `UIViewControllerBasedStatusBarAppearance` in Info.plist, which `denext mobile add
system-bars` writes. On the web it does nothing: the browser owns its toolbars (set a
`theme-color` meta for their tint).
symbols.returns: A promise that settles once the plugin applied it. It rejects with a TypeError for an unknown style, bar or animation, or if the plugin rejects.
examples:
```ts
import { setSystemBars } from "denext/mobile";

await setSystemBars({ style: "dark" }); // light icons over a dark header
await setSystemBars({ hidden: true, bar: "status", animation: "none" }); // full-screen video
```

symbols.doc: Store data as the snapshot widget kind renders, and refresh that kind's widgets.
symbols.docFull:
Store `data` as the snapshot widget `kind` renders, and refresh that kind's widgets.

Inside the native shell with the plugin (`denext mobile add widget --name <kind>`): iOS keeps
the JSON in the App Group's shared defaults (`denext.widget.<kind>`) and reloads the kind's
WidgetKit timelines; Android keeps it in the `denext_widgets` shared preferences and updates
the kind's placed widgets. The generated widget shows `title` and `body` strings; edit its
view to show more. Elsewhere it does nothing.

A configurable widget (iOS 17+) reads the snapshot stored for the values the user chose:
store one per combination you want to tailor with `options.params`, and one without `params`
as the fallback (and for iOS 14–16 and Android, where widgets are static).

params.name: options
params.doc: params: the configurable widget's parameter values this snapshot is for.

symbols.doc: Options for setWidgetData.
symbols.docFull: Options for {@linkcode setWidgetData}.

symbols.doc: Open the share sheet.
symbols.docFull:
Open the share sheet.

- Inside the native shell with `@capacitor/share` installed (`denext mobile add share`),
  the OS share sheet.
- In a Deno Desktop window under denext's pinned runtime (2.9.7-denext.20 or later), the OS
  share sheet over the window for a `text` or `url`: macOS `NSSharingServicePicker`, Windows
  `DataTransferManager` (it reports no more than that the sheet was shown: `"shared"`). Linux has
  none, so the paths below run. To share files, use `shareFromWindow` from
  `denext/desktop/window`.
- Otherwise `navigator.share` where the browser has it (and `canShare` accepts the data).
- Otherwise the text and URL are copied to the clipboard (joined by a space), and the
  result is `"copied"` so the UI can say so.

A dismissed sheet resolves `"cancelled"` rather than rejecting.

symbols.name: showContextMenu
symbols.signature: showContextMenu(items: readonly ContextMenuItem[], options?: ContextMenuOptions): Promise<string | null>
symbols.doc: Open a context menu and resolve the chosen item's id, or null if it was dismissed.
symbols.docFull:
Open a context menu and resolve the chosen item's `id`, or `null` if it was dismissed.

- Inside the native shell with the `DenextContextMenu` plugin (`denext mobile add
  context-menu`), the OS menu: on iOS a `UIMenu` at `(x, y)` (the edit-menu presentation,
  iOS 16+; an action sheet on iOS 15) with SF Symbol `systemIcon`s, subtitles, destructive
  and disabled items and submenus; on Android a Material `PopupMenu` anchored at `(x, y)`
  (submenus as labelled groups, destructive items in the error color). For the long-press
  menu that lifts the pressed element (`UIContextMenuInteraction` with its preview), bind the
  element with {@linkcode useContextMenu} instead.
- Inside a Deno Desktop window with the `contextMenu` capability (`denext desktop add
  context-menu`) and denext's pinned runtime, the OS's own menu at `(x, y)`: submenus,
  disabled items, subtitles appended to the label, `destructive` items in red (macOS, Linux and
  the CEF backend; runtime 2.9.7-denext.20), an `iconPng` next to the label where the backend
  draws icons, and `null` when the user dismisses it (`icon` and `systemIcon` are not drawn there;
  a `title` is a disabled first item). Without the capability, or under the stock runtime, the
  in-page popover below.
- Otherwise (the web, and SSR-safe) an accessible in-DOM popover: `role="menu"`
  with a `role="menuitem"` per item (a submenu is a `role="group"` labelled by its item),
  opened at `(x, y)` or under `anchor`. It is keyboard navigable (Up/Down to move,
  Enter/Space to choose, Escape to dismiss), dismisses on an outside pointer press, respects
  `disabled` (shown, not selectable) and `destructive`, and removes every node and listener it
  added when it resolves.

Every path renders **every** item, so no menu action is silently dropped. Aborting
`options.signal` closes the in-page popover and the shell's native menu (the plugin's
generation-2 `dismiss`), which then resolve `null`.

params.name: items
params.doc: The menu entries (every one is rendered).

params.name: options
params.doc: x/y or anchor for placement, an optional title, and haptic.

symbols.returns: The chosen item's id, or null when dismissed (or in a non-DOM context, or when items is empty).

members.name: rekey
members.doc:
Change the SQLCipher passphrase of a database opened with `encryptionKey` (or keyed with
`PRAGMA key`), as `PRAGMA rekey = '…'` does. In the shell, `@capacitor-community/sqlite` keeps
ONE passphrase for every encrypted database of the app, so this re-encrypts each of them under
`newKey` and then stores it as the plugin's passphrase (in the Keychain / Keystore). Each file
is rewritten inside SQLCipher's own transaction: a process killed during one keeps that file
under the old passphrase, but one killed between two files leaves the app's databases split
between the passphrases (keep one encrypted database per app if you rotate). Keep the new
passphrase beside the old one before calling this and drop the old one once it resolves; after
a crash, open with the old one first and, on `WRONG_KEY`, with the new one (see the mobile
docs). Refused with `KEY_REQUIRED` when the database is not keyed, `UNSUPPORTED`
inside a transaction, and `ENCRYPTION_UNAVAILABLE` on the web and Deno Desktop (no
SQLCipher) or with a plugin that cannot change its passphrase.

members.doc: Close it. Later calls reject.

symbols.name: SqliteEncryptionError

symbols.docFull:
A refused encryption request: `ENCRYPTION_UNAVAILABLE` (this backing has no SQLCipher, or the
plugin has encryption off; nothing ran), `WRONG_KEY` (another passphrase than the one the
plugin keeps), `KEY_REQUIRED` (the database is encrypted: run `PRAGMA key` first; or a rekey
of a database that was never keyed) or `UNSUPPORTED` (a key pragma other than
`PRAGMA key = '…'` / `PRAGMA rekey = '…'` as the first statement, such as `PRAGMA hexkey`, or
a rekey inside a transaction).

Open it encrypted (SQLCipher) with this passphrase, as `PRAGMA key = '…'` does: only in the
shell, through `@capacitor-community/sqlite` with encryption on in `capacitor.config.ts`

symbols.name: uploadFile
symbols.signature: uploadFile(url: string, path: string, options?: UploadFileOptions): Promise<UploadFileResult>
symbols.doc: Upload a file to a URL, with progress.
symbols.docFull:
Upload a file to a URL, with progress.

- Inside the native shell with denext's `DenextTransfer` plugin (`denext mobile add
  file-transfer`), the OS's background transfer service sends it (a `URLSession` background
  session on iOS, WorkManager on Android), straight from the file: it carries on while the
  app is in the background, and CORS does not apply.
- Otherwise the page sends it (`XMLHttpRequest`, for upload progress; `fetch` where there is
  none), read from the app's storage (the native filesystem plugin, the desktop runtime, or
  OPFS). CORS applies.

Uploads cannot pause; a cancelled or failed one starts over when resumed.

params.name: url
params.doc: The http(s) URL to send it to.

params.name: path
params.doc: The file's path inside directory; no .. segments.

params.name: options
params.doc: directory (default "data"), method (default "POST"), as ("multipart", the default, or "binary"), field, fileName, mimeType, fields, and the transfer's id, headers, onProgress, signal and background.

symbols.returns: The response's status, headers and body. It rejects on a non-2xx response (a FileTransferError with the status and body), on a network error, and with the signal's reason when signal aborts it.

symbols.signature: useBackSwipe(onBack: () => void, opts?: BackSwipeOptions): (el: Element | null) => void
symbols.doc: Swipe right to go back. Returns a ref callback: attach it to the element that should recognize the gesture (often the page's scroll container). A touch that travels rightward at least minDistance CSS px (default 72), with horizontal travel at least ratio (default 1.4) × vertical travel, fires onBack once, as soon as it qualifies.
symbols.docFull:
Swipe right to go back. Returns a ref callback: attach it to the element that should
recognize the gesture (often the page's scroll container). A touch that travels rightward at
least `minDistance` CSS px (default 72), with horizontal travel at least `ratio` (default
1.4) × vertical travel, fires `onBack` once, as soon as it qualifies.

It yields, and never fires, when the touch starts inside an editable element (`input`,
`textarea`, `select`, contenteditable) or inside an element scrolled away from its left
edge (`scrollLeft > 0`), so carousels and code blocks keep their own horizontal pans. Only
touch pointers count (`pointerType === "touch"`); mouse and pen are ignored.

`onBack` and `opts` are held in refs: changing them between renders never re-binds, and the
returned ref callback is stable. Give the element `touch-action: pan-y` so the browser does
not claim horizontal pans for itself (which would cancel the pointer stream).

params.name: onBack
params.doc: Called when a back swipe is recognized, e.g. () => router.back().

symbols.returns: A ref callback for the element to watch.

  add keep-awake`), the native flag. Several mounted callers share it: the screen may sleep
  again once the last one unmounts or turns `active` off.
- In a Deno Desktop window (`denext desktop add keep-awake`), an OS assertion held by the
  desktop runtime (`caffeinate`, `SetThreadExecutionState` or `systemd-inhibit`), which
  also keeps the machine from sleeping.
- Otherwise the Screen Wake Lock API (`navigator.wakeLock`), re-acquired whenever the page
  becomes visible again, since the browser releases it on every hide. Where the browser has
  no wake lock, or refuses one, it does nothing.

The values are the same expressions SAFE_AREA_CSS uses, measured through a hidden fixed element, so they need viewport-fit=cover too. All zero during SSR and before mount.
symbols.docFull:
The device's safe-area insets in CSS px (`{ top, right, bottom, left }`), kept up to date on
rotation, window and visual-viewport resizes, and when Capacitor updates the insets it
injects (on Android the bottom inset drops to 0 while the keyboard is up). The values are the
same expressions {@linkcode SAFE_AREA_CSS} uses, measured through a hidden fixed element,
so they need `viewport-fit=cover` too. All zero during SSR and before mount.

Use {@linkcode SAFE_AREA_CSS} for layout (CSS applies the insets without a render); use this
when JavaScript needs the numbers: positioning a canvas, a sheet's resting height, a
gesture's edge zone.

Install Clerk's native bridge in the Capacitor shell (see the module docs). Call it once, before
the page's Clerk code loads clerk-js — from `instrumentation-client.ts` in an App Router app, or
at the top of a SPA entry. Outside the shell (the web, Deno Desktop) it installs nothing.

and the scheme's registration), `<scheme>://app/` on the Clerk instance's native redirect
allowlist, and the shell's page origin (`capacitor://localhost` on iOS, `https://localhost` on
Android) in its allowed origins: native mode sends `Authorization` and the WebView adds
`Origin`, and the Frontend API refuses both together from an origin it does not allow.

symbols.docFull:
Install every update on offer, reporting each step to `onProgress`: on a phone the new UI, on
Deno Desktop the whole app (or, when no newer app is on offer, the UI overlay), in a browser
the newer deploy. It never
throws; a target that failed is listed in `failures` (and reported as `stage: "failed"`).

When installing replaces the running page (a phone's UI switch, a browser reload, a desktop
app's install-and-relaunch), the promise does not settle. A desktop UI overlay alone is
served from the next launch: the result says `restartRequired`. A second call while one runs
finds the first's download in progress and reports it (`busy` on desktop).

symbols.name: StackAnimation
symbols.doc: How a screen enters and leaves a stack. The names follow react-native-screens' native-stack animation option:
symbols.docFull:
How a screen enters and leaves a stack. The names follow `react-native-screens`'
native-stack `animation` option:

- `"default"`: the platform's own (`"ios_from_right"` on iOS and the web,
  `"shared_axis_x"` on Android).
- `"ios_from_right"` / `"ios_from_left"`: the iOS push, with the screen below sliding a
  third of the way under and dimming (parallax).
- `"slide_from_right"` / `"slide_from_left"` / `"simple_push"`: both screens slide by a
  full width, no parallax (`"simple_push"` is `"slide_from_right"`).
- `"slide_from_bottom"`: the screen rises from the bottom edge (a full-screen modal).
- `"fade"`: a cross-fade.
- `"fade_from_bottom"`: Android 8's rise-and-fade.
- `"shared_axis_x"`: Material's shared-axis X (fade through with a short horizontal shift).
- `"none"`: no animation.

symbols.doc: Start an exhaustive match over a literal union or a discriminated union:
symbols.docFull:
Start an exhaustive match over a literal union or a discriminated union:

```ts
type Shape = { kind: "circle"; r: number } | { kind: "square"; side: number };
const area = match(shape)
  .with({ kind: "circle" }, (s) => Math.PI * s.r ** 2)
  .with({ kind: "square" }, (s) => s.side ** 2)
  .exhaustive(); // drop a case and this line stops compiling
```

symbols.name: postgresConnection
symbols.signature: postgresConnection(url: string, schemaOption: string | undefined): { url: string; options: DenoSqlOptions; schema: string | undefined }
symbols.doc: A Postgres URL with Prisma's own parameters read into Deno.SQL options and removed, as PrismaDenoSql does before it connects. schema becomes the search_path, connection_limit the pool's max, connect_timeout (or pool_timeout) the connectionTimeout, and pgbouncer=true turns prepared statements off; Prisma-only parameters a server would refuse (socket_timeout, statement_cache_size, sslaccept, …) are dropped. symbols.docFull:
A Postgres URL with Prisma's own parameters read into `Deno.SQL` options and removed, as
{@linkcode PrismaDenoSql} does before it connects. `schema` becomes the `search_path`,
`connection_limit` the pool's `max`, `connect_timeout` (or `pool_timeout`) the
`connectionTimeout`, and `pgbouncer=true` turns prepared statements off; Prisma-only
parameters a server would refuse (`socket_timeout`, `statement_cache_size`, `sslaccept`, …)
are dropped. Use it to open a `Deno.SQL` client of your own from a Prisma `DATABASE_URL`.

```ts
const { url, options } = postgresConnection(Deno.env.get("DATABASE_URL")!, undefined);
const adapter = new PrismaDenoSql(new Deno.SQL(url, { ...options, max: 20 }));
```

The `client:*` directive props: a Flight route's island hydration markers, and in SPA mode the
deferred mount of a code-split component. The build strips every `client:*` key before it
reaches the component or the DOM; they are authoring markers, not real props.

Each key admits an explicit `undefined`, as React's own `Attributes` do: under
`exactOptionalPropertyTypes` a props type that spells its optional keys `?: T | undefined`
(Base UI's, any mapped `Partial`) is spread onto elements whose `Attributes` include these.

members.name: parse
members.signature: parse(argv: string[], extraVerbs?: readonly string[]): ParseOutcome
members.doc:
Parse a full argv (as in `Deno.args`) into an actionable {@linkcode ParseOutcome}.
Resolves the leading verb — the first bare token, skipping the value of a valued
{@linkcode GLOBAL_FLAGS} entry (`--cwd <dir>`) — then parses every other token against
that command's flag schema merged with {@linkcode GLOBAL_FLAGS}, so a global flag may
sit before the verb. `--help`/`-h` and `--version`/`-v` are recognized before and after
the verb; a help flag BEFORE the verb never runs it: `denext --help build` is build's
help, and a leading token that is not a verb (`denext --help ./app`) is top-level help.

plus `project` — the verbs a project contributes, which the CLI reads from the last
discovery's cache rather than importing the project for. A registered verb carrying a
non-core {@linkcode CommandSpec.source} (a plugin verb or a config entry) joins them,
and a name the registry already has is never repeated.

symbols.name: buildNextCompatModules
symbols.doc: Build react→denext-rewritten SSR bundles for a set of route source modules, each RE-EXPORTING the source module's shape (default + named exports: metadata/generateMetadata/segment-config/…) rather than wrapping it in a render(). The main SSR loader (createNextCompatServerLoader) returns these instead of the raw source, so the whole route subtree — including npm React libraries imported inside it — runs on denext's single React.
symbols.docFull:
Build react→denext-rewritten SSR bundles for a set of route source modules,
each RE-EXPORTING the source module's shape (`default` + named exports:
`metadata`/`generateMetadata`/segment-config/…) rather than wrapping it in a
`render()`. The main SSR loader ({@link createNextCompatServerLoader}) returns
these instead of the raw source, so the whole route subtree — including npm
React libraries imported inside it — runs on denext's single React.

All modules are bundled in ONE code-split pass ({@link bundleNextCompatModules})
so they share one denext runtime chunk → a single denext instance at runtime.

Callers manage the esbuild lifecycle (dev keeps the service warm; a one-shot
build should wrap in {@link withEsbuild}). The denext runtime is prebuilt once
per call into `outDir/server/runtime/`.

SSR bundles inline a prebuilt denext runtime; the hook dispatcher lives on
globalThis (see `src/runtime/hooks.ts`), so this bundled denext copy shares the
one dispatcher denext's source SSR renderer installs → hooks in the rendered
(npm React) components resolve correctly.
symbols.returns: Map of absolute source path → absolute server bundle path.

symbols.name: captureRequestContext
symbols.signature: captureRequestContext(init: { headers?: Record<string, string> }): <T>(fn: () => T) => T
symbols.doc: Capture the current request so its session can be read again later, outside it — what a plugin holding a long-lived connection (a WebSocket it upgraded) uses to re-check who is on the other end: the returned function runs fn in a fresh request context for a copy of this request (its URL, its headers — cookies included — and its client address, with the app's proxy trust and limit policy), so auth(), cookies() and clientIpForLimits() answer as they did for the original. Capture BEFORE Deno.upgradeWebSocket, which consumes the request. Outside a request the function runs fn as it is.

Capture the current request so its session can be read again later, outside it — what a
plugin holding a long-lived connection (a WebSocket it upgraded) uses to re-check who is on
the other end: the returned function runs `fn` in a fresh request context for a copy of this
request (its URL, its headers — cookies included — and its client address, with the app's

members.doc: End every subscription to `key` (or one peer's); the client sees `denied`. Cluster-wide.

members.name: discard
members.doc:
Drop THIS instance's publishes of `key` that its Live hub has not yet sent to a subscriber:
those inside the hub's coalescing window, or still in the transport. Later publishes are
delivered as usual. Per instance: another instance's publishes of the key — in its hub's
window, or on their way through a shared transport — are not reached, nor are frames already
held for a connected subscriber. A key whose next subscriber must not get what was published
for an earlier one (a subscription re-authorized under other claims, on any instance) is
protected by stamping its publishes with a `grant` and having `authorize` answer one
({@linkcode ChannelPublishOptions.grant}); `discard` is the local complement, not that
guarantee.

members.doc:
Rendering mode. Omit (the default) for the App Router (SSR/SSG) pipeline.
`"spa"` builds {@link SpaConfig.entry} as a pure client-side-rendered app —
React but not Next: no `app/` directory, no SSR, no Flight. denext bundles the
entry, emits an HTML shell around it, serves it with a history-API fallback, and
(via `denext export` / `deno desktop`) packages it as a static app. Use it to
host an existing Vite-style React SPA on denext's toolchain and runtime.

members.doc: Serve the app under a sub-path (e.g. `/docs`). Stripped before routing.

members.name: trailingSlash
members.doc:
Enforce a trailing slash on page URLs (308-redirect to normalize). Unset or `false`
(Next's default) redirects `/about/` → `/about`.

members.name: assetPrefix
members.doc: Prefix for client bundle/asset URLs (e.g. a CDN origin).

members.name: scheduledJobs
members.doc:
Cron schedules for background jobs: a map of a 5-field cron expression to the job name(s)
to run on it (a job is `jobs/<name>.ts` exporting `defineJob(...)`). Registered at server
startup via `Deno.cron` when the runtime exposes it (Deno Deploy, or `--unstable-cron`) and a
dependency-free minute-tick scheduler otherwise. A task may also declare its own `schedule`.

```ts
scheduledJobs: { "0 3 * * *": "cleanup", "0 0 * * 1": ["digest", "warm-cache"] }
```

members.name: jobs
members.doc:
Scheduled/background job behaviour. Currently run history, which is off unless asked for.

```ts
jobs: { history: true }
```

members.name: images
members.doc:
Image-optimization config. Remote sources are refused by default (local-only,
SSRF-safe); allowlist hosts here to enable optimizing remote images.

members.name: tailwind
members.doc:
Tailwind CSS integration. When set, denext manages the Tailwind v4 standalone
binary and compiles `input` → `output` automatically on `dev`/`build`.

members.name: mdx
cache
members.doc:
Cache Components / ISR data + page cache store. Omit to let denext resolve the
default at startup — the durable `node:sqlite` store when a writable filesystem is
available, else the in-memory store. Set {@link CacheConfig.store} to force a choice,
or pass your own {@link CacheStore}.

members.name: hsts
members.doc:
`Strict-Transport-Security` (HSTS) header tuning, applied to responses served
over HTTPS. Defaults to `max-age=31536000` (1 year, host-only — no
`includeSubDomains`/`preload`, a safe default that can't brick sibling
subdomains). Set fields to opt into a stronger policy, or `false` to omit the
header entirely (e.g. when your edge sets it).

members.name: csp
members.doc:
App-wide Content-Security-Policy default (three-state), overridable per file:
- `"strict"` (default) — denext's hash-based strict policy on buffered pages.
- `"off"` — emit no CSP header at all (set your policy at the edge, or for
  Next.js-style "CSP is the app's job" behavior). A route can still opt back in
  with its own `csp` export.
- a {@link CspSetting} object — the strict policy plus these global opt-ins
  (`scriptSrc`, `styleSrc`, `imgSrc`, `connectSrc`, `fontSrc`, `frameSrc`,
  `mediaSrc`, `workerSrc`; e.g. `{ frameSrc: ["https://js.stripe.com"] }` for
  Stripe's Payment Element iframes).

A route's `csp` export overrides this for that route. Streamed responses (PPR /
incremental streaming) carry the **same** strict hash-based CSP, computed from the
buffered shell prefix plus the hashed swap-runtime constant (see
{@link resolveStreamingCsp}); the one inherent limit is that an inline
`<style>`/`<script>` appearing inside a streamed hole (flushed after the head) is
not covered by the header — see [KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md]. Absent ⇒ `"strict"`.

members.name: publicEnv
members.doc:
Public-env vars to always embed in the page island, in addition to the ones
the build detects the client references. Use this to force-include a key the
client reads via a computed expression (`publicEnv()["NEXT_PUBLIC_" + x]`),
which the build can't see. Referenced keys are shipped automatically; this only
adds to that set.

members.name: streaming
members.doc:
Incremental (Suspense) streaming, **on by default**; set `false` to opt out.
A page with a pending Suspense boundary flushes its shell first and streams each
boundary's content as it resolves; a fully synchronous page (no holes) is still
delivered buffered, so it stays shared-cacheable. Streamed responses carry the
same strict hash-based CSP as buffered ones (the swap runtime is a hashed
constant), survive a failing boundary (its fallback stays), and cover Flight
routes. ISR/PPR-cacheable routes (revalidate/force-static) and soft navigations
take their own path first, so streaming never bypasses the page cache. A shipped,
default-on capability — not an experiment.

members.name: live
members.doc:
Live Server Components security policy: authorization hooks and resource caps
for the `<Live>` / `useLive` / `usePresence` WebSocket hub. See {@link LiveConfig}.
Presence/data are default-deny in production without a policy here — so this is a
**security-policy** field, not an on/off experiment.

members.name: apiBatch
members.doc:
The typed-API batch endpoint (`POST /_denext/api-batch`: N GET/HEAD calls from
`createApiClient` in one round trip). Same-origin only; caps on items, body, fan-out
concurrency, and per-item response size. See {@link ApiBatchConfig}.

members.name: apiMaxBodyBytes
members.doc:
The request-body cap for route handlers (`route.ts`), in bytes — default 1 MiB. A route
raises or lifts its own with `export const maxBodyBytes = N | false`; a `defineApi`
endpoint with `maxBodyBytes` in its definition overrides both. Over the cap → 413.

members.name: cors
members.doc:
Cross-origin (CORS) access to route handlers and the native `denextAuth` endpoints —
what a Capacitor shell or a front end on another origin needs. Off by default (no CORS
headers at all). A route overrides it with `export const cors = { … } | false`. See
{@link CorsConfig}.

members.name: appLinks
members.doc:
The domain-association files for the app's universal links (iOS) and App Links (Android):
`denext start` and `denext dev` serve `/.well-known/apple-app-site-association` and
`/.well-known/assetlinks.json` from it (`application/json`, `200`, never redirected), and
`denext export` writes both into the export. Pair it with `denext mobile add deep-links
--domain <host>`. See {@link AppLinksConfig}.

members.name: actionMaxBodyBytes
members.doc:
The request-body cap for Server Actions, in bytes — default 1 MiB (Next's default). Raise
it only for actions that accept large payloads (multipart uploads); over the cap → 413
before the action runs. `denext start`/`dev` forward it to the server; a custom server
passes `actionMaxBodyBytes` to `createApp()` itself.

members.name: canonicalOrigin
members.doc:
The app's public origin (e.g. `"https://example.com"`), pinned outright: absolute URLs
(canonical, `og:image`), the Server Action origin check and HSTS all use it instead of
the `Host` / forwarded headers — the robust choice behind a proxy that rewrites `Host`.
A full origin (scheme + host, no path). Unset, the `DENEXT_CANONICAL_ORIGIN` env var is
read at boot (config > env > derived from the request).

members.name: trustForwardedHeaders
members.doc:
Trust `X-Forwarded-Proto` / `X-Forwarded-Host` from a reverse proxy when deriving the
request origin (absolute URLs, the Server Action origin check, HSTS), and
`X-Forwarded-For` / an inbound `X-Request-Id` for `clientIp()`, `requestId()` and the
rate limiters (`denextAuth` and `rateLimit()` inherit it unless they set their own). Enable
ONLY when clients cannot reach denext directly — a client that can spoofs them. The origin
part is ignored when {@link DenextConfig.canonicalOrigin} is set. Unset,
`DENEXT_TRUST_PROXY=1` turns it on (config > env > `false`).

members.name: rateLimitHeader
members.doc:
A request header the fronting proxy sets to the client address — `"cf-connecting-ip"`
(Cloudflare), `"fly-client-ip"` (Fly.io), `"x-real-ip"` (nginx) — that every **per-address
limit** keys on: `rateLimit()`, `denextAuth`'s per-IP budgets,
`live.limits.maxConnectionsPerIp`, `@denext/backend` realtime's signed-out quota and
`clientIpForLimits()`. Supabase Auth's `GOTRUE_RATE_LIMIT_HEADER`, for denext. When a request
carries an IP address in it (its last comma-separated value), that address is the limit key,
IPv6 bucketed by /64 and an IPv4-mapped address as its IPv4 — a loopback/private one too.

A request **without** it (or with a value that is not an IP address) did not come through
the proxy that sets it, so it falls back to the rule without this option (the trusted
`x-forwarded-for` hop, else the socket peer) and one warning is logged — where Supabase Auth
applies no limit at all to it, which would let anyone who reaches the server directly skip
every limit by leaving the header out.

The header is believed only from a **trusted proxy**: a socket peer inside
{@link DenextConfig.rateLimitTrustedProxies}, or — with none listed — a loopback/private peer
while {@link DenextConfig.trustForwardedHeaders} is on. From any other peer it is ignored and
the limit keys on that peer (one warning), so a client that reaches the server directly (a
leaked origin IP, an exposed app port) cannot pick a fresh bucket per request by sending its
own value. Supabase Auth's `GOTRUE_RATE_LIMIT_HEADER` trusts the header from anyone; denext
does not, because that one misconfiguration fails open silently. With neither trust rule set
the header is never believed and a warning says so at boot.

It only names the LIMIT address: `clientIp()` still follows `trustForwardedHeaders`. Unset,
the `DENEXT_RATE_LIMIT_HEADER` env var is read at boot (config > env > none).

members.name: rateLimitTrustedProxies
members.doc:
The proxies whose {@link DenextConfig.rateLimitHeader} is believed: CIDR ranges or single
addresses (`["173.245.48.0/20", "2400:cb00::/32"]` for Cloudflare's published ranges,
`["10.0.0.0/8"]` for an nginx or Fly proxy on a private network). A request whose socket peer
is outside every range keys its per-address limits on that peer instead. Unset (or empty):
a loopback/private peer when `trustForwardedHeaders` is on, else none. Unset, the
`DENEXT_RATE_LIMIT_TRUSTED_PROXIES` env var (comma-separated) is read at boot
(config > env > none).

members.name: rateLimitLocalAddresses
members.doc:
Apply per-address limits (`rateLimit()`, `denextAuth`'s per-IP budgets,
`live.limits.maxConnectionsPerIp`, `@denext/backend` realtime's signed-out quota,
`clientIpForLimits()`) to a loopback, private, link-local or unique-local socket peer too,
counted by its own address. Default `false`: such a peer is usually a reverse proxy every
visitor shares, so its limit would be site-wide, and the limits are skipped for it with a
warning. Turn it on where those peers are real clients — a LAN or VPN deployment, a
container network with no proxy in front. A trusted forwarded hop or a
{@link DenextConfig.rateLimitHeader} address still takes precedence. Unset,
`DENEXT_RATE_LIMIT_LOCAL_ADDRESSES=1` turns it on (config > env > `false`).

members.name: allowedDevOrigins
members.doc:
`denext dev` only: extra hosts allowed to reach the dev server's `/_denext/*` assets (the
bundles, the module graph, the reload stream, the Live hub), beyond loopback. Each entry is
an origin (`"http://192.168.1.5:3000"`) or a bare host (`"192.168.1.5"`, `"mac.local"`,
`"mac.local:3000"`); matching is on the hostname. Wildcards are not supported: list each
host. Mirrors Next.js's `allowedDevOrigins`. An entry may also be a Deno Desktop app's
custom-scheme origin (`"myapp://app"`, validated as `desktop.app.origin` is), which admits a
request whose `Origin` is exactly that value — for a backend project that a separate desktop
app talks to. The project's own `desktop.app.origin` is admitted without listing it.

Without it the dev server refuses those assets to any non-loopback `Host` (the DNS-rebinding
defense, cf. CVE-2025-48068), so a phone or another machine gets a dead page. You rarely
need to set it by hand: `denext dev --lan` and an explicit `--host` allow the address they
bind, and `--allowed-dev-origin <origin>` adds entries for one run. A listed host is
trusted as a dev client: anything on the network that can reach it (and send that `Host`)
can read the app's transformed source, as a loopback client can. Ignored by `denext start`.

members.name: requestTimeout
members.doc:
Per-request deadline in milliseconds — default 30 000. A request still running past it
is aborted and answered `503`; the per-request `AbortSignal` fires so cooperative work
(`fetch(url, { signal })`) cancels. `0` disables the deadline. Unset, the
`DENEXT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` env var is read at boot (config > env > default).

members.name: maxConcurrency
members.doc:
In-process concurrency ceiling: the max number of client requests one instance handles
at once. A request arriving at capacity is shed immediately with `503` + `Retry-After`
(never queued). Bounds work up to the point the `Response` is produced (a streaming
body's client-read time is not counted); background ISR regeneration is exempt. A
complement to — not a replacement for — the edge/load-balancer ceiling. Default: no
limit. Unset, the `DENEXT_MAX_CONCURRENCY` env var is read at boot (config > env >
unlimited).

members.name: slotBackstop
members.doc:
With {@link DenextConfig.maxConcurrency} set and {@link DenextConfig.requestTimeout} `0`,
the milliseconds after which a never-settling request's concurrency slot is force-freed
(default 120 000). It frees only the slot — the render is not aborted, since the request
timeout was opted out of. Inert while a request timeout is in place.

members.name: cacheKeyParams
members.doc:
Allowlist of query-parameter names that fork the ISR page-cache key. When set, only these
params make a distinct cached entry; every other param (`?utm_*`, `?fbclid`, a random
cache-buster) is ignored for keying — but still reaches the render via `searchParams`, so
list every param whose value changes cacheable output. Unset, every param participates.

members.name: cdnCacheHeaders
members.doc:
Send shared-cache headers with ISR pages — **off by default** (opt-in). With `true`, a page
served from the ISR cache (and the render that stores it) answers `Cache-Control: public,
s-maxage=<seconds it stays fresh>, stale-while-revalidate=31536000` (`public,
s-maxage=31536000` for `force-static`), so a CDN in front caches it as long as denext would.
Never for a request carrying a `Cookie` or `Authorization`, a response that sets a cookie, a
non-200, a dynamic render, a response whose `Cache-Control` middleware or a `headers()` rule
already set, or a request a `middleware.ts` matched (`{ evenWithMiddleware: true }` sends it
there too).

The risk: a CDN keys a page on its URL alone, so a page gated on anything else the cached
render didn't read — an IP allow-list, an auth proxy's header, geolocation,
`Accept-Language` — is served from the CDN to everyone once one allowed visitor fetched it.
Turn it on only for pages every visitor may see.

members.name: compress
members.doc:
Compress dynamic responses (rendered HTML, Flight/JSON payloads, route-handler text/JSON/
JS/CSS/SVG/XML) — **on by default**, like Next.js's `compress`. gzip by default (as
Next.js); brotli (quality 5: markedly smaller output for about two to three times gzip's
CPU) only when listed in `{ encodings }` (`{ encodings: ["br", "gzip"] }`). Negotiated from
`Accept-Encoding` (q-values; a tie goes to the earlier listed coding) through `node:zlib`,
flushed explicitly; streamed (Suspense/PPR) HTML is compressed chunk by chunk with a
flush per chunk, so it still reaches the browser progressively. Skipped for bodies under
1 KiB, `text/event-stream`, already-compressed types (images, fonts, video, archives),
a response that already has a `Content-Encoding`, `Cache-Control: no-transform`, range
responses, `HEAD` and `204`/`304`. A page, layout or route handler opts out with
`export const compress = false`. Build-time precompressed client bundles (`.gz`) are
served as-is. Set `false` when a proxy in front (nginx, Cloudflare, a CDN) compresses.

members.name: nodeResolve
members.doc:
denext's tolerant node_modules resolver for the compat (npm-React) build — default ON.

Every bare npm specifier is resolved straight from the app's installed `node_modules`
using denext's own resolver, a strict superset of Deno's `npm:` loader: it honors
`exports` wildcard globs, falls back to a plain subpath, and returns nothing on a miss
(so the deno-loader still gets its shot). This is what makes an unmodified
pnpm/npm/yarn/bun app build with no catalog-concretizing and no hand-patching of
dependency `exports` — the "seamless migration" contract. Set `false` only to force
app deps back through Deno's strict `npm:` loader (escape hatch). The pre-2.0 home,
`experimental.nodeResolve`, was removed in 3.0 (setting it is a config error).

members.name: cacheComponents
members.doc:
Cache Components (Next.js 16): the `"use cache"` directive is compiled into
cross-request caching on the server (`src/build/use-cache-transform.ts`), plus the
PPR render path — dynamic-by-default rendering with cacheable `use cache` islands (a
cached shell with per-request dynamic holes spliced in). A stable, **opt-in**
feature, deliberately **off by default**: caching stays a choice, because a cache
bug's failure class (a poisoned or cross-user shell) is severe and must not be
imposed on apps that never asked. When off, every `"use cache"` directive is inert
(a plain no-op string statement) and rendering is unchanged.

Documented bounds (see KNOWN-LIMITATIONS): as in Next.js, reading request data
(`cookies()`/`headers()`) inside `use cache` throws (`"use cache: private"` may read
them); a streamed hole can't add an
inline `<style>`/`<script>` or hoist an in-boundary `<title>`/`<meta>` into the
already-flushed head. With `cacheKeyParams` set, reading a `searchParams` name outside
it postpones like `cookies()` (outside every Suspense boundary, the page renders per
request and is not stored).

Next.js's `experimental.cacheComponents` spelling is kept as an obsolete alias for
migrated Next apps (see {@linkcode resolveCacheComponents}); this top-level field wins.

members.name: cacheLife
members.doc:
Named `cacheLife()` profiles (Next.js 16's `cacheLife` key), each `{ stale, revalidate,
expire }` in seconds (`Infinity` for never): `cacheLife("biweekly")` inside a
`"use cache"` function picks one. A name that matches a built-in profile (`default`,
`seconds`, `minutes`, `hours`, `days`, `weeks`, `max`) overrides it; a field left out of
a custom profile falls back to the `default` profile's. Validated at load as Next.js does
(`false` is refused, `expire` must be at least `revalidate`).

members.name: reactCompiler
members.doc:
The build-time auto-memoization compiler (a React-Compiler-style pass), an opt-in
optimization that is off by default. Conservative by construction: it bails to
identity whenever a transform isn't provably safe, so it only ever adds memoization,
never changes behavior.

Next.js 15's `experimental.reactCompiler` spelling is honored, with a dev warning, when
this field is absent (the pre-2.0 `experimental.compiler` was removed in 3.0).

members.name: asyncContext
members.doc:
Scope async `startTransition` by transition IDENTITY instead of a time window, so a
post-`await` update is attributed to its transition while an unrelated urgent update in
the pending window keeps its priority. Off by default.

Enables a build-time transform that makes denext's first-party {@link AsyncContext}
survive `await` (src/build/async-context-transform.ts). It instruments every `await`
in client code (a small per-await cost); the default time-window behavior is unchanged
when off. Removes the async-`startTransition` gap in KNOWN-LIMITATIONS when on.

Graduated from `experimental.asyncContext` in 2.5; that spelling was removed in 3.0
(setting it is a config error).

members.name: features
members.doc:
Compile-time feature flags: `feature("KEY")` (from `denext/feature`) always returns the
configured value, and a call with a string-literal KEY is folded to a literal where the
build can, so the bundler dead-code-eliminates the untaken branch. A key not listed
reads `false`.

The server and every client bundle are seeded with this map. The fold (DCE) covers the
native App Router's component (`.tsx`/`.jsx`) modules, the SPA bundle, and dev; the
compat drop-in App Router path and non-component modules on the native path read the
seeded value without DCE. Flag names and states are embedded in the client bundle.

Graduated from `experimental.features` in 2.5; that spelling was removed in 3.0
(setting it is a config error).

members.name: optimizePackageImports
members.doc:
npm packages whose barrel (`index`) imports are rewritten to the files that define each
name, as Next.js's `optimizePackageImports` does: `import { Check } from "lucide-react"`
becomes an import of `lucide-react`'s `icons/check.js`, so the bundler never loads the
barrel. Your list is ADDED to a built-in default (lucide-react, date-fns, lodash-es, …);
a `"!pkg"` entry removes a package from it, and `false` turns the optimization off.

That keeps an icon library's thousand re-exports out of the module graph — and, when the
package also code-splits every icon (`lucide-react/dynamic`), out of the startup chunk
list. Applied to the esbuild bundles (the compat client and server bundles and SPA mode,
in production builds and compat dev rebuilds), for app source and for npm modules that
import a listed package. The unbundled per-module dev server and the native `deno bundle`
path do not apply it.

The built-in default is `lucide-react`, `date-fns`, `lodash-es`, `ramda`, `rxjs`,
`@tabler/icons-react`, `@heroicons/react/{20,24}/solid`, `@heroicons/react/24/outline`,
`react-icons/*`, `@mui/icons-material`, `recharts`, `react-use`, `@headlessui/react`,
`effect`; an entry ending in `/*` matches every subpath of the package, and `"!pkg"`
removes exactly the entry `pkg` (`"!react-icons/*"` drops the wildcard). Only named value
imports are rewritten, and only names the barrel re-exports from another module (a name
the barrel defines itself stays on the barrel); a barrel that runs code of its own
(including a decorator), carries a directive, or cannot be analysed is left untouched.

**Listing a package asserts its modules are side-effect free** (Next.js's contract too):
the modules beside the one a name comes from are never loaded, so a top-level side effect
in one of them no longer runs. Next's `experimental.optimizePackageImports` spelling is
honored, with a dev warning, when this field is absent.

Packages whose own `package.json` declares them side-effect free (`"sideEffects": false`, or
an array naming none of the modules the barrel loads) are looked through automatically,
unlisted: the barrel must be the file the build resolves the specifier to, a name it
re-exports from another package stays on the barrel, and every module the barrel would have
loaded must be side-effect free. That also keeps a lazy route's modules out of the startup
chunks when the startup graph imports other names from the same barrel. `"!pkg"` excludes a
package from the automatic mode too, and `"!*"` turns the automatic mode off.

members.name: nextScriptWorkers
members.doc:
Run `<Script strategy="worker">` in a web worker through Partytown, as Next.js does (its
`experimental.nextScriptWorkers`, honored with a dev warning when this field is absent).
The app installs Partytown itself — `@qwik.dev/partytown`, or Next's
`@builder.io/partytown`, in `node_modules` — and `denext dev` / `build` / `export` serve its
files from the app's own origin under `/_denext/~partytown/`, so the strict default CSP
needs no opt-in. Off (the default), or with no Partytown installed, worker scripts run on
the main thread as `afterInteractive`, with a dev warning naming the fix.

members.name: resolveAlias
members.doc:
Module aliases for the esbuild bundles, optionally sensitive to the importing file, as
Metro's `resolveRequest` and Vite's `resolve.alias` express them. A key is an import
specifier, matched exactly; its value is where that import goes: a package or package
subpath (`"uniwind/components/web"`), or a `./` file of the project. The object form's
`except` lists packages whose OWN imports of the key keep the original module, the shape a
library that wraps the module it replaces needs (uniwind's `react-native`).

```ts
resolveAlias: {
  "react-native": { to: "uniwind/components/web", except: ["uniwind"] },
  "legacy-sdk": "./src/web/legacy-sdk.ts",
}
```

Applied ahead of every other resolver in SPA and React Native mode, the next-compat App
Router's client and server bundles, and `denext dev`'s dependency bundles; the target is
resolved through the same build, so its own resolution rules apply. The native App
Router path (`deno bundle`) resolves through the import map instead: use `deno.json`
`imports`, and `scopes` for an importer-sensitive entry.

members.name: momentumSafeScroll
members.doc:
Keep iOS momentum scrolling alive while scroll-anchoring code corrects the scroll offset —
default ON. In iOS WebKit (Safari, WKWebView, Capacitor) any programmatic scroll write
during a touch fling (`scrollBy`, `scrollTo`, assigning `scrollTop`) stops the fling dead,
and virtualized lists (LegendList, react-virtuoso, TanStack Virtual) issue exactly such
writes to compensate for rows measured taller or shorter than estimated. The client
runtime therefore defers those writes during a gesture (see `installMomentumSafeScroll`
in `denext/mobile`) and applies them in one step once the scroller comes to rest.

It installs only on iOS/iPadOS WebKit, loaded as its own chunk, so other platforms pay a
user-agent check and nothing more. Set `false` to opt out.

members.name: lists
members.doc:
Which engine runs the DOM list packages. `"denext"`: `@legendapp/list/react` (LegendList's
DOM build), imported by the app or by its packages, runs on denext's `VirtualList` with
LegendList's props, ref methods (`scrollToEnd`, `scrollToIndex`, `getState`, …) and cell
hooks, in SPA mode and on the App Router (server render included); the app's source stays
unchanged. `"library"` (the default): the real package. Applies to apps that use npm React
(the esbuild build path). React Native mode's own list packages are `reactNative.lists`.

members.name: platformExtensions
members.doc:
Platform-specific files: an import of `./BigButton` (or `./BigButton.tsx`) resolves to
`BigButton.ios.tsx` in the iOS export, `BigButton.desktop.tsx` in a desktop package,
`BigButton.web.tsx` on the web, and to the plain file where a target has no variant. The
probe order per target (most specific first): web `.web`; ios `.ios` → `.mobile` → `.web`;
android `.android` → `.mobile` → `.web`; macos / windows / linux the OS → `.desktop` →
`.web`. Applies to the app's own modules (packages in `node_modules` keep their own
resolution). `{ native: true }` also probes React Native's `.native` after the OS on ios and
android (off by default: `.native` files are usually native code, which a WebView cannot
run). In React Native mode the app's `.ios` / `.android` files are native code too, so they
are not probed unless `{ osFiles: true }`. `false` turns platform files off. See
{@link https://denext.dev/docs/platform-files}.

members.name: mobile
members.doc:
Capacitor shell settings for `denext mobile build` and `denext mobile assets`: build flavors
(per-flavor app id, name, server URL, icon and splash). See
{@link https://denext.dev/docs/mobile-build}.

members.name: desktop
members.doc:
Deno Desktop native capabilities: the allowlist the desktop runtime's capability bridge
serves (default deny) and the source the package scripts derive least-privilege `--allow-*`
from. Written by `denext desktop add <cap>`. Distinct from {@link SpaConfig.desktop} (packaging
settings such as the icon); the two may be unified in a later release. Docs:
https://denext.dev/docs/desktop

members.name: compile
members.doc:
`denext build --compile`: the single-executable server build (`deno compile` on denext's
Deno toolchain). What the binary embeds beyond what denext finds itself, and the `--allow-*`
baked into it beyond the least-privilege baseline. See
{@link https://denext.dev/docs/deployment-targets#a-single-binary-with-denext-build---compile}.

members.name: start
members.doc:
The production server (`denext start`, the `build --compile` executable, the generated Docker
image and systemd unit): its idle memory trim and its resource limits. See
{@link https://denext.dev/docs/deployment-targets#idle-memory-trim}.

members.name: deploy
members.doc:
Deploy adapter: `denext build` runs its `prepare` with the typed deploy manifest
(`.denext/deploy-manifest.json`) after every build, and `denext deploy` pushes with it. A
preset from `denext/deploy` (`docker()`, `fly()`, `denoDeploy()`, `genericHost()`,
`staticHost()`) or your own adapter. See {@link https://denext.dev/docs/deploy#deploy-adapters}.

members.name: reactNative
members.doc:
Build a React Native / Expo app's source for the web through `react-native-web`, in SPA
mode (`mode: "spa"`) or on the App Router. `true` turns on the defaults; an object sets
options.

- `react-native` (and every `react-native/…` subpath) resolves to the installed
  `react-native-web`, for every importer, even when a real `react-native` is installed.
  A deep `react-native/Libraries/…` import maps to react-native-web's equivalent where one
  exists, else to a stub that throws, naming the import, when it is called.
- Web platform files win: `.web.tsx`, `.web.ts`, `.web.jsx` and `.web.js` are probed
  before the plain extensions, for relative and alias imports and for package subpaths.
- `.js` files are parsed as JSX (React Native libraries ship JSX in `.js`).
- `__DEV__` (true in dev, false in a production build), `global` → `globalThis` and
  `process.env.EXPO_OS` → `"web"` are defined at build time.
- The SPA shell gets Expo web's root style (see {@link ReactNativeConfig.rootStyle}).

The build always takes the esbuild (compat) path. Install `react-native-web` in the
project; native-only modules still need web shims of your own.

On the App Router, the server bundle, the client islands and the hydrated routes all
resolve this way, so Server Components and `"use client"` components can both import
`react-native`; react-native-web's style sheet is written into each server-rendered
`<head>` (`<style id="react-native-stylesheet">`). `expo-router` imports fail there (`app/`
is the App Router's), `dev` uses the bundled loop, and `fonts` and
`compatibilityMode: false` are refused.

members.name: classComponents
members.doc:
How the client bundle gets the React class-component runtime (`class X extends
React.Component`: lifecycle, setState batching, class error boundaries). It is a
code-split chunk (`denext/class-runtime`), so the default needs no configuration.
Unset, `denext build` scans your sources and installs it eagerly when a class is found,
otherwise a page loads it on demand; `true` always installs it eagerly; `false` never
ships it — the runtime is dead-code-eliminated and a class used anyway throws a guided
error.

- **unset** (default): loaded **on demand**. `denext build` scans your app's own sources
  (and sibling workspace packages) for `Component`/`PureComponent` and, when it finds
  one, installs the runtime eagerly; otherwise the generated entry fetches the chunk
  only for a page whose server render produced a class component — so a class that
  lives in an npm dependency you never name still works in production, and a
  function-only page never downloads it.
- **`true`**: always install it eagerly (skips the scan and the on-demand round trip).
- **`false`**: never ship it. In the next-compat (esbuild) build the flag is a `define`,
  so the entire runtime is dead-code-eliminated — zero bytes — and a class used anyway
  throws a guided error.

members.name: compatibilityMode
members.doc:
Run the app through the **next-compat** SSR/client pipeline, which rewrites
every `react`/`react-dom`/`next/*` import (including those inside npm React
libraries) to denext at bundle time so the whole app runs on one denext React
— the drop-in path for real Next.js App Router projects. `true`/`false` force
it; the default `"auto"` enables it when `node_modules/react` exists or
`package.json` lists `react`/`next`. A pure denext-native app keeps the
zero-overhead source-load path.

(Renamed from `nextCompat`; the old key is no longer accepted.)

members.name: plugins
members.doc:
denext plugins (e.g. a Pages Router). Each is set up once before routes are
scanned and may contribute routes, claim requests, and emit build assets — see
{@linkcode DenextPlugin}. Apps with no plugins pay nothing.

members.name: commands
members.doc:
Project-local CLI verbs: `denext <name>` runs the entry's `run`, with the same
flag parsing, `--help` rendering, and "did you mean" suggestions a built-in verb
gets. The shorthand for a one-off project script — a plugin (`addCommand`) is
only needed when the verb ships as a reusable package.

They are listed under "Project commands" by `denext commands` and included in
`denext completions <shell>` (`denext --help` deliberately imports nothing and
points at `denext commands`). A **built-in verb always wins a name collision**:
an entry named `dev` or `build` is ignored, never shadowing the core verb.
Loading them costs one config read, paid only when the CLI must enumerate every
verb (`commands`, `completions`) or hits a verb it doesn't recognize — never for
a script (`denext main.ts`) or a Deno verb, which run without importing the config.

An entry may not take the name of a Deno verb that runs or installs code (`run`,
`x`, `eval`, `serve`, `compile`, `install`, `uninstall`, `upgrade`, `task`): the
config is refused. One named after another Deno verb (`bench`, `doc`, …) runs in
its place only once `denext commands` has listed it (the listing in
`.denext/commands.json` must match the current config, `deno.json` and
`deno.lock`); until then `denext <name>` runs Deno's.

symbols.name: DenextPlugin
symbols.doc: A denext plugin. Declared in denext.config.ts as plugins: [myPlugin()]; its setup runs once per process, before the first route scan.
symbols.docFull:
A denext plugin. Declared in `denext.config.ts` as `plugins: [myPlugin()]`; its
{@linkcode setup} runs once per process, before the first route scan.

members.name: name
members.doc: Unique plugin name (used to de-duplicate registration across a process).

members.name: setup
members.doc: Wire the plugin into denext's seams. Runs once, before routes are scanned.

symbols.name: DEPLOY_MANIFEST_FILE
symbols.doc: The manifest's file name, under the build directory (.denext/deploy-manifest.json).
symbols.docFull: The manifest's file name, under the build directory (`.denext/deploy-manifest.json`).

symbols.name: DEPLOY_MANIFEST_VERSION
symbols.doc: The manifest format version DeployManifest.version carries.
symbols.docFull: The manifest format version {@linkcode DeployManifest.version} carries.

symbols.name: DeployAdapter
symbols.doc: A deploy adapter: prepare writes a target's files from the manifest, and the optional deploy pushes them with the target's own CLI. Declare one in denext.config.ts as deploy: { adapter: fly({ app: "my-app" }) }, or contribute one from a plugin with addDeployAdapter.
symbols.docFull:
A deploy adapter: {@linkcode prepare} writes a target's files from the manifest, and the
optional {@linkcode deploy} pushes them with the target's own CLI. Declare one in
`denext.config.ts` as `deploy: { adapter: fly({ app: "my-app" }) }`, or contribute one from a
plugin with `addDeployAdapter`.

members.name: name
members.doc: The adapter's name (its output directory under `.denext/deploy/`).

members.name: prepare
members.doc:
Write the target's files. Throw an `Error` whose message starts with `denext:` to refuse the
app (the static preset does, for routes that need a server).

members.name: deploy
members.doc: Push the prepared output (`denext deploy`). Absent: the target has no CLI denext drives.

symbols.name: DeployAssetGroup
symbols.doc: One directory of files the server serves as they are, with the Cache-Control it sends.
symbols.docFull: One directory of files the server serves as they are, with the `Cache-Control` it sends.

members.name: urlPrefix
members.doc: The URL prefix the files are served under (`/_denext/client/`, `/`).

members.name: dir
members.doc: The directory, project-relative (`.denext/client`, `public`).

members.name: cacheControl
members.doc: The `Cache-Control` the production server sends for these files.

members.name: immutable
members.doc: Whether the files are content-hashed (safe to cache forever).

members.name: files
members.doc: The files, relative to {@linkcode dir}, sorted (precompressed `.gz` siblings left out).

symbols.name: DeployCache
symbols.doc: The data / page (ISR) cache store the config chooses.
symbols.docFull: The data / page (ISR) cache store the config chooses.

members.name: store
members.doc:
`"default"` (`node:sqlite` in `.denext/` where the disk is writable, else memory),
`"sqlite"`, `"memory"`, or `"custom"` (a store object, e.g. Redis or Deno KV).

symbols.name: DeployCompile
symbols.doc: What denext build --compile produced.
symbols.docFull: What `denext build --compile` produced.

members.name: output
members.doc: The executable, project-relative.

members.name: target
members.doc: The `deno compile --target` triple (absent: the build machine's).

members.name: permissions
members.doc: The `--allow-*` baked into it.

symbols.name: DeployContext
symbols.doc: What an adapter's prepare and deploy receive.
symbols.docFull: What an adapter's `prepare` and `deploy` receive.

members.name: manifest
members.doc: The deploy manifest of the build.

members.name: projectDir
members.doc: The project root (absolute).

members.name: outDir
members.doc: The adapter's output directory (absolute): `.denext/deploy/<adapter name>/`.

members.name: dryRun
members.doc: `--dry-run`: say what would be written or run, and write / run nothing.

members.name: writeFile
members.signature: writeFile(path: string, contents: string, options?: DeployWriteOptions): Promise<boolean>
members.doc:
Write a generated file (UTF-8). Resolves to whether it was written: `false` when dry-running
or when a hand-edited project file was left alone.

params.name: options
params.doc: Where it goes (the adapter's directory by default).

members.name: log
members.doc: Print a progress line.

members.name: warn
members.doc: Print a warning (something the target cannot do, a file left alone).

members.name: env
members.doc: Read an environment variable (credentials come from here, never from a file).

members.name: which
members.doc: The first of `names` on `PATH`, as an absolute path, or `null`.

members.name: run
members.signature: run(command: readonly string[], options?: DeployRunOptions): Promise<number>
members.doc:
Run a command with the terminal attached and the process's environment, resolving to its
exit code (a dry run prints it and resolves to `0`).

members.name: exportStatic
members.doc: Run `denext export` on the project and resolve to the export directory (absolute).

symbols.name: DeployEnvVar
symbols.doc: An environment variable the app reads.
symbols.docFull: An environment variable the app reads.

members.name: name
members.doc: The variable.

members.name: required
members.doc:
Whether the app cannot run without it: a secret the detected stack needs (`AUTH_SECRET`,
`DATABASE_URL`, …) or a read the source asserts (`Deno.env.get("X")!`).

members.name: public
members.doc: A `DENEXT_PUBLIC_` / `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable: shipped to the browser.

members.name: sources
members.doc: Where it was found: project-relative files, or `"stack"` for the detected services.

symbols.name: DeployImages
symbols.doc: The built-in image optimizer.
symbols.docFull: The built-in image optimizer.

members.name: optimizer
members.doc: Whether `<Image>` requests go through the server's optimizer (`images.unoptimized` off).

members.name: endpoint
members.doc: The optimizer's endpoint.

members.name: remoteHosts
members.doc: The remote hosts it may fetch (`images.remotePatterns` / `images.domains` hostnames).

symbols.name: DeployRouteKind
symbols.doc: How a route is served, as a host needs to know it: - "static" — rendered once (at build or on the first request) and the same for everyone: denext export writes it, and a CDN may cache it until the next deploy. - "isr" — cached and re-rendered in the background every DeployRoute.revalidate seconds (export const revalidate = N): needs the server. - "dynamic" — rendered per request (dynamic = "force-dynamic", a request API such as cookies(), or a dynamic segment with no generateStaticParams): needs the server. - "route-handler" — a route.ts (or a metadata route such as sitemap.ts): needs the server. - "middleware" — the root middleware.ts / proxy.ts: runs before every matched request.
symbols.docFull:
How a route is served, as a host needs to know it:
- `"static"` — rendered once (at build or on the first request) and the same for everyone:
  `denext export` writes it, and a CDN may cache it until the next deploy.
- `"isr"` — cached and re-rendered in the background every {@linkcode DeployRoute.revalidate}
  seconds (`export const revalidate = N`): needs the server.
- `"dynamic"` — rendered per request (`dynamic = "force-dynamic"`, a request API such as
  `cookies()`, or a dynamic segment with no `generateStaticParams`): needs the server.
- `"route-handler"` — a `route.ts` (or a metadata route such as `sitemap.ts`): needs the server.
- `"middleware"` — the root `middleware.ts` / `proxy.ts`: runs before every matched request.

symbols.doc: Install the family-identity check and hook-signature guard into the reconciler. Idempotent; called once by the dev route entry before its first render. A no-op in production (this module is never imported there).
symbols.docFull:
Install the family-identity check and hook-signature guard into the reconciler.
Idempotent; called once by the dev route entry before its first render. A no-op
in production (this module is never imported there).

The signature guard fires during a refresh render when an edited component's
hook signature changed — a different hook count OR a same-count reorder / kind
change (each cell is tagged with its hook kind and the full sequence is compared)
— reusing its hook cells would be unsafe, so it falls back to a full page reload
(the correct, if blunt, recovery for a hooks-shape edit).

members.doc: The locale served without a URL prefix, e.g. `"en"`.

members.name: localePrefix
members.doc:
How the default locale is represented in URLs:
- `"as-needed"` (default) — the default locale is served **unprefixed** (`/about`),
  every other locale is prefixed (`/fr/about`).
- `"always"` — **every** locale is prefixed, including the default (`/en/about`);
  an unprefixed path redirects to the detected (or default) locale's prefix.

members.name: messages
members.doc:
Optional message catalogs keyed by locale, powering `useTranslations()`. The
active locale's catalog is provided to the render and embedded in the
hydration payload. Server components may also load catalogs directly.

members.name: hreflang
members.doc:
Automatically emit `<link rel="alternate" hreflang>` alternates (one per
locale, plus `x-default`) and a per-locale canonical for every page. On by
default when i18n is configured; set `false` to opt out. A page that sets its
own `alternates.languages` always takes precedence over the generated set.

members.name: domains
members.doc:
Serve a locale per **domain** without a URL prefix (Next's `i18n.domains`):
`example.fr/about` renders French with no `/fr`. Each entry pins a host to a
`defaultLocale` (served unprefixed on that host); a host's other `locales` (if
listed) are still prefixed there. Locales not tied to any domain keep the normal
prefix behavior on the primary host. The host is the request's (`X-Forwarded-Host`
only under `trustForwardedHeaders`), compared against these domains only;
`canonicalOrigin` does not override it (it governs absolute URLs).

The rendered-page store for Incremental Static Regeneration. A thin façade
over the active {@link CacheStore}: the prod server consults it before
rendering and populates it afterward for cacheable routes. Injecting a shared
store via {@linkcode setCacheStore} makes ISR work across replicas
transparently (replicas of one build share its build id).

members.name: constructor

params.name: buildId
params.doc: The build whose pages this cache holds — denext start passes the id denext build wrote. A cached page references that build's hashed client chunks, which the next deploy no longer serves, so each build reads and writes only its own entries (a redeploy starts cold; the previous build's entries age out through the store's eviction). Omitted, entries are keyed by path alone.

store error is logged and treated as a miss, so a cache outage degrades to
live rendering rather than failing the request.

members.name: emitFile
members.doc:
Publish a generated file at the site root: the build-time analogue of a Vite plugin's
`this.emitFile({ type: "asset", fileName, source })` from `generateBundle`. In
`denext export` the file lands in the export directory (next to `public/`'s files, after
them, so an emitted file replaces a same-named public one); in `denext build` it lands in
`<outDir>/emitted/`, which `denext start` serves at the same URL, ahead of `public/`.
Resolves once the file is written. Rejects a path outside the site root and one the build
publishes itself: `index.html`, denext's own output under `_denext/` (`client/`, `pages/`,
`fonts/`, `ota.json`, `platform.txt`, `desktop-preload.js`), the `spa.assetsDir` directory and,
in an export, any file the build already wrote there (a rendered page, a client chunk).
An asset given by `name` instead of `fileName` gets a content-hashed name
({@linkcode EmittedHashedAsset}), which may sit in the `spa.assetsDir` directory. Resolves to
the file name it was published under.

symbols.docFull:
A build-time step that emits the plugin's client bundles/assets into `outDir`, and publishes
generated files at the site root with {@linkcode PluginBuildContext.emitFile}. Runs at
`denext build` and at `denext export` (App Router, SPA and Pages Router alike).

extend `denext <command>` — not only the request/route/build seams. The command
is discovered when the CLI encounters an unknown verb in a project whose config
lists this plugin, and eagerly (under a time budget) when the CLI has to
enumerate every verb — `denext --help`, `denext completions <shell>`. A name that
collides with a built-in verb is ignored (core verbs always win). A name or alias
of one of Deno's code-running verbs (`run`, `x`, `eval`, `serve`, `compile`,
`install`, `uninstall`, `upgrade`, `task`) throws: `denext <name>` always means
Deno's there. Any other Deno verb's name (`bench`, `doc`, …) is dispatched to the
plugin only once `denext commands` has listed it. The stored spec
is a copy stamped with `source: "plugin"`, which groups it under "Project
commands" in the help table.

members.name: addDeployAdapter
members.doc:
Contribute a deploy adapter (see `denext/deploy`): `denext build` runs its `prepare` after
the build, with the deploy manifest, when `denext.config.ts` names no `deploy.adapter` of its
own, and `denext deploy` uses it. The first one a plugin contributes wins.

members.name: addDeployRoutes
members.doc:
Contribute the routes this plugin serves to the deploy manifest
(`.denext/deploy-manifest.json`'s `routes`), so a deploy adapter sees them: a router plugin's
pages (`"static"` when `denext export` writes them, else `"dynamic"`) and its endpoints
(`"route-handler"`). `source` is called when the manifest is collected (after `denext build`,
and by `denext deploy`), and its routes are sorted in with the App Router's.

Optional, so a plugin that calls it as `ctx.addDeployRoutes?.(…)` still runs on a host from
before it existed.

members.name: addDeployAssets
members.doc:
Contribute the files this plugin serves as they are to the deploy manifest
(`.denext/deploy-manifest.json`'s `assets`): a router plugin's client bundle under its own URL
prefix, each group with the `Cache-Control` the plugin sends (`immutable` when the names are
content-hashed). `source` is called when the manifest is collected; a group with no files is
left out.

Optional, so a plugin that calls it as `ctx.addDeployAssets?.(…)` still runs on a host from
before it existed.

members.name: addTeardown
members.doc:
Register a disposer to run when the server drains — the symmetric shutdown
for anything {@linkcode DenextPlugin.setup} opened (a file watcher, a
connection, a timer). Disposers run most-recently-registered first. Per-plugin
state itself needs no special seam: a handler/step/teardown registered inside
`setup` closes over `setup`'s scope, so they already share state.

members.name: servesRoutes
members.doc:
Declare that this plugin serves the app's pages from a route tree of its own (a Pages Router
`pages/` tree, a TanStack Start or React Router route config), so the app needs no `app/`
directory: `denext doctor` passes its "app directory" check naming the plugin, where it
otherwise fails a project without one. A plugin that only adds endpoints beside the app's
pages (an API, docs, auth, storage) does not call it, however many request handlers it adds.

Optional, so a plugin that calls it as `ctx.servesRoutes?.()` still runs on a host from
before it existed.

symbols.name: revalidateTag
symbols.signature: revalidateTag(tag: string, profile?: string | CacheLifeProfile): Promise<void>
symbols.doc: Invalidate every cached data entry and page carrying tag.
symbols.docFull:
Invalidate every cached data entry and page carrying `tag`.

- **`revalidateTag(tag)`** (single arg) hard-purges the entries — the original
  (Next.js-deprecated but still supported) form.
- **`revalidateTag(tag, profile)`** soft-expires them with stale-while-revalidate
  timing from the `cacheLife` `profile` (a name like `"max"`/`"hours"` or an inline
  `{ stale, revalidate, expire }`): entries are served **stale** while refreshed in
  the background, matching Next.js 16. Stores without soft-expire support
  ({@link CacheStore.expireByTag}) fall back to a hard purge.

With the in-memory default the change is applied synchronously; with an **async
store you should `await` the returned promise**. Inside a request it is also
drained via the deferred queue.

params.name: profile
params.doc: Optional cacheLife profile for stale-while-revalidate behavior.

symbols.name: tapChannel
symbols.signature: tapChannel<T>(channel: Channel<T> | string, key: string, handlers: ChannelTapHandlers<T>): () => void
symbols.doc: Observe a channel's publishes on the SERVER: every payload published to key on any instance — through the installed transport, decoded, in seq order per instance — until the returned disposer runs. The seam a plugin uses to bridge channel pushes into another protocol (a GraphQL subscription in @denext/graphql, an SSE stream, a queue) without a second event bus. Survives setChannelTransport (re-binds to the new transport).
symbols.docFull:
Observe a channel's publishes on the SERVER: every payload published to `key` on any
instance — through the installed transport, decoded, in `seq` order per instance — until
the returned disposer runs. The seam a plugin uses to bridge channel pushes into another
protocol (a GraphQL subscription in `@denext/graphql`, an SSE stream, a queue) without a
second event bus. Survives `setChannelTransport` (re-binds to the new transport).

Not authorization: `authorize` gates socket SUBSCRIBERS; a server-side tap sees every
publish to the key. A tap that serves a viewer goes through `tapChannelAuthorized` (from
`denext/server`), which runs the channel's `authorize` for that viewer first.
symbols.returns: A disposer that stops the tap.

symbols.name: tapChannelAuthorized
symbols.signature: tapChannelAuthorized<T>(channel: Channel<T> | string, key: string, options: AuthorizedTapOptions<T>): Promise<() => void>
symbols.doc: Subscribe a viewer to one key of a channel on the server, behind the channel's authorize — the same gate, context and key the Live socket applies to a useChannel subscriber. Call it inside the viewer's request (a resolver, a route handler): authorize(ctx, key) runs there with ctx = { origin, url, cookie, peerId } from that request, and again, lazily, on the first payload after the channel's re-authorization TTL, in a copy of that request's context.

symbols.name: decode
symbols.signature: decode(spec: WidgetSpec, entries: readonly FormEntry[], prefix?: string): unknown
symbols.doc: Parse a posted body back into the config value its widget stands for.
symbols.docFull:
Parse a posted body back into the config value its widget stands for.

Type driven throughout: numbers are parsed (and range-checked), toggles become booleans, chip
and list rows are reassembled by index, map rows by their `~key` field, and a union by the
branch its discriminator names. A field nothing posted stays `undefined`, which the config
writer reads as "leave this key alone".

members.name: bareAt
members.doc:
The field name whose label something above already shows.

Two places need this, and they are the same situation: a config tab that already says
`i18n` above the form, and a union's branch, which renders at its parent's path — so the
picker labels the key and the branch would label it again, pill, help and validation message
and all. Keyed by NAME rather than by depth, so a branch nested anywhere is covered.

Only the field with exactly this name is bared; its children keep their own labels, which is
what tells you where one key ends and the next begins.

Render a component view to a pre-escaped fragment — synchronously, with no hydration markers
